4.10 Further reading

R for Data Science (2nd ed.), https://r4ds.hadley.nz. The chapter “Logical vectors” covers comparisons, &, |, and ! in more depth, and “Data import” covers reading CSV files with readr.
Hands-On Programming with R by Garrett Grolemund, free at https://rstudio-education.github.io/hopr/. Its chapter “R Notation” is a gentle, thorough guide to indexing vectors and data frames.
Advanced R (2nd ed.) by Hadley Wickham, https://adv-r.hadley.nz. The chapter “Subsetting” is the complete reference, for when you are ready for it.




Selecting part of a vector or data frame with square brackets: by
position (vect[3]), by a condition
(vect[vect > 10]), or by name
(vect["Fozzie"]).
A sequence of values that R stores together, made with c(),
such as c(71, 75, 68).
An operator that combines TRUE and FALSE
values: & (AND, both must be true), | (OR,
either can be true), and ! (NOT).
R’s table: rows are observations and columns are variables. A tibble is
the tidyverse’s version of a data frame.
A plain-text table in which each line is a row and commas separate the
values. Read one into R with read.csv() or
read_csv().
In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as
months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic,
such as median income; each Census variable has a code.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
A small area of about 1,200 to 8,000 people (4,000 on average), drawn to
be fairly stable over time. The workhorse unit for neighborhood
analysis.
Finding and fixing the mistakes (bugs) in code: read the error message,
find the line, make a guess, and test it.
One run of R, from start to finish. A new session starts with an empty
Environment and no packages loaded; knitting always starts a fresh one.
An index with a minus sign, such as vect[-3], which drops
that position and returns the rest.
:, which makes a sequence of whole numbers:
6:8 is c(6, 7, 8).
Another name for logical (TRUE or FALSE)
values, after the mathematician George Boole.
An operator that compares two values and returns TRUE or
FALSE: >, <,
>=, <=, == (equal to), and
!= (not equal to).
An input to a function, written inside its parentheses.
Code that takes inputs (arguments), does a job, and returns an output,
such as mean(temps).
A vector of TRUE and FALSE values, such as the
result of vect > 10. Inside square brackets it keeps the
TRUE positions.
R repeating a shorter vector until it matches the length of a longer
one, so vect[c(TRUE, FALSE)] keeps every other element.
A table listing the result of a logical operator for every combination
of TRUE and FALSE inputs.
Combining two tables by matching rows on a shared key column, such as
attaching Census data to boundaries by GEOID with
left_join().
One thing that was measured or recorded, such as a student, a county, or
a flight. In a data frame, each row is an observation.
The kind of value R is storing. The four main atomic types are logical,
integer, numeric, and character; class() tells you which
you have.
R converting values from one data type to another. Mixing types in one
vector coerces them all to the type that can hold everything, usually
character.
A note for people that R ignores. In R, a comment starts with
#.
The integrated development environment (IDE) where you write and run R.
R does the computing; RStudio is the workspace around it.
The RStudio pane (top right) that lists the variables and data currently
in memory.
A family of R packages (including dplyr,
ggplot2, and readr) for reading,
cleaning, reshaping, summarizing, and plotting data, all designed to
work together.
The first line of a data file, when it holds the column names.
The character that separates values in a text file of data, such as a
comma in a CSV file or a tab.
The location of a file on your computer, such as
data/counties.csv. When you knit, paths are read relative
to the folder the .Rmd file is saved in.
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
A set of lines and blocks of code that work together to do a whole job.
R runs a program from top to bottom, so order matters.

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
text:
5.1 Blocks group lines of code
What is the first virtue of a programmer? Ingenuity? Grit? Devotion to R? Larry Wall, who created the Perl programming language, gave a surprising answer: laziness. He meant a particular kind of laziness: refusing to do the same work twice. A lazy programmer writes a piece of code once and reuses it, instead of typing (or copying and pasting) the same steps again and again.
This chapter covers the R tools that let you be productively lazy. Blocks group lines of code together. if statements decide whether a block runs, and loops decide how many times it runs. Functions, which you have been calling since Chapter 2, give a block a name so you can run it again with new inputs.
A block is the code between a pair of curly braces, { }. R reads everything from the opening brace to the matching closing brace and treats it as one unit:
All three lines run together, and R prints 10. On their own, braces don’t change much. Their power comes when you attach them to an if, a loop, or a function, which decide whether, or how many times, the block runs. A block either runs completely or is skipped completely.
Two habits make blocks easy to read:
The most common blocks are if statements, while loops, for loops, and functions. We’ll take them in that order.

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
text:
Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



Indent the lines inside a block by two spaces. RStudio does this for you when you press Enter after a {. The indentation shows at a glance where a block starts and ends.
Check your braces. Every { needs a matching }. A missing closing brace is one of the most common errors in R. When it happens, the Console shows a + prompt, because R is waiting for the rest of the block. Press Esc to start again.

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
section: 5.2 if statements run a block only when a test is TRUE
text:
5.2 if statements run a block only when a test is TRUE
An if statement has two parts: a test in parentheses and a block in braces. R works out the test. If it is TRUE, the block runs. If it is FALSE, R skips the whole block.
if (test) {
  # runs only when test is TRUE
}
Before you run the code below, predict the value of x at the end:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
x starts at 10. Is 10 less than 100? Yes, so the first block runs and x becomes 11. Is 11 less than 5? No, so the second block is skipped. x ends at 11.

5.2.1 Adding else
Add else to give R a second block for when the test is FALSE. Exactly one of the two blocks runs:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
You can chain tests with else if. R checks them from the top and runs the first block whose test is TRUE:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


5.2.2 Writing good tests
The test uses the comparison and logical operators from Chapter 4: <, >, <=, >=, ==, !=, &, and |. Two mistakes come up again and again:

= is not ==. x = 5 assigns 5 to x. To ask “is x equal to 5?”, write x == 5.
The test must be one TRUE or FALSE. if (c(1, 8) > 5) is an error, because the test gives two answers, FALSE TRUE, and R doesn’t know which one to use. To decide something for every element of a vector, use the vectorized ifelse() instead:


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
section: 5.3 while loops repeat a block while a test is TRUE
text:
5.3 while loops repeat a block while a test is TRUE
A while loop looks like an if statement, but instead of running its block once, it goes back to the test after every run. As long as the test is TRUE, the block runs again:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
R checks the test (is 11 less than 100?), runs the block (x becomes 12), checks the test again, and so on. When x reaches 100 the test is FALSE and the loop stops, so x is 100.






WarningWatch out for infinite loops



The block must change something in the test, or the test never becomes FALSE and the loop never ends. If R seems stuck, click the red stop sign at the top of RStudio’s Console, or press Esc.


In practice, R users rarely write while loops. A for loop, or a function that works on a whole vector at once, is almost always simpler.
crumbs: Unit 1: R and Spatial Data Science

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
section: 5.4 for loops run a block once for each item
text:
5.4 for loops run a block once for each item
A for loop doesn’t have a TRUE or FALSE test. Instead, it walks through a vector one item at a time. On each pass, the loop variable takes the next item:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
On the first pass county is "Orange", on the second "Durham", and on the third "Wake". After the last item the loop stops on its own, so a for loop can’t run forever. That makes it safer than a while loop.
Use a for loop when you know what you want to repeat over: a set of files, counties, or years. This loop reads each CSV file in a folder and prints how many rows it has:
files <- list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

for (f in files) {
  d <- read.csv(f)
  print(nrow(d))
}

5.4.1 Saving results from a loop
print() only shows a result. To keep the results, make an empty vector before the loop and fill in one element on each pass. seq_along() gives the positions 1, 2, 3, … of a vector, which makes a good loop variable:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


5.4.2 Do you need a loop?
Many R functions are vectorized: they already work on every element of a vector at once. The loop above does the same job as one line:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Before you write a loop, check for a vectorized way to do the job. x + 1, sqrt(x), round(x), ifelse(), and the dplyr verbs you’ll meet in Unit 2 all work on whole vectors or columns. Reach for a loop when there isn’t one, such as reading many files or downloading data for many years.






TipThink about it



Later in the book, Chapter 13 downloads American Community Survey data with tidycensus. How could a for loop help you download the same table for 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023, and save each year to its own file?

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
section: 5.5 Functions name a block so you can reuse it
text:
5.5 Functions name a block so you can reuse it
A function is a block with a name, inputs, and an output. You have already called many functions, such as mean(), round(), and read.csv(). Now that you know what a block is, you can write your own. Every function has the same parts:
name <- function(argument1, argument2) {
  # the body: a block of code
  result <- ...
  result          # the last value is the output
}

Name. You create a function the same way you create any object, with <-.
Arguments. The inputs, in parentheses after the word function. Inside the body they are placeholders for whatever you pass in.
Body. The block between the braces.
Return value. The value of the last line in the block is what the function returns. You can also write return(result) to make it explicit.

Here is the smallest useful function, addSeven(). Running the first three lines only creates the function; nothing is printed. The function runs when you call it:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Because + is vectorized, addSeven(c(1, 2, 3)) returns 8, 9, 10 without a loop.

5.5.1 A preview: the weighted mean center
In Chapter 17 you’ll use a function, meanCenter(), that finds the weighted mean center of a map layer. You don’t need to follow its spatial steps yet, but you can already pick out its parts. Its name is meanCenter, its arguments are layer and weights, its body turns polygons into centroids and takes the weighted mean of their coordinates, and its last line, mean_center, is the return value:
meanCenter <- function(layer, weights) {
  # convert the polygons into points
  points <- st_centroid(layer)
  # weighted mean of the x and y coordinates
  mc_x <- weighted.mean(st_coordinates(points)[, 1], weights)
  mc_y <- weighted.mean(st_coordinates(points)[, 2], weights)
  # create a point with the same CRS as the input layer
  mean_center <- st_sfc(st_point(c(mc_x, mc_y)))
  mean_center <- st_set_crs(mean_center, st_crs(layer))
  mean_center
}

mc_pop <- meanCenter(nc_counties, nc_counties$popE)


5.5.2 More than one argument, and defaults
Separate several arguments with commas. You can give an argument a default value with =. The function uses the default unless you pass something else:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


5.5.3 Putting blocks inside functions
A function’s body can hold any block, including if statements and loops. A common use is to check the input and stop with a helpful message if it’s wrong. stop() ends the function with an error:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
section: 5.6 A function’s arguments are separate from variables outside it
text:
5.6 A function’s arguments are separate from variables outside it
What do these lines print? Predict, then run them:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
addSeven(1) returns 8, and numbers is still 10. Inside the function, numbers means whatever you passed in, here 1. Each time a function runs, R gives it a fresh, private workspace, called its local environment, and throws that workspace away when the function finishes. The numbers in your own workspace, the global environment, is never touched.
This idea, which variables a piece of code can see, is called scope. It is why functions are safe to reuse: they don’t overwrite your variables unless you save their result with <-. If you want to keep what a function returns, assign it:

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
text:
5.8 Check your understanding

In R, a block of code is marked by: Parentheses ( )Curly braces { }Square brackets [ ]Quotation marks
What is x after this code runs? x <- 10; if (x < 100) { x <- x + 1 }; if (x < 5) { x <- x - 1 } 
A while loop whose block never changes anything in its test will: Run onceNever runRun forever, until you stop itGive an error right away
A for loop stops on its own after the last item in its vector. TRUEFALSE
To test whether x equals 5 inside an if, you write if (x ___ 5). Fill in the blank. 
Which is the simplest way to add 1 to every element of a numeric vector x? A for loopA while loopx + 1An if statement
A function returns the value of the last line in its body, unless you use return() earlier. TRUEFALSE
After numbers <- 10, addSeven <- function(numbers) { numbers + 7 }, and addSeven(1), what is numbers?

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
text:
5.9 Summary

A block is code inside curly braces { } that R runs as one unit. Indent it, and match every { with a }.
An if statement runs its block only when its test is TRUE. else gives a second block for FALSE, and else if chains more tests. The test must be one TRUE or FALSE; use ifelse() for a whole vector.
A while loop repeats its block while its test is TRUE. Something in the block must move the test toward FALSE, or the loop never ends.
A for loop runs its block once for each item in a vector, then stops. Fill a vector made before the loop to keep the results.
Many R functions are vectorized, so check for one before you write a loop.
A function is a named block: name <- function(arguments) { body }. The last line is the return value. Arguments can have default values.
A function’s arguments live in its own local environment, so a function never changes your variables unless you assign its result.
crumbs: Unit 1: R and Spatial Data Science

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
text:
5.10 Exercises

Predict, then run. Without running it, predict what this prints, then check: x <- 1; while (x < 50) { x <- x * 2 }; x.
Grades. Write a function, letterGrade(score), that uses if, else if, and else to return "A" for 90 or more, "B" for 80 to 89, "C" for 70 to 79, and "F" below 70. Why does letterGrade(c(95, 72)) give an error? Rewrite it with nested ifelse() so that it works on a vector.
Loop or not? Write a for loop that converts c(32, 50, 68, 86, 104) from degrees Fahrenheit to Celsius, (f - 32) * 5 / 9, and stores the results. Then do the same thing in one line without a loop.
Running total. Use a for loop to find the running total of births in c(1091, 487, 3188, 508, 1421): the first value, then the first two added up, and so on. Check your answer with cumsum().
Checking inputs. Add an if statement and stop() to toKm() so that it gives a helpful error when distance is negative.
Standard distance again. (Come back to this one after Chapter 17.) Chapter 17’s standardDistance(x, y) function returns the standard distance of a set of points. Add a check that x and y are the same length, and stop with a message if they aren’t.

title: 5  Blocks, Loops, and Functions
text:
5.11 Further reading

R for Data Science (2nd ed.), by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund, free at https://r4ds.hadley.nz. The “Functions” and “Iteration” chapters show more ways to write functions and to avoid loops.
Hands-On Programming with R, by Garrett Grolemund, free at https://rstudio-education.github.io/hopr/. Its chapters on if and else, loops, and environments go further into the ideas in this chapter.
Programming Perl (3rd ed.), by Larry Wall, Tom Christiansen, and Jon Orwant (O’Reilly, 2000), where Wall describes the three virtues of a programmer: laziness, impatience, and hubris.

block.

FALSE. Stop it with Esc or RStudio’s red stop sign.

R is vectorized, so distance / air_time divides row by row.

function(x, factor = 1.609).

title: Unit 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
Chapter 6: Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
This unit introduces the tidyverse, a family of R packages that share one way of working with data. Using a year of flights from New York’s three airports (the nycflights13 data), you learn the dplyr verbs that filter, sort, select, change, and summarize a data frame, chained together with the pipe. The unit ends by turning those tables into graphs with ggplot2.
This chapter introduces the tidyverse and the data science workflow it is built around. You look at a data frame with glimpse(), keep the rows you want with filter(), and chain steps together with the pipe, |>. It also explains missing values (NA) and how they affect filtering.

title: Unit 2: Into the Tidyverse
section: Chapter 7: Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
text:
Chapter 7: Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
dplyr verbs work on either rows or columns. This chapter sorts rows with arrange(), finds unique values with distinct(), keeps the columns you need with select(), and calculates new columns with mutate(). Sorting a new column turns out to be a quick way to spot outliers worth checking.

title: Unit 2: Into the Tidyverse
section: Chapter 8: Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
text:
Chapter 8: Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
summarize() collapses many rows into summary statistics, and group_by() makes it give one answer for each group, such as each month or each airline. The chapter compares two ways of handling missing values, na.rm = TRUE and drop_na(), and shows why the average of averages can mislead and how a weighted average fixes it.

text:
Chapter 9: Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
ggplot2 builds graphs from the grammar of graphics: data, aesthetics that map columns to visual properties, and geoms that draw the marks, added in layers with +. This chapter makes scatterplots, bar charts, and boxplots, explains the difference between setting and mapping an aesthetic, splits plots into small multiples with facets, and finishes plots with colors, labels, themes, and ggsave().

title: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
text:
6.1 What is the tidyverse?
In Chapter 4 you selected rows of a data frame with square brackets, as in grades[grades$exam2 > 90, ]. That works, but it gets long and hard to read quickly: the data frame’s name appears again for every condition, and every step needs a new variable. This chapter introduces the tidyverse, a set of packages designed to make that kind of work shorter and easier to read, and three tools from it that you will use in almost every assignment from here on: glimpse() to see what is in a data frame, filter() to keep the rows you need, and the pipe, |>, to chain steps together.
The examples use real data: every flight that left New York City’s three airports in 2013, from the nycflights13 package. By the end of the chapter you will be able to answer questions such as “how many flights left LaGuardia in June?” in four short lines.
crumbs: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe

title: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
text:
6.1.1 The data science workflow
The tidyverse is a family of R packages built for data science. Its packages share a design philosophy, a grammar, and a way of storing data, so they fit together. They are organized around the workflow in Figure 6.1, from the book R for Data Science (Wickham et al. 2023):







flowchart LR
  A["Import"] --> B["Tidy"]
  B --> C
  subgraph C["Understand"]
    direction LR
    T["Transform"] --> V["Visualize"]
    V --> M["Model"]
    M --> T
  end
  C --> D["Communicate"]




Figure 6.1: The data science workflow, after Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund (2023). Data are imported and tidied, then transformed, visualized, and modeled, often several times over, before the results are communicated. This chapter is about tidying and transforming.





First you import data into R. Then you tidy it into a consistent shape, with one variable per column and one observation per row. Then you go round a loop of transforming it (keeping the rows you need, making new columns, summarizing), visualizing it, and modeling it, until you understand it. Finally you communicate what you found, usually in an R Markdown report. This chapter lives in the Tidy and Transform boxes: getting data into shape and pulling out the rows you need.


6.1.2 The core packages
One command, install.packages("tidyverse") (or one trip to the Packages tab), installs the core tidyverse packages (Table 6.1).



Table 6.1: The core tidyverse packages.









Package
What it is for




dplyr
Transforming data frames: keeping rows, choosing columns, making new columns, summarizing


ggplot2
Plots and charts


tidyr
Reshaping data into a tidy form


readr
Reading files such as CSVs, with read_csv()


tibble
The tidyverse’s version of the data frame


stringr
Working with text


forcats
Working with categories (factors)


lubridate
Working with dates and times


purrr
Repeating a task over many inputs






This chapter uses dplyr, which supplies glimpse() and filter(). Posit publishes a one-page cheatsheet for dplyr, Data transformation with dplyr, linked on the course Canvas page and at https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/. filter() is on the front page under Manipulate Cases (Extract Cases). It is worth keeping open while you work.


6.1.3 Loading the tidyverse
Load the tidyverse at the top of every R Markdown file, the same way as any other package:
library(tidyverse)
The first time you do, R prints a block of messages like this (your version numbers may differ):
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.1.4     ✔ readr     2.1.5
✔ forcats   1.0.0     ✔ stringr   1.5.1
✔ ggplot2   3.5.1     ✔ tibble    3.2.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.3     ✔ tidyr     1.3.1
✔ purrr     1.0.2
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
These messages are normal. They are not errors, even though some are printed in red. The first block lists the packages that were loaded. The second, Conflicts, says that two packages contain a function with the same name, and which one R will use. Here, dplyr’s filter() masks the filter() in base R’s stats package (a function for time series). From now on, when you type filter(), you get dplyr’s version, which is the one you want. If you ever need the other one, you can name its package explicitly with two colons: stats::filter().


6.1.4 Tidying data is a set of verbs
What do we actually do when we tidy data? We select, extract, arrange, sort, combine, group, join, and summarize. dplyr gives each of these jobs its own function, named with a verb (Table 6.2).



Table 6.2: The main dplyr verbs.










dplyr verb
What it does
Covered




filter()
Keeps the rows that meet a condition
This chapter


select()
Picks columns
Next chapter


arrange()
Sorts rows
Next chapter


mutate()
Makes new columns, or changes existing ones
Next chapter


group_by() and summarize()
Collapse groups of rows into summary values
Later


left_join() and friends
Combine two tables
Later in the course






Every dplyr verb works the same way: its first argument is a data frame, the arguments after it say what to do, and it returns a new data frame. That consistency is what makes the pipe, later in this chapter, work so well.

title: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
section: 6.2 Seeing inside a data frame with glimpse()
text:
6.2 Seeing inside a data frame with glimpse()

6.2.1 The flights data
The nycflights13 package contains a data frame called flights: one row for every flight that departed from New York City’s three airports (Newark, EWR; John F. Kennedy, JFK; and LaGuardia, LGA) in 2013. You might use it to compare flights by day, by airport, or by how late they left. Install it once from the Packages tab, then load it along with the tidyverse:
library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights13)
The live code boxes in this chapter load dplyr, the part of the tidyverse this chapter uses, rather than the whole tidyverse, because it loads faster in a web browser. Everything works the same way in RStudio with library(tidyverse). The first time you run a box, it takes a little while to download the flights data.


6.2.2 glimpse()
flights has more than 300,000 rows, far too many to print. Typing flights shows only the first few rows and as many columns as fit across the screen. glimpse() is the tidyverse’s way to see everything that is in a data frame at once. It turns the data on its side: each column becomes one line of output, showing the column’s name, its type, and its first few values. Run it:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The first two lines give the size: 336,776 rows and 19 columns. Below them is one line per column. The type of each column is in angle brackets, abbreviated (Table 6.3).



Table 6.3: Column types as glimpse() shows them.










In glimpse()
Type
Example columns in flights




<int>
integer (whole numbers)
year, month, day, dep_time


<dbl>
numeric (“double”), may have decimals
dep_delay, arr_delay, distance


<chr>
character (text)
carrier, origin, dest, tailnum


<dttm>
a date and time
time_hour






The columns this chapter uses are month and day (numbers, so June is 6, not "June"), origin (the three-letter code of the airport the flight left from), and dep_delay, the departure delay in minutes. A negative dep_delay means the flight left early.
glimpse() is one of several ways to look at a data frame. head(flights) prints the first six rows; str(flights), from Chapter 4, is base R’s version of glimpse(); and in RStudio, View(flights) opens the whole table in a spreadsheet-like tab. Get in the habit of looking at every data frame before you work with it. Most surprises (a number stored as text, a column you didn’t expect, far fewer rows than you thought) show up in a glimpse.

title: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
text:
6.3 Keeping rows with filter()

6.3.1 One condition
filter() keeps the rows of a data frame that meet a condition. Its first argument is the data frame, and the arguments after that are one or more logical conditions:
filter(data, condition)
It returns only the rows where the condition is TRUE. Here are the flights that left on the first day of a month:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
flights is the data frame, and day == 1 is the logical condition. Notice that, inside filter(), you refer to the columns by name alone, day rather than flights$day: filter() knows to look for them in the data frame. The result has 11,036 rows, the flights on the 1st of each of the twelve months.
The condition uses ==, which tests whether two things are equal. A single = sets an argument, and writing filter(flights, day = 1) is one of the most common mistakes in R. dplyr catches it and tells you, with an error that says you have used = instead of == and asks “Did you mean day == 1?”
filter() doesn’t change flights; it returns a new data frame. To keep the result, store it with <-, and give it a new name, so that you still have the original:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


6.3.2 Several conditions
Give filter() more than one condition, separated by commas, and it keeps the rows where all of them are TRUE. A comma inside filter() means AND, exactly like &. These two lines both find the flights on January 1:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Both return 842 rows. For OR, use |. This finds the flights in June or July:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Conditions on text work the same way, but the text needs quotation marks, as always: origin == "LGA", not origin == LGA. Without the quotes, R looks for a column or variable named LGA and doesn’t find one.

title: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
text:
6.4 The pipe

6.4.1 Chaining steps with |>
Most questions take several steps. Suppose you want to know how many flights left LaGuardia early, or on time, on January 1, 2013. That takes three filters and a count. You could save a new data frame after every step, or nest the functions inside one another, but both get hard to read.
You met the pipe, |>, in an earlier chapter. It takes the output of one function and feeds it in as the first argument of the next. Because every dplyr verb takes a data frame as its first argument and returns one, verbs can be chained with pipes as long as you like:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Read the pipe out loud as “and then”: take flights, and then keep January 1, and then keep LaGuardia, and then keep the flights that left on time or early (a delay of zero or less), and then count the rows. The answer is 172 flights. Each step narrows the rows further, and the code reads in the same order as the question.


6.4.2 Don’t repeat the data frame
With the pipe, the data frame goes in front of the pipe, not inside filter(). These two lines do exactly the same thing:
filter(flights, day == 1)
flights |> filter(day == 1)
In the second, |> passes flights into filter() as its first argument. So inside a pipe chain you never write filter(flights, ...). If you do, flights is passed in twice, once by the pipe and once by you, and R reports an error.






TipThis is not a pipe



René Magritte’s 1929 painting The Treachery of Images shows a pipe above the words Ceci n’est pas une pipe, “This is not a pipe.” It isn’t: it’s a picture of one. In the same spirit, |> isn’t really a pipe either. It’s an operator, a piece of R grammar that rewrites x |> f(y) as f(x, y) before the code runs. The plumbing metaphor is just a good way to picture it: data flow in at one end and out at the other.
You may also see %>% in older code and online answers. It is the original pipe, from the magrittr package (named after Magritte), and does almost the same job. The native pipe |> was added to R itself in version 4.1, and it is the one this course requires.

title: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
section: 6.5 Missing values: why the counts don’t match
text:
6.5 Missing values: why the counts don’t match

6.5.1 The same question, two ways
Here is the January 1 LaGuardia question again, answered first with base R brackets, as in Chapter 4, and then the tidy way with filter() and the pipe:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The base R way needs more typing, and more places for a typo: flights$ for every condition, and a new object at every step. The tidy way reads top to bottom. But look at the answers. Base R finds 174 flights, and filter() finds 172. They don’t match. Why?


6.5.2 NA: a missing value
The answer is missing values. In R, a value that is unknown or missing is written NA (“not available”). Flights that were cancelled never departed, so their departure delay is unknown: dep_delay is NA. Two of the January 1 LaGuardia flights were cancelled.
What is NA <= 0? R can’t say whether an unknown number is less than zero, so the answer is itself unknown: NA, not TRUE or FALSE. Each approach handles that differently (Table 6.4):

Base R brackets don’t drop a row when the condition is NA. They return a row in which every value is NA, so the result has two extra rows of missing values, 174 in all.
filter() keeps only the rows where the condition is TRUE. It quietly drops rows where the condition is NA, so it finds 172.




Table 6.4: How base R brackets and filter() treat each result of a condition.












Condition is TRUE
Condition is FALSE
Condition is NA




Base R df[condition, ]
Row kept
Row dropped
A row of NAs is returned


filter(df, condition)
Row kept
Row dropped
Row dropped






You can see the two extra rows by looking at the last rows of the base R result:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


6.5.3 Deciding what happens to NAs
Neither approach is wrong, but they give different answers, and nothing warns you. That is annoying, and it is exactly the kind of quiet difference that leads to wrong results in a report. The lesson is to check the number of rows after every filter, and to decide on purpose what should happen to missing values.
If you do want to keep the rows with a missing delay, say so in the condition, with the function is.na(), which returns TRUE when a value is NA:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Read the second filter as “keep the flight if its delay is missing or it left on time or early.” Now filter() also returns 174. To count the missing values themselves, filter for them: filter(flights, is.na(dep_delay)) returns all 8,255 flights in 2013 with no departure delay recorded.
Note that you can’t test for NA with ==. dep_delay == NA is always NA, whatever dep_delay is, because R can’t tell whether something equals an unknown value. Always use is.na().

title: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
text:
6.6 Practice: counting flights
Put it all together. These steps follow the in-class exercise.
Step 1: set up. In RStudio, use the Packages tab to install nycflights13 and tidyverse, if you haven’t yet. Start a new R Markdown file, and load both in the first chunk:
library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights13)
You will see the tidyverse’s startup messages. Remember that they are not errors.
Step 2: count all the flights. The dplyr function count() counts the rows of a data frame, so pipe flights into it:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
There were 336,776 flights from New York City’s airports in 2013.
Step 3: flights in June. Add a filter() before count() that keeps month 6. Remember that month is stored as a number, so write 6, not "June". Try it before you look at the answer:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Show the answer to step 3

flights |>
  filter(month == 6) |>
  count()
There were 28,243 flights in June.

Step 4: June flights from LaGuardia. Now keep only the June flights that left from LaGuardia. LaGuardia’s airport code is "LGA", and it is text, so it needs quotation marks. You can add a second filter(), or put both conditions in one, joined with a comma or &:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Show the answer to step 4

All three of these return the same count, 8,596 flights. Pick the one you find easiest to read.
# Two filters, one after the other
flights |>
  filter(month == 6) |>
  filter(origin == "LGA") |>
  count()

# One filter, with a comma (AND)
flights |>
  filter(month == 6, origin == "LGA") |>
  count()

# One filter, with & (AND)
flights |>
  filter(month == 6 & origin == "LGA") |>
  count()
Read the first version as “take flights, and then keep June, and then keep LGA, and then count.” If you got a much bigger number, check for missing quotation marks around "LGA", or a single = where you need ==.

title: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
text:
6.8 Summary

The tidyverse is a family of packages for data science that work together, organized around the workflow import, tidy, transform, visualize, model, and communicate. Load it with library(tidyverse); the startup and conflict messages are normal.
dplyr gives each data-tidying job a verb. Every verb takes a data frame first and returns a data frame.
glimpse() shows a data frame’s size and every column’s name, type (<int>, <dbl>, <chr>, <dttm>), and first values. Look at every data frame before you work with it.
filter() keeps the rows where a condition is TRUE. Use == to test equality, quotation marks around text, and commas or & for AND, | for OR.
The pipe |> passes the result on its left into the first argument of the function on its right. Read it as “and then.” Inside a pipe chain, don’t repeat the data frame.
NA marks a missing value. Base R brackets return a row of NAs when a condition is NA; filter() drops it. Check row counts, and use is.na() when you want to keep or find missing values.

title: 6  Into the Tidyverse: glimpse, filter, and the Pipe
text:
6.9 Exercises
Use the flights data from nycflights13 for these exercises, and answer each with a pipe chain.

Glimpse. Run glimpse(flights). Which columns hold times? Which hold distances? What does a negative value in arr_delay mean?
One airport. How many flights left Newark ("EWR") in 2013? How many left JFK? Which of the three airports was busiest?
Christmas Day. How many flights left New York City on December 25, 2013? How many of them left more than an hour late?
Raleigh–Durham. The dest column holds each flight’s destination airport. How many flights flew to Raleigh–Durham ("RDU") in 2013? How many of them have a missing dep_delay? What do you think happened to those flights?
AND or OR? Predict which of these returns more rows, then check. Explain the difference in words.
flights |> filter(month == 6 & month == 7) |> count()
flights |> filter(month == 6 | month == 7) |> count()
Long delays. How many flights left more than two hours late? Write the same filter in base R with square brackets, as in Chapter 4. Do the two methods agree? Why or why not?
Fix the code. Each chain below has one mistake. Find and fix it.
flights |> filter(origin = "LGA") |> count()
flights |> filter(flights, month == 6) |> count()
flights |> filter(origin == LGA) |> count()
flights |> filter(dep_delay == NA) |> count()

title: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
text:
7.1 Verbs for rows and verbs for columns
In the last chapter you met the tidyverse, looked inside the flights data with glimpse(), and kept the rows you needed with filter(). This chapter adds four more dplyr verbs. Two of them work on rows: distinct() finds the unique values in a column, and arrange() sorts the rows. The other two work on columns: select() keeps the columns you name, and mutate() makes new ones. With filter(), these five verbs cover most of the day-to-day work of getting data into shape.
The examples keep using the nycflights13 data, so you can build each answer one step at a time. By the end of the chapter you will be able to answer questions such as “where can I fly from JFK in under three hours?” and “what was the fastest flight out of New York in 2013?”
crumbs: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate

title: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
text:
7.1.1 Two kinds of verb
Every dplyr verb takes a data frame as its first argument and returns a new data frame, which is why they chain together so well with the pipe. But they change different things. Some verbs change which rows you have, or the order they are in. Others change which columns you have (Table 7.1).



Table 7.1: The five dplyr verbs in this chapter and the last, grouped by what they work on. Every example is code you will run in this chapter.











Works on
Verb
What it does
Example




Rows
filter()
Keeps the rows that meet a condition
filter(origin == "JFK")


Rows
distinct()
Keeps one row for each unique value
distinct(dest)


Rows
arrange()
Sorts the rows
arrange(dest, origin)


Columns
select()
Keeps the columns you name
select(origin, dest)


Columns
mutate()
Adds new columns
mutate(avg_speed = distance / air_time * 60)






Keeping the two groups in mind helps you plan a pipe chain. If the question is about which flights, you need a row verb. If it is about which information about each flight, you need a column verb.


7.1.2 Where this fits
These verbs all belong to the Transform step of the data science workflow you met in the last chapter. None of them changes what a row means: before and after, each row of flights is one flight. They only change which flights you keep, the order they are in, and which facts about each flight you can see. That relies on the data being tidy: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value has its own cell.
crumbs: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate

title: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
text:
7.2 Finding unique values with distinct()

7.2.1 One column
flights has 336,776 rows, but most of the values in a column like origin repeat thousands of times. distinct() keeps one row for each unique value. Give it the data frame and the column to check:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Read it as “take flights, and then keep one row for each different origin.” The answer is three rows: the three New York City airports, Newark (EWR), LaGuardia (LGA), and John F. Kennedy (JFK). Notice that the result has only the column you named. distinct() answers the question “which values are there?”, so it drops the other columns.


7.2.2 Building up a question
distinct() is most useful at the end of a pipe chain, after filter() has kept the rows you care about. Here is one question, asked four ways, each a little narrower than the last.
Where can I fly from New York? Every row of flights is one departure, so the same destination appears thousands of times. distinct(dest) keeps each destination once:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The result has 105 rows: 105 destination airports. They are all domestic. Most are in the 50 states, and a few are in US territories, such as San Juan (SJU) in Puerto Rico and St. Thomas (STT) in the US Virgin Islands.
Where can I fly from JFK? Put a filter() in front, so that distinct() only sees the JFK flights:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
JFK serves 70 of the 105 destinations.
Where can I fly from JFK in 3 hours or less? air_time is the time in the air, in minutes, so 3 hours is 180 minutes. Add a second filter:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
That leaves 50 destinations. <= means “less than or equal to,” so this keeps flights of exactly 180 minutes too. For “less than 3 hours,” strictly, use <. In this case both give the same 50 destinations, but they won’t always, so write the one that matches your question.
And sorted by airport code? The result above is in the order the destinations first appear in the data, which is hard to scan. The next section shows how to sort it.


7.2.3 Several columns
Give distinct() more than one column and it keeps each unique combination of their values. Which airports are linked by a direct flight from New York?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
There are 224 origin and destination pairs. That is more than 105, because many destinations are served from more than one New York airport: Atlanta, for example, appears three times, once with each origin.
To count unique values, pipe the result into nrow(), as in flights |> distinct(dest) |> nrow(), which returns 105. If you want to keep the other columns, distinct() has an argument for that, .keep_all = TRUE, which keeps the first row it finds for each unique value.
crumbs: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate

title: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
text:
7.3 Sorting rows with arrange()

7.3.1 Sorting by one column
arrange() sorts the rows of a data frame by the column you name. Add it to the end of the JFK question to list the destinations alphabetically:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The same 50 rows now start with ACK (Nantucket), ATL (Atlanta), and AUS (Austin). arrange() changes the order of the rows, never how many there are. It sorts in ascending order by default: A to Z for text, smallest to largest for numbers.


7.3.2 Sorting every row
arrange() works on any data frame, not only on the result of distinct(). Take out distinct(), and arrange() sorts every one of the 64,248 short JFK flights by destination:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
All 19 columns are still there, and the rows with the same dest now sit together, starting with the flights to Nantucket. Comparing this result with the last one shows that it was distinct(), not arrange(), that collapsed 64,248 flights into 50 destinations.


7.3.3 Largest first
To sort in descending order, largest first or Z to A, wrap the column in desc(). Which flights left latest?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The longest departure delay in 2013 was 1,301 minutes, nearly 22 hours, on a flight from JFK to Honolulu on January 9. (The select() at the end keeps a few columns so the result fits on the screen. It is the subject of the next section.)
For a numeric column, a minus sign does the same job: arrange(-dep_delay) sorts from largest to smallest. The minus sign only works on numbers, though, while desc() also works on text, so desc() is the safer habit.
Missing values always go to the end, whichever direction you sort. The flights with no dep_delay (the cancelled flights) are at the bottom of both arrange(dep_delay) and arrange(desc(dep_delay)).


7.3.4 Sorting by two columns
What does this code do? Read it one step at a time, and predict the order of the Atlanta (ATL) rows before you run it.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
distinct(origin, dest) keeps the 224 unique pairs. arrange(dest, origin) sorts them by destination first. When two rows have the same destination, which is called a tie, it uses the second column, origin, to decide their order. All three New York airports fly to Atlanta, so ATL appears three times, and those three rows are sorted by origin: EWR, JFK, LGA. You can name as many columns as you like; each one breaks the ties left by the one before.

title: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
text:
7.4 Keeping columns with select()

7.4.1 Naming the columns you want
flights has 19 columns, too many to see at once. select() keeps the columns you name, in the order you name them, and every row:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The result has all 336,776 rows but only 4 columns. Storing it with <- under a new name, flights_dates, leaves the original flights unchanged.
select() and filter() are easy to mix up, because in everyday English you “select” the rows you want. Remember that filter() picks rows and select() picks columns.


7.4.2 Dropping and finding columns
Typing out every column you want gets tedious with wide data. select() has shortcuts (Table 7.2).



Table 7.2: Shortcuts for choosing columns with select().









Code
What it keeps




select(-tailnum)
Every column except tailnum


select(year:day)
Every column from year to day, in the order they sit in the data frame


select(starts_with("dep"))
Columns whose names start with dep: dep_time and dep_delay


select(ends_with("delay"))
Columns whose names end with delay: dep_delay and arr_delay


select(contains("time"))
Columns whose names contain time anywhere






starts_with(), ends_with(), and contains() are selection helpers: functions that only work inside select() (and a few other tidyverse functions), and that pick columns by their names. You can combine any of these, separated by commas:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
crumbs: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate

title: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
text:
7.5 Making new columns with mutate()

7.5.1 Average speed
mutate() adds new columns to a data frame, calculated from the columns it already has. Its arguments take the form new_name = calculation. How fast was each flight? distance is in miles and air_time is in minutes, so distance divided by air time is miles per minute, and multiplying by 60 gives miles per hour:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
mutate() did the calculation for every one of the 336,776 flights at once. That is because arithmetic in R is vectorized: dividing one column by another divides each value by the value in the same row, without a loop. The new column goes at the end of the data frame. Here, select() keeps it and the columns it was made from, so you can check the arithmetic: the first flight flew 1,400 miles in 227 minutes, or about 370 miles per hour.
The 9,430 flights with no air_time (most of them cancelled) get an avg_speed of NA, because any arithmetic with a missing value gives a missing value.


7.5.2 Several columns at once
Separate several new columns with commas. A later column can use one made earlier in the same mutate():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This gives the same speeds as before, in two steps. If you give a new column the name of one that already exists, mutate() replaces the old column with the new values, so pick new names unless you mean to overwrite.


7.5.3 Slowest and fastest
Put mutate(), arrange(), and select() together to find the slowest flights:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The slowest flight, from LaGuardia to Philadelphia, averaged about 77 miles per hour. Philadelphia is less than 100 miles from New York, so a flight there spends most of its time taking off, circling, and landing.
Change arrange(avg_speed) to arrange(desc(avg_speed)) to find the fastest:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






ImportantThink about it



The fastest flight averaged 703 miles per hour: a Delta flight from LaGuardia to Atlanta on May 25, which flew 762 miles in 65 minutes. A passenger jet usually cruises at about 550 to 580 miles per hour. The typical LaGuardia to Atlanta flight in 2013 took 112 minutes, at about 408 miles per hour.
Do you believe it? A strong tailwind can push a plane’s speed over the ground well above its cruising speed, but a 65-minute flight to Atlanta is still extraordinary. It could also be an error in the recorded air time. Either way, a value that is far from all the others, an outlier, deserves a second look before you report it. Sorting with arrange() is one of the quickest ways to find them.

title: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
text:
7.6 Practice: the longest flight
Put it all together. These steps follow the in-class exercise.
Step 1: set up. Start a new R Markdown file, and load the packages in the first chunk:
library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights13)
Then take a quick look at the data with glimpse(flights).
Step 2: the longest flight. What is the longest domestic flight from New York? Sort by distance, largest first, and keep the columns that answer the question. Try it before you look at the answer:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Show the answer to step 2

flights |>
  arrange(desc(distance)) |>
  select(origin, dest, distance, air_time)
The longest flight is from JFK to Honolulu (HNL), 4,983 miles. Every one of the top rows is that same route, because it was flown every day. Add distinct(origin, dest, distance) after the arrange() to see the longest routes rather than the longest flights: the second is Newark to Honolulu, 4,963 miles.

Step 3: how fast was it? Add a mutate() that calculates avg_speed, and include it in the select().

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Show the answer to step 3

flights |>
  arrange(desc(distance)) |>
  mutate(avg_speed = distance / air_time * 60) |>
  select(origin, dest, distance, air_time, avg_speed)
The first flight in the list took 659 minutes, an average of about 454 miles per hour. But the next took 638 minutes and the one after 616, so the speeds differ. Over the year, JFK to Honolulu flights averaged between about 433 and 516 miles per hour. The distance is the same every day, so the difference is all in air_time. Why might the same route take an hour longer on one day than another? Think about the wind over the Pacific, and the route each flight was cleared to fly.

title: 7  Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate
text:
7.8 Summary

dplyr verbs work either on rows (filter(), distinct(), arrange()) or on columns (select(), mutate()). Each takes a data frame first and returns a data frame, so they chain with the pipe.
distinct() keeps one row for each unique value of the columns you name, or each unique combination if you name several. It keeps only those columns.
arrange() sorts rows, in ascending order by default. Wrap a column in desc() for descending order. With several columns, each one breaks the ties left by the one before. Sorting never adds or removes rows, and missing values go last.
select() keeps the columns you name, in that order. - drops a column, : keeps a range, and starts_with(), ends_with(), and contains() pick columns by name. filter() picks rows; select() picks columns.
mutate() adds new columns calculated from existing ones, with new_name = calculation. The calculation is done for every row at once. Arithmetic with NA gives NA.
Sorting a new column with arrange() is a quick way to find outliers. Check them before you trust them.

Airlines. How many different airlines (carrier) flew out of New York in 2013? Which airlines flew from LaGuardia to Raleigh–Durham ("RDU")?

title: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
text:
8.1 Tidy data and the verbs so far
So far, every verb you have used gives back one row for each flight, or fewer flights, or the same flights in a new order. But many questions are about many flights at once. What was the average departure delay in 2013? Which month had the worst delays? Which plane was late most often? This chapter introduces the verbs that answer them: summarize(), which collapses many rows into a few numbers, and group_by(), which makes summarize() give one answer for each group. Along the way you will meet drop_na(), a third way to deal with the missing values you met two chapters ago.
The examples still use the nycflights13 data, and the chapter ends with a question that looks simple but has a trap in it: how fast did planes fly each month?
crumbs: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na

title: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
text:
8.1.1 Tidy data
dplyr’s verbs expect tidy data, which follows three rules (Wickham et al. 2023):

Each variable is a column.
Each observation is a row.
Each value is a cell.

flights is tidy. Each row is one flight, each column is one thing recorded about it, such as dep_delay or carrier, and each cell holds one value. Because every month is in the same column, and every delay in the same column, a single line of code can work on all of them at once. That is what makes this chapter’s verbs possible.


8.1.2 Three new verbs
Table 8.1 adds this chapter’s verbs to the ones you already know.



Table 8.1: The dplyr verbs so far, and this chapter’s three new ones.










Works on
Verb
What it does




Rows
filter()
Keeps the rows that meet a condition


Rows
arrange()
Sorts the rows


Rows
distinct()
Keeps one row for each unique value


Rows
group_by()
Groups the rows that share a value (new)


Rows
drop_na()
Removes the rows with missing values (new)


Columns
select()
Keeps the columns you name


Columns
mutate()

Columns

drop_na() comes from the tidyr package rather than dplyr, but library(tidyverse) loads both, so you don’t need to do anything extra. The live code boxes in this chapter load dplyr and tidyr separately, because that is faster in a web browser.

title: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
text:
8.2 Summarizing with summarize()

8.2.1 One number from many rows
How late, on average, did flights leave New York in 2013? summarize() collapses a whole data frame into a single row of summary statistics. Inside it, name the new column and say how to calculate it:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The answer is one row and one column: across all 336,776 flights, the average departure delay was about 12.6 minutes. delay is the name we chose for the result; you can call it anything. mean(dep_delay) is the calculation.
na.rm = TRUE (“remove NAs”) tells mean() to skip the missing values. Without it, the answer is NA, because the 8,255 cancelled flights have no departure delay, and any calculation that includes an unknown number gives an unknown answer. Try it: delete , na.rm = TRUE and run the box again.
summarize() is also spelled summarise(). The two are the same function; use whichever spelling you like.


8.2.2 Summary functions
The calculation inside summarize() can be any function that takes a column and returns one number (Table 8.2).



Table 8.2: Functions to use inside summarize(), with their results for departure delays in 2013. All but n() need na.rm = TRUE for dep_delay.










Function
What it returns
dep_delay in 2013




mean()
The average
12.6 minutes


median()
The middle value: half are above, half below
−2 minutes


min(), max()
The smallest and largest values
−43 and 1,301 minutes


quantile(x, 0.25)
The value below which a given share falls; here the 25th percentile
−5 minutes


sd()
The standard deviation: how spread out the values are
40.2 minutes


var()
The variance, the standard deviation squared
1,617


sum()
The total



n()
The number of rows
336,776






n() is different from the others: it takes no arguments, and it counts rows rather than looking at a column. It only works inside dplyr verbs such as summarize().
Look at the first two rows of the table. The mean delay is 12.6 minutes, but the median is −2 minutes: more than half of all flights left early. How can both be true? Delays are skewed. Most flights leave a few minutes early or late, but a few leave hours late, and those few pull the mean up a long way. The median only cares about the middle flight, so it ignores them. When a variable has a long tail like this, report the median as well as the mean, or instead of it.


8.2.3 Several statistics at once
Separate several statistics with commas. Each becomes its own column, still in a single row:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The longest delay was 1,301 minutes, almost 22 hours. The shortest is negative: one flight left 43 minutes before its scheduled time. One maximum for the whole year is a start, but it would be more useful to know the longest delay in each month. That is the job of group_by().

title: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
section: 8.3 One result per group with group_by()
text:
8.3 One result per group with group_by()

8.3.1 Grouping, then summarizing
group_by() sorts the rows into groups that share a value. On its own it changes nothing you can see. But every verb after it then works on each group separately. Put group_by(month) in front of the summarize() from the last section:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The summarize() code is exactly the same, but now there are 12 rows, one per month, instead of one. group_by(month) split the 336,776 flights into 12 groups, and summarize() ran once for each. The grouping column, month, stays in the result so you can tell the rows apart. The longest delay of the year was in January, and the longest in June was 1,137 minutes.
Which month had the worst delays on average? Group by month, take the mean, and sort:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
July (21.7 minutes) and June (20.8) were the worst; October and November, at around 6 minutes, were the best. Summer thunderstorms are a likely suspect. n() counts the flights in each group, here between about 25,000 and 29,000 a month.
You can group by any column, and by more than one: group_by(origin) gives one row per airport, and group_by(origin, month) gives one row for each airport in each month, 36 rows in all.


8.3.2 group_by() on its own
What does group_by() do without summarize()?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Nothing seems to change: there are still 336,776 rows and 19 columns, with the same values. The only difference is a new line at the top, Groups: month [12]. The data frame is now a grouped data frame: it carries a hidden note saying that its rows belong to 12 groups by month.
That note matters, because every verb that comes later works within each group, until you remove it with ungroup(). That is what you want right before summarize(), but it can surprise you later in a chain. For example, mutate(mean_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE)) on a grouped data frame gives each flight the mean delay for its month, not for the year. When you have finished working by group, add ungroup():
flights |>
  group_by(month) |>
  mutate(month_mean = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()
summarize() removes one level of grouping for you, so after group_by(month) |> summarize(...) the result is no longer grouped. After group_by(origin, month), it is still grouped by origin, and dplyr prints a message to say so.
crumbs: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na

title: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
text:
8.4 Removing missing values with drop_na()

8.4.1 Two ways to skip NAs
You have now seen na.rm = TRUE many times. drop_na(), from tidyr, is another way to deal with missing values: it removes every row where a column you name is NA. These two chains give exactly the same 12 rows:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
In the second, drop_na(dep_delay) removes the 8,255 flights with no departure delay before summarize() sees them, so max() and min() never meet an NA and don’t need na.rm.


8.4.2 They are not the same thing
Here the results match, but the two approaches do different things (Table 8.3).



Table 8.3: How na.rm = TRUE and drop_na() differ.











na.rm = TRUE
drop_na()




Where it goes
Inside one summary function
As its own step in the pipe chain


What it changes
Only that one calculation
The data: whole rows are removed for every later step


Columns affected
The one being summarized
All columns, because whole rows go






The difference shows up when you count. n() counts rows, whether or not they have missing values. With na.rm = TRUE, n() still counts the cancelled flights; after drop_na(dep_delay), it doesn’t. Neither is wrong, but they answer different questions (“how many flights were scheduled?” against “how many flights have a delay recorded?”), so choose on purpose.


8.4.3 Name your columns
drop_na() with no columns named removes every row that has an NA in any column. That can remove more than you meant to:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
drop_na(dep_delay) keeps 328,521 flights. drop_na() keeps only 327,346, because it also removes flights that departed but have no arrival delay or air time recorded. Always name the columns your question needs.

title: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
section: 8.5 Practice: how fast did planes fly each month?
text:
8.5 Practice: how fast did planes fly each month?

8.5.1 The obvious way
Here is a question that combines everything so far: what was the average air speed of flights from New York in each month? A first attempt might calculate the speed of every flight with mutate(), then take the mean for each month:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
That runs without errors and gives one speed per month: about 370 miles per hour in January. But is it the right answer?


8.5.2 The average of averages
The problem isn’t the code; it is the statistics. mean(speed) gives every flight an equal say. A half-hour hop to Philadelphia counts as much as a 6-hour flight to San Francisco. Short flights spend most of their time climbing and descending, so they are slow, and there are a lot of them, so they drag the average down.
What does “the average speed in January” really ask for? A good definition is the total distance flown in January, divided by the total time spent in the air:
\[
\text{speed}_{\text{month}} = \frac{\sum \text{distance}_{\text{month}}}{\sum \text{air\_time}_{\text{month}}} \times 60
\]
This is a weighted average of the flights’ speeds. Each flight counts in proportion to its air time, so a 6-hour flight counts twelve times as much as a 30-minute one.


8.5.3 Sum first, then divide
To calculate it, add up the distances and air times in each month with summarize(), and then divide the totals with mutate():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The order matters: summarize() runs first to get one total per month, and mutate() then works on those 12 rows. In January the speed is 394 miles per hour, against 370 from averaging the flights’ speeds, and the weighted speed is higher in every month. Long flights, which spend most of their time at cruising speed, now count in proportion to the time they spend in the air.
Here drop_na(distance, air_time) does more than clean up. Every cancelled flight still has a distance, because the route is known, but no air_time. If you used sum(air_time, na.rm = TRUE) without dropping those rows, the total distance would include miles that were never flown, and January’s speed would come out at about 401 miles per hour, too fast. Dropping the rows keeps the distances and the times about the same flights.

title: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
text:
8.8 Summary

dplyr’s verbs work on tidy data: each variable a column, each observation a row, each value a cell.
summarize() collapses a data frame into one row of summary statistics, with name = function(column). Separate several statistics with commas.
Useful summary functions include mean(), median(), min(), max(), quantile(), sd(), var(), sum(), and n(). Skewed data, like flight delays, can have a mean far from the median.
group_by() splits the rows into groups. On its own it changes nothing you can see, but summarize() after it gives one row per group. Use ungroup() when you have finished working by group.
na.rm = TRUE skips missing values in one calculation. drop_na() removes whole rows with missing values from the data. Always name the columns in drop_na().
The average of averages gives every row an equal say. To find a rate such as speed for a group, sum first, then divide: that is a weighted average.
crumbs: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na

title: 8  Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na
text:
8.9 Exercises
Use the flights data from nycflights13 for these exercises, and answer each with a pipe chain.

Busiest airport. Use group_by() and summarize() with n() to count the flights from each of the three New York airports. Then try flights |> count(origin). What does count() do?
Most popular destinations. Which three destinations had the most flights from New York in 2013?
Delays by airport. For each origin, calculate the mean and median departure delay. Which airport had the worst delays? Do the mean and the median agree?
Arrivals. Calculate the mean arrival delay (arr_delay) for each airline (carrier), and sort from worst to best. How many flights does each airline have? Would you trust the average for an airline with very few flights?
Two groups. Group by origin and month and count the flights. Which airport was busiest in which month? Is the result still grouped?
Counting NAs. Without using drop_na(), count how many flights in each month have a missing dep_delay. (Hint: sum(is.na(dep_delay)).) Which month had the most cancelled flights?
Fix the code. Each chain below has one mistake. Find and fix it.
flights |> summarize(mean(dep_delay))          # result is NA
flights |> group_by(month) summarize(n = n())
flights |> summarize(n = n(month))
flights |> group_by(month) |> summarize(delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE) |> arrange(delay)

text:
8.10 Further reading

R for Data Science (2nd ed.) (Wickham et al. 2023), free at https://r4ds.hadley.nz. The “Data transformation” chapter covers group_by() and summarize() with the flights data, and the “Data tidying” chapter explains tidy data.
The tidyr website, https://tidyr.tidyverse.org, has the reference page for drop_na().
Posit’s Data transformation with dplyr cheatsheet, https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/, shows summarize(), group_by(), and the summary functions under Summarize Cases and Group Cases.




R’s table: rows are observations and columns are variables. A tibble is
the tidyverse’s version of a data frame.
One number that describes many values, such as their mean, median,
maximum, or count. summarize() calculates them.
Code that takes inputs (arguments), does a job, and returns an output,
such as mean(temps).
A value that is unknown, written NA (“not available”) in R.
Most calculations with NA give NA; test for it
with is.na().
An average in which some values count more than others. Total distance
divided by total air time weights each flight’s speed by its air time.
A dplyr function named for the job it does to a data frame, such as
filter(), select(), arrange(),
and mutate().
An R package of data on every flight that left New York City’s three
airports in 2013, including the flights data frame.
The operator |>, which passes the result on its left as
the first argument of the function on its right. Read it as “and then.”
The tidyverse package for transforming data frames: filtering rows,
choosing columns, adding new columns, joining tables, and summarizing.
Data arranged so that each variable is a column, each observation is a
row, and each value has its own cell.
In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as
months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic,
such as median income; each Census variable has a code.
One thing that was measured or recorded, such as a student, a county, or
a flight. In a data frame, each row is an observation.
A value counted once, however many times it repeats.
distinct() keeps one row for each unique value, or each
unique combination of values.
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
The value below which a given share of the values fall: a quarter of
values are below the 25th percentile. quantile() in R.
A measure of how spread out values are around their mean, in the same
units as the values. sd() in R.
A measure of spread: the standard deviation squared, so its units are
squared too. var() in R.
An input to a function, written inside its parentheses.
The average: the sum of the values divided by how many there are. A few
very large or small values can pull it a long way.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
Lopsided: most values are bunched at one end, with a long tail of
unusual values at the other, which pulls the mean away from the median.
A data frame made by group_by(). It looks the same, but
later verbs work on each group separately until you call
ungroup().
Largest to smallest for numbers, Z to A for text. Ask
arrange() for it with desc(), as in
arrange(desc(dep_delay)).
A document format (.Rmd) that mixes formatted text with
chunks of R code. Knitting it runs the code and builds a finished
report.
A vector of TRUE and FALSE values, such as the
result of vect > 10. Inside square brackets it keeps the
TRUE positions.
A one-page summary of a package or tool. Posit publishes them for dplyr,
ggplot2, RStudio, and more.



Wickham, Hadley, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund. 2023. R for Data Science: Import, Tidy, Transform, Visualize, and Model Data. 2nd ed. O’Reilly Media. https://r4ds.hadley.nz.
