title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.1 The grammar of graphics
In the last three chapters you used dplyr to filter, sort, and summarize the nycflights13 data. Tables of numbers answer precise questions, but they are a poor way to see a pattern. Do flights that leave late also arrive late? Which airline flies the longest routes? Is there a weekly rhythm to the number of flights? A graph answers each of these at a glance.
This chapter introduces ggplot2, the tidyverse package for graphs. Everything in it builds on one short template, and the same ideas carry straight over to the maps in the next chapter.
crumbs: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.1.1 ggplot2 expects tidy data
ggplot2 is built for tidy data, the same shape dplyr produces: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value is a cell. Every variable you want on an axis, or as a color, or to split a plot by, must be its own column. flights is already tidy: one row per flight and one column per thing recorded about it. If a variable is spread over several columns (say, one column per year), you would reshape it first with pivot_longer() from tidyr.


9.1.2 What is ggplot2?
ggplot2 is part of the tidyverse, so library(tidyverse) loads it. The package is called ggplot2, but its main function is ggplot(). It was written by Hadley Wickham, based on Leland Wilkinson’s book The Grammar of Graphics, and it has three things going for it:

A readable graph takes very little code, because the defaults are good.
You can still change every part of the graph when you need to.
Graphs are built in layers, joined with +, so you can start simple and add one piece at a time.



9.1.3 Every graph has the same parts
The grammar of graphics is the idea that any chart, from a scatterplot to a map, can be described with the same small set of parts (Table 9.1).



Table 9.1: The parts of the grammar of graphics.










Part
What it is
In ggplot2




Data
The tidy table you plot
ggplot(data = flights)


Aesthetics
Visual properties, such as x position, y position, color, or size, that a column is shown with
aes(x = dep_delay, y = arr_delay)


Geoms
The marks that show the data: points, bars, lines, boxes
geom_point(), geom_bar()


Scales
How data values turn into visual values: which colors, which axis breaks
scale_fill_manual(), scale_x_log10()


Facets
Splitting the data into small plots, one per group
facet_wrap()


Coordinates
Where the marks land on the page
coord_flip(), or a map projection






The key word is aesthetic: a visual property of a mark. aes() is where you connect the columns in your data to those properties. A bar chart and a scatterplot can share the same data and the same coordinates; only the geom changes.


9.1.4 Choosing a geom
ggplot2 has more than 40 geoms. To pick one, first ask what kinds of variables you are plotting (Table 9.2). The answer narrows it down to two or three choices.



Table 9.2: Choosing a geom from the kinds of variables.









You are plotting
Try




One continuous variable
geom_histogram(), geom_density()


One categorical variable
geom_bar()


Two continuous variables
geom_point(), geom_smooth()


A categorical x and a continuous y
geom_boxplot(), geom_col()


Change over time
geom_line()






Posit’s ggplot2 cheatsheet groups all the geoms this way. In RStudio, find it under Help > Cheat Sheets.


9.1.5 The template
Every ggplot follows the same template:
ggplot(data = <DATA>) +
  <GEOM_FUNCTION>(mapping = aes(<MAPPINGS>))
Swap in a data frame, a geom function, and the mappings, and you have a plot. Building one takes five steps, but only the first three are required:

Start with tidy data: ggplot(data = flights).
Map variables to aesthetics: aes(x = dep_delay, y = arr_delay).
Add a geom to draw them: + geom_point().
Adjust the scales and coordinates, for example + scale_x_log10().
Add labels: + labs(title = "...").

Two rules trip people up. First, the + must go at the end of a line, not the start of the next one; otherwise R thinks the command has ended. Second, ggplot2 uses + to add layers, while dplyr uses |> to pass data along. You can pipe data into ggplot(), but after that, every layer is joined with +.
The argument names data = and mapping = are optional, so ggplot(flights) + geom_point(aes(x = dep_delay, y = arr_delay)) works too. Most code you find online leaves them out.
crumbs: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.2 Scatterplots and aesthetics

9.2.1 A first scatterplot
Do flights that leave late arrive late? To keep the plot readable, start with the October flights, and drop the cancelled ones, which have no delay values:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Each point is one October flight. The points form a rising band: flights that leave late arrive late, by about the same amount. Without drop_na(), the plot would look the same, but ggplot2 would warn that it had removed rows with missing values.
What does a point far above the band mean? A flight that arrived much later than its departure delay predicts, perhaps because it was held in the air or waited a long time on the runway.


9.2.2 Adding a trend line
geom_smooth() draws a trend line. Layer it on top of the points with another +:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Two things changed. The mapping moved into ggplot(). Mappings set there apply to every layer, so geom_point() and geom_smooth() both use the same x and y, and you don’t have to repeat them. And the layers draw in order, so the line sits on top of the points.
By default, geom_smooth() fits a smooth curve, with a gray band showing its 95% confidence interval. R prints a message saying which method it used. For a straight regression line, use geom_smooth(method = "lm"), and to hide the band, add se = FALSE.


9.2.3 Setting an aesthetic
To make the points blue and the line red, give each geom a color outside aes():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This is setting an aesthetic: every mark gets the same fixed value, whatever the data say. It is a design choice, not a data choice. Each geom takes its own settings, so here the points are blue, and the line is red and thicker (linewidth = 2).
Note the quotes around "blue" and "red". R knows 657 color names (run colors() to see them all), and it also takes hex codes such as "#2C5080".


9.2.4 Mapping an aesthetic
Now give each origin airport its own color. Move color inside aes(), and give it a column instead of a color:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This is mapping an aesthetic: the color now comes from the data. ggplot2 picks one color for each value of origin, and builds the legend for you. Because color is mapped in ggplot(), geom_smooth() also splits by airport, and draws three trend lines.
Table 9.3 sums up the difference. It is the most important idea in this chapter.



Table 9.3: Setting an aesthetic against mapping one.











Setting
Mapping




Where
In the geom, outside aes()
Inside aes()


Value
A fixed value: color = "blue"
A column: color = origin


Result
Every mark looks the same
Marks differ by the data, with a legend












WarningA common mistake



What happens if you write aes(color = "blue")? Inside aes(), ggplot2 treats "blue" as a data value, as if every row had a column whose value was the word “blue”. It makes a one-item legend called blue, and colors the points with its first default color, which is a salmon pink. Try it in the box above. If your points come out the wrong color with a strange legend, check whether a setting has slipped inside aes().








TipThink about it



Move color = origin out of ggplot(aes()) and into geom_point(aes()) instead. Before you run it, predict: how many trend lines will you get now? Why?




9.2.5 Too many colors
Try mapping color to the airline, carrier. With all 16 airlines, the colors become hard to tell apart, so this code keeps six large ones first:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The data flow into ggplot() through the pipe, and from there on the layers are joined with +. Even with six carriers, the points pile on top of each other. Color works best for about five groups or fewer. Facets, later in this chapter, are a better fix.
crumbs: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.3 Bar charts and boxplots

9.3.1 Counting with geom_bar()
How many October flights did each airline fly? A bar chart compares counts across categories:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
You only map x. geom_bar() counts the rows for each carrier itself, the same as count(carrier) would, and plots the counts as the bar heights. If you already have a table of counts, for example from group_by() and summarize(), use geom_col(aes(x = carrier, y = n)) instead, which draws the heights you give it.
United (UA), ExpressJet (EV), and JetBlue (B6) flew the most, with about 5,000 flights each. Hawaiian (HA) flew just 21. The carrier codes are hard to read; the airlines table in nycflights13 has the full names, which you could join in.


9.3.2 fill and color
For bars, boxes, and polygons, fill colors the inside, and color only the outline. (For points and lines, color is the one to use.) Map fill to the carrier:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Each bar now has its own color and a legend entry. But the legend only repeats the x axis, so it adds nothing. Hide it with show.legend = FALSE inside geom_bar(). Color earns its place when it shows a different variable from x.


9.3.3 Stacked bars
Map fill to a different variable from x. Here x is the day of the month, and the colors show which of five carriers flew that day:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Each bar splits into colored segments, one per carrier, and the bar’s height is still the total number of flights that day. This is a stacked bar chart. The regular dips are Saturdays, when airlines schedule fewer flights.
Stacking makes the totals easy to read, but the middle segments are hard to compare, because they don’t sit on a shared baseline. The position argument gives two alternatives:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
position = "fill" stretches every bar to the same height, so you compare proportions. The y axis would still say “count”, although it now shows a share, which is why the code relabels it with labs(). position = "dodge" puts each day’s bars next to each other on a shared baseline, so you can compare counts directly. With 31 days and five carriers it gets crowded; dodging works best with only a few categories on x.


9.3.4 Boxplots
Which airlines fly the longest routes? A boxplot compares a continuous variable across categories. Map a categorical x and a continuous y:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
A boxplot summarizes each group in five numbers. The box runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile, so it holds the middle half of the flights. The thick line is the median. The whiskers reach the furthest points within 1.5 times the height of the box, and anything beyond them is drawn as a dot: an outlier.
United (UA) flies the longest routes, with a median of about 1,400 miles, and its outliers near 5,000 miles are its flights from Newark to Honolulu. Southwest (WN) flies the shortest, with a median of about 750 miles. A boxplot hides the shape of the data inside the box; geom_violin() is an alternative that shows it.
crumbs: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.4 Small multiples with facets

9.4.1 facet_wrap()
Sixteen colors on one chart are impossible to tell apart. A better idea is small multiples: one small chart per group, all with the same axes. In ggplot2 this is called faceting:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
facet_wrap(~ carrier) draws one panel per carrier. The tilde, ~, makes a formula: read ~ carrier as “split by carrier”. The panels share their axes, so you can compare them directly. nrow or ncol sets the shape of the grid, as in facet_wrap(~ carrier, ncol = 4).
alpha = 0.3 makes each point 70% transparent, so places where many points overlap look darker, and you can see where most flights fall. Look at the panel for HA (Hawaiian Airlines): it is nearly empty, because Hawaiian flew only one flight a day from New York. You would never have spotted that in a single chart with 16 colors.


9.4.2 facet_grid()
To split by two categorical variables, use facet_grid(rows ~ columns):
flights |>
  ggplot(aes(x = distance, y = air_time)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(origin ~ month)
This makes 3 rows (one per airport) by 12 columns (one per month): 36 panels. Read across a row to follow one airport through the year, or down a column to compare the airports in one month. At this size the axis labels overlap; fixes include filtering to a few months, or setting fewer breaks with scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1000)). facet_grid(~ month) makes columns only.
Use facet_wrap() for one variable with many levels, and facet_grid() when you want to cross two variables.

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.5 Finishing a plot

9.5.1 Choosing your own colors
Every mapped aesthetic has a scale, which controls how data values turn into visual values. To pick the colors yourself, replace the default fill scale with scale_fill_manual():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Naming each value ("EWR" = ...) guarantees each airport keeps its color, even if the order of the data changes. Match the scale to the aesthetic: scale_fill_manual() for fills, scale_color_manual() for points and lines.
The six-character codes are hex codes: two characters each for the red, green, and blue in the color. Choosing colors that work for everyone is harder than it looks. About one man in twelve has some form of color blindness. Websites such as https://colorbrewer2.org suggest sets of colors that work for color-blind readers and in grayscale, and scale_fill_viridis_d() uses the viridis palette, which is designed for both.


9.5.2 Adding labels with labs()
A column name such as dep_delay means something to you, but not to your reader. labs() sets every label in one call:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The argument names match the aesthetics: x, y, color, fill. Here color = "Origin airport" renames the legend, because color is the mapped aesthetic. A good habit for every plot you hand in: a title, axis labels with units, and the data source in the caption.


9.5.3 Themes
A theme controls everything that isn’t data: the background, the grid lines, the fonts. Add one as another layer. theme_minimal() removes the gray background, and theme_bw() and theme_classic() are worth trying too:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


9.5.4 Saving a plot with ggsave()
You could export a plot from RStudio’s Plots pane, but then it comes out at whatever size the pane happens to be. ggsave() makes the size and resolution part of your code, so the figure is the same every time you knit:
# Create your plot
ggplot(data = october_flights) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = dep_delay, y = arr_delay, color = origin)) +
  theme_minimal()

# Save it as a high-resolution PNG file
ggsave(filename = "nyc_flights_delays_october.png",
       width = 8,
       height = 6,
       dpi = 300)   # good for print or presentations
ggsave() saves the last plot you made. width and height are in inches, and dpi is the resolution in dots per inch: 300 is print quality. The file extension sets the type: .png, .pdf, .svg, or .jpg. The file goes into your working directory, which for an R Markdown file is the folder the .Rmd file is in. To save a plot that isn’t the last one, store it first, p <- ggplot(...), and then ggsave("file.png", plot = p).

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.6 Practice: June flights
These steps follow the in-class exercise.
Step 1: set up. Start a new R Markdown file, load the packages, and look at the data:
library(nycflights13)
library(tidyverse)

glimpse(flights)

flights |>
  distinct(carrier)
Step 2: plot. Graph air_time against distance for the June flights. Add a trend line, color the points by origin airport, and label the axes with units. Try it first:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Show the answer to step 2

flights |>
  filter(month == 6) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = distance, y = air_time)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = origin), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth() +
  labs(x = "Distance (miles)", y = "Air time (minutes)",
       color = "Origin airport",
       title = "Air time against distance, June 2013")
The points fall close to a straight line, because air time grows with distance at roughly cruising speed. Points far off the line are worth asking about. Here color is mapped in geom_point() only, so there is a single trend line for all three airports.

Step 3: challenge. Which plane (tailnum) has the worst on-time record? This is a dplyr question, not a plotting one: you answered a version of it at the end of the last chapter. Once you have a table of planes with their share of late flights, try plotting it: a histogram of share_late shows whether a few planes are unusually bad, or whether lateness is spread across the whole fleet.

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.7 Check your understanding

In ggplot2, which function connects columns in your data to visual properties such as x, y, and color? 
geom_point(color = "blue") is an example of: Mapping an aestheticSetting an aestheticFacetingA scale
Writing aes(color = "blue") makes all the points blue. TRUEFALSE
Which geom counts the rows in each category for you? geom_col()geom_bar()geom_point()geom_boxplot()
For a bar chart, which aesthetic colors the inside of each bar? 
Which bar position stretches every bar to the same height, so you can compare shares? “stack”“dodge”“fill”“identity”
In a boxplot, the thick line across the box shows the: MeanMedianMaximum25th percentile
facet_wrap(~ carrier) draws one panel for each carrier, with shared axes. TRUEFALSE
In a chain of ggplot2 layers, the + goes at the start of each new line. TRUEFALSE



Show hint for question 3

Inside aes(), "blue" is treated as a data value, not a color. ggplot2 makes a legend entry called blue and uses its default color, a salmon pink. To make the points blue, set the color outside aes(): geom_point(color = "blue").

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.8 Summary

ggplot2 builds graphs from the grammar of graphics: data, aesthetics that map columns to visual properties, and geoms that draw the marks, joined in layers with +.
The template is ggplot(data) + geom_function(aes(mappings)). Mappings in ggplot() apply to every layer.
Choose the geom from the kinds of variables: geom_point() and geom_smooth() for two continuous variables, geom_bar() for counts of a category, geom_boxplot() for a continuous variable across categories.
Setting an aesthetic (outside aes()) gives every mark the same value. Mapping one (inside aes()) ties it to a column and makes a legend.
For bars, fill is the inside and color the outline. position = "fill" compares shares; position = "dodge" compares counts.
Facets (facet_wrap(), facet_grid()) make small multiples, a better choice than many colors.
Finish every plot with readable colors (scale_fill_manual()), labels (labs()), and a theme, and save it with ggsave().

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.9 Exercises
Use the flights data from nycflights13 for these exercises.

Histogram. Make a histogram of distance with geom_histogram(). Change binwidth to 100, then 500. What do you notice about the distances flown from New York?
Sorted bars. Make a bar chart of the number of flights from each origin airport. Then make one for the 10 most common destinations (dest). (Hint: count(), slice_max(), and geom_col().)
Delays by month. Use group_by() and summarize() to find the mean departure delay for each month, then plot it with geom_line() and geom_point(). Which months were worst?
Set or map? Make a scatterplot of distance against air_time for the January flights. First set every point to dark green. Then map color to origin. Then map size to dep_delay. Which of these makes a useful plot?
Facets. Make boxplots of dep_delay for each origin, then facet them by month. Use coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-20, 100)) to zoom in. What does zooming in show you that the full plot doesn’t?
Finish and save. Take your favorite plot from these exercises, give it a title, axis labels with units, and a caption, apply theme_minimal(), and save it as a PNG file 7 inches wide and 5 inches tall.
Fix the code. Each chunk below has one mistake. Find and fix it.
ggplot(flights) + geom_point(aes(x = dep_delay, y = arr_delay), color = "origin")
ggplot(flights, aes(x = carrier))
  + geom_bar()
flights |> ggplot(aes(x = carrier)) |> geom_bar()

title: 9  Into the Tidyverse: Graphs with ggplot2
text:
9.10 Further reading

R for Data Science (2nd ed.) (Wickham et al. 2023), free at https://r4ds.hadley.nz. The “Data visualization” chapter introduces ggplot2 with a different data set, and the “Layers” chapter goes further into geoms, facets, and positions.
The ggplot2 website, https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org, has the reference page for every function in this chapter.
Posit’s Data visualization with ggplot2 cheatsheet, https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/, lists the geoms by the kinds of variables they plot.
ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis (3rd ed.), by Hadley Wickham, Danielle Navarro, and Thomas Lin Pedersen, free at https://ggplot2-book.org, explains the grammar of graphics in depth.




The idea that any chart can be described with the same small set of
parts: data, aesthetic mappings, geoms, scales, facets, and coordinates.
ggplot2 is built on it.
A visual property of a mark, such as its x position, y position, color,
fill, size, or shape. In ggplot2, aes() connects columns to
aesthetics.
Tying an aesthetic to a column, inside aes(), as in
aes(color = origin). The look of each mark then comes from
the data, and ggplot2 adds a legend.
Short for geometric object: the marks a ggplot draws to show the data,
such as points (geom_point()), bars
(geom_bar()), or boxes (geom_boxplot()).
A plot of two continuous variables against each other, with one point
per observation. In ggplot2, geom_point().
A chart that compares counts or amounts across categories with bars.
geom_bar() counts rows for you; geom_col()
draws heights you give it.
A chart that summarizes a distribution: the box spans the middle half of
the values, a line marks the median, and dots beyond the whiskers are
outliers.
Giving every mark the same fixed value, outside aes(), as
in geom_point(color = "blue"). It is a design choice, not a
data choice.
A set of small charts, one per group, that share the same axes so they
can be compared directly. ggplot2 calls this faceting.
The tidyverse package for transforming data frames: filtering rows,
choosing columns, adding new columns, joining tables, and summarizing.
An R package of data on every flight that left New York City’s three
airports in 2013, including the flights data frame.
The tidyverse package for making plots and maps by adding layers.
A family of R packages (including dplyr,
ggplot2, and readr) for reading,
cleaning, reshaping, summarizing, and plotting data, all designed to
work together.
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
Data arranged so that each variable is a column, each observation is a
row, and each value has its own cell.
In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as
months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic,
such as median income; each Census variable has a code.
One thing that was measured or recorded, such as a student, a county, or
a flight. In a data frame, each row is an observation.
Code that takes inputs (arguments), does a job, and returns an output,
such as mean(temps).
One piece of a plot or map, added with + and drawn on top
of the layers before it. In GIS, a layer holds one theme of features,
such as roads or soils.
The rules that turn data values into visual values: which colors, which
classes, which axis breaks. Every mapped aesthetic has one, and
functions such as scale_fill_manual() or
tm_scale_intervals() change it.
A method for flattening the curved graticule onto a flat map. Every
projection distorts shape, area, distance, or direction.
A one-page summary of a package or tool. Posit publishes them for dplyr,
ggplot2, RStudio, and more.
The integrated development environment (IDE) where you write and run R.
R does the computing; RStudio is the workspace around it.
R’s table: rows are observations and columns are variables. A tibble is
the tidyverse’s version of a data frame.
The operator |>, which passes the result on its left as
the first argument of the function on its right. Read it as “and then.”
An input to a function, written inside its parentheses.
A value that is unknown, written NA (“not available”) in R.
Most calculations with NA give NA; test for it
with is.na().
A range that is likely to contain the true value of something estimated
from data. geom_smooth() shades a 95% confidence interval
around its trend line.
A statistical model of how one variable (such as home price) changes
with one or more others (such as distance to downtown).
A six-character code for a color, such as #3182bd: two
characters each for its red, green, and blue.
The key that explains what the colors, sizes, or shapes on a plot or map
mean. ggplot2 and tmap build one for every mapped aesthetic.
Combining two tables by matching rows on a shared key column, such as
attaching Census data to boundaries by GEOID with
left_join().
A closed shape that represents an area, such as a county, a lake, or a
census tract.
A bar chart where each bar is split into colored segments, one per
group, so the bar’s height is the total.
The value below which a given share of the values fall: a quarter of
values are below the 25th percentile. quantile() in R.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
A value far from all the others. It may be real or an error, so check it
before you report it.
The settings for everything on a plot that isn’t data: background, grid
lines, fonts. Add one with a layer such as theme_minimal().
To build an R Markdown file into a finished document (HTML, PDF, or
Word). Knitting reruns every code chunk from the top in a fresh R
session.
Dots per inch: the resolution of a saved image. 300 dpi is print
quality.
A document format (.Rmd) that mixes formatted text with
chunks of R code. Knitting it runs the code and builds a finished
report.
A chart that divides a variable’s range into bins and draws a bar for
how many values fall in each. geom_histogram() in ggplot2.
A block of R code inside an R Markdown file, starting with
```{r} and ending with three backticks.



Wickham, Hadley, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund. 2023. R for Data Science: Import, Tidy, Transform, Visualize, and Model Data. 2nd ed. O’Reilly Media. https://r4ds.hadley.nz.

title: Unit 3: Maps and Geographic Data
text:
Chapter 10: Thematic Maps with tmap
This unit moves from tables and graphs to maps. It starts by making thematic maps in R with the tmap package, using campus data on UNC’s trees, sidewalks, and buildings. It then steps back from the code to ask how the real world becomes geographic data in the first place: the vector and raster data models, and the file formats that store them. Next comes location itself: how a datum, a coordinate system, and a map projection turn places on a round Earth into coordinates on a flat map. The unit ends by getting geographic data from the places that publish it: the US Census Bureau, through the APIs that let your code download its data directly, and the ArcGIS servers that publish many government GIS layers.
A thematic map shows how one theme varies from place to place. This chapter reads spatial data into R as sf objects, which are tidy data frames with a geometry column, and maps points, lines, and polygons with tmap’s tm_shape(), tm_dots(), tm_lines(), and tm_polygons(). It covers coloring features by an attribute, choosing classes, combining layers, adding a title, scale bar, and north arrow, and switching between static and interactive maps.

title: Unit 3: Maps and Geographic Data
text:
Chapter 11: What Is Geographic Data?
Every map is a model of the world. This chapter follows data abstraction from real-world entities to features a computer can store, and compares the two main data models: vector data (points, lines, and polygons with attributes) and raster data (grids of cells). It explains map scale, cell size and resolution, and the common file formats (shapefile, GeoJSON, KML, and GeoTIFF), and why metadata matter.

title: Unit 3: Maps and Geographic Data
text:
Chapter 12: Location and Coordinate Systems
To store a location, a computer needs a model of the Earth, a grid on it, and a way to flatten it. This chapter covers geodesy and the ellipsoid, the datums used in North America (NAD27, NAD83, and WGS84), latitude and longitude, and converting between decimal degrees and degrees, minutes, and seconds. It explains why every map projection distorts shape, area, distance, or direction, how to choose one for a task, and how to check and change a layer’s coordinate reference system in R with st_crs() and st_transform().

title: Unit 3: Maps and Geographic Data
text:
Chapter 13: Census Data and APIs
US Census data come from the decennial census, a full count every ten years, and the American Community Survey, a continuous sample with a margin of error on every estimate. This chapter explains how Census geography nests from states down to tracts and blocks, how APIs work, and how the tidycensus package downloads tidy, map-ready Census data. It also shows how to carry margins of error through calculations and compare data across years.

title: Unit 3: Maps and Geographic Data
text:
Chapter 14: ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
Governments publish many of their GIS layers on ArcGIS REST services. This chapter shows how to find a layer’s URL and read its REST page, then download it into R as an sf object with arcpullr’s get_spatial_layer(). It covers SQL where clauses that download only the features you need, the server’s record limit, and the other ways arcpullr can query a layer.



An R package for making thematic maps quickly, with sensible defaults.
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
A sequence of values that R stores together, made with c(),
such as c(71, 75, 68).
Spatial data stored as a grid of cells (pixels), each holding a value,
such as a satellite image or an elevation model. In R, the
terra package handles rasters.
A model that fixes an ellipsoid to the real Earth, so that a latitude
and longitude point to one place on the ground. NAD83 and WGS84 are
datums.
The rules that tie coordinates to places on the Earth, including how the
round Earth is flattened onto a map (the projection). Layers must share
a coordinate system before you can combine them.
A method for flattening the curved graticule onto a flat map. Every
projection distorts shape, area, distance, or direction.
Application Programming Interface: a set of rules for how one program
asks another for data or services, such as your R script asking the
Census Bureau’s server for a table.
“Simple features”: the R package for spatial vector data. An sf object
is a data frame with a geometry column holding each row’s point, line,
or polygon.
R’s table: rows are observations and columns are variables. A tibble is
the tidyverse’s version of a data frame.
A closed shape that represents an area, such as a county, a lake, or a
census tract.
The level of detail at which you study something: addresses,
neighborhoods, counties, or states. A pattern that is clear at one scale
can vanish or reverse at another.
Spatial data stored as points, lines, and polygons, each with a table of
attributes. In R, the sf package handles vector data.
An open, plain-text format for vector features, written in JSON.
Coordinates are longitude first, then latitude, in WGS84.
Keyhole Markup Language: the XML-based format behind Google Earth. A
.kmz file is a zipped KML file.
The standard file format for raster data: a TIFF image with its location
and coordinate system stored inside the file.
Data about data: who made a dataset, when, how, and what each part
means. In a YAML header, it describes the document.
The science of measuring the Earth’s size, shape, orientation, and
gravity. Every coordinate rests on a geodetic model of the Earth.
A sphere flattened at the poles: the smooth mathematical shape used to
model the Earth, defined by its semi-major and semi-minor axes.
The North American Datum of 1927, based on the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and
a single origin point in Kansas.
The North American Datum of 1983, based on the GRS80 ellipsoid and
maintained through a network of permanent GPS stations (CORS).
The World Geodetic System of 1984, the datum GPS uses. GeoJSON and KML
give coordinates as WGS84 longitude and latitude.
The angle north or south of the Equator, from 0° to 90°. Lines of equal
latitude are parallels.
The angle east or west of the Prime Meridian, from 0° to 180°. Lines of
equal longitude are meridians.
Coordinates written as signed decimal numbers, such as −79.05°. Negative
means south latitude or west longitude.
Coordinates written as whole degrees, minutes (1/60 of a degree), and
seconds (1/3,600 of a degree), with a letter N, S, E, or W, such as 79°
3′ 21″ W.
The full count of everyone in the US, every ten years. It asks only a
few questions but covers every person.
The Census Bureau’s continuous survey of a sample of households every
year. It asks many more questions than the decennial census, but every
value is an estimate with a margin of error.
A subset of a population that is surveyed to estimate something about
the whole population. Smaller samples give less certain estimates.
How far a sample estimate might be from the true value. ACS margins of
error use a 90% confidence level: there is a 90% chance the true value
lies within the estimate plus or minus the MOE.
A small area of about 1,200 to 8,000 people (4,000 on average), drawn to
be fairly stable over time. The workhorse unit for neighborhood
analysis.
An R package that downloads US Census data through the Census API and
returns it as a tidy data frame, with boundaries attached if you ask.
The most common style of web API: each dataset has its own URL, you ask
for data with ordinary web requests, and the answer usually comes back
as JSON.
An R package that downloads layers from ArcGIS REST services as sf
objects, with get_spatial_layer().
Structured Query Language, the language of databases. ArcGIS
where clauses use it: fcounty = 'Orange'.

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.1 Spatial data are tidy data
The last chapter turned tables into graphs with ggplot2. This chapter turns them into maps. A thematic map shows how one theme, such as tree height, the age of buildings, or the population of cities, varies from place to place. It is the most common kind of map in spatial data science, and in R the quickest way to make one is the tmap package.
The examples use three layers of data about the UNC Chapel Hill campus: its trees, its sidewalks, and its buildings. Between them they cover the three kinds of vector data, points, lines, and polygons, so by the end of the chapter you will have mapped all three.

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.1.1 Features and attributes
Spatial data follow the same tidy rules as any other data frame. In a spatial layer, each row is one feature: one tree, one stretch of sidewalk, one building. Each column is one attribute of those features: a tree’s species or height, a building’s year built or number of floors.
What makes the data spatial is one extra column. The sf package (“simple features”) stores each feature’s shape in a geometry column, as a point, a line, or a polygon. Everything else about an sf object is an ordinary data frame. That means the tidyverse verbs you already know, such as filter(), mutate(), and count(), work on spatial data too, and they keep the geometry attached to each row.


10.1.2 tmap: the thematic mapper
tmap was written by Martin Tennekes. Like ggplot2, it builds a map in layers, joined with +:

tm_shape() names the data to draw.
A layer function draws it: tm_dots() for points, tm_lines() for lines, and tm_polygons() for polygons.
More functions add the parts of a finished map: tm_title(), tm_scalebar(), tm_compass(), and tm_layout().

tmap reads sf objects directly, and the same code makes a static map for a report or an interactive web map you can zoom into. This book uses tmap version 4, which changed many argument names. If you find older code online that uses col = for polygon colors or tm_layout(title = ...), it was written for version 3. It will often still run, but tmap prints a message suggesting the new form.
Load three packages at the top of every script:
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)


10.1.3 Our data: three campus layers
The three layers come from UNC’s open data portal, https://gisdata-uncadmin.opendata.arcgis.com (Table 10.1). Download each one as a GeoJSON file and save it in the same folder as your R Markdown file.



Table 10.1: The three UNC campus layers.











Layer
Geometry
One feature is
Attributes used here




Tree Inventory
Points
One campus tree
COMMONNAME, HEIGHT


Sidewalks
Lines
One sidewalk segment
SURFACE_


Building Footprints
Polygons
One building outline
YEARBUILT, FLOORS






read_sf() reads each file into an sf object:
buildings <- read_sf("Building_Footprints.geojson")
sidewalks <- read_sf("Sidewalks.geojson")
trees <- read_sf("Tree_Inventory.geojson")
Run glimpse(trees) to see the attributes, and check that the last column is geometry. Run st_crs(trees) to see the layer’s coordinate system. GeoJSON files always use longitude and latitude, so all three layers share a coordinate system and will line up when you draw them together.


10.1.4 tmap and ggplot2 on the same trees
ggplot2 can draw maps too, with geom_sf(). Here is the same tree layer drawn by each package (Figure 10.1):
trees |>
  tm_shape() + tm_dots()

trees |>
  ggplot() + geom_sf()











(a) tmap: tm_shape() + tm_dots()











(b) ggplot2: ggplot() + geom_sf()







Figure 10.1: The same trees drawn by tmap and by ggplot2.



Both start from the same sf object. tmap gives a clean map frame by default, and has built-in scale bars, north arrows, and an interactive mode. ggplot2 adds axes and a gray panel, as it would for any plot. ggplot2 is the more general tool, and you can make fine maps with it, but for everyday thematic maps tmap takes less code. The rest of this chapter uses tmap.

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.2 Points: mapping trees with tm_dots()

10.2.1 Color trees by height
Each tree in the inventory is one point. To color the trees by height, pass the name of a column to fill, in quotes:
trees |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_dots(fill = "HEIGHT") +
  tm_layout(bg.color = "gray")






Figure 10.2: Campus trees colored by height. tmap breaks the heights into classes and colors them from light (short) to dark (tall).



Two details matter. First, the column name goes in quotes, fill = "HEIGHT". (ggplot2’s aes() takes column names without quotes, but tmap wants them as text.) Second, because HEIGHT is a number, tmap uses a sequential palette, a ramp from light to dark, so that taller trees look darker. It also breaks the heights into a few classes, 0–19, 20–39 and so on, and builds the legend.
tm_layout() controls the map as a whole rather than one layer. Here bg.color = "gray" makes the background gray, so the palest dots still show up.






TipThink about it



Look at Figure 10.2. Where on campus are the tallest trees? Can you think of a reason why?




10.2.2 Color trees by species
Now try a text column, the species name:
trees |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_dots(fill = "COMMONNAME")






Figure 10.3: Campus trees colored by species. With 158 species, colors repeat and the legend crowds the map.



For a text column, tmap uses a qualitative palette: distinct colors with no order, one per category. That works for a handful of categories. With 158 species, the colors repeat and the legend takes up as much room as the map, so you can’t tell which tree is which (Figure 10.3). There are two fixes: map only the most common species, or lump the rare ones together.


10.2.3 Fix 1: map only the top five species
First, find the most common species with count():
trees |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(COMMONNAME, sort = TRUE)



Table 10.2: The ten most common values of COMMONNAME.





COMMONNAME
n




oak
778


holly
570


loblolly pine
513


NA
498


maple
259


willow oak
234


pine
229


crape myrtle
223


hickory
217


dogwood
183






st_drop_geometry() turns the sf object back into an ordinary data frame. That isn’t required, but it makes counting much faster, because otherwise sf tries to merge the points of every species into one shape. Oak, holly, and loblolly pine lead, and 498 trees have no species name (Table 10.2).
Then filter() to the top five, and map them:
trees |>
  filter(COMMONNAME %in% c("oak", "holly", "loblolly pine", "maple", "willow oak")) |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_dots(fill = "COMMONNAME", size = 0.05) +
  tm_title("UNC Trees") +
  tm_layout(bg.color = "lightgray")






Figure 10.4: The five most common species. Five colors are easy to tell apart, but most of the trees have gone.



Ordinary tidyverse verbs work on sf objects and keep the geometry, so the filtered trees go straight into tm_shape(). size = 0.05 sets the size of the dots, and tm_title() adds a title. The legend is readable now, but the map has lost more than half the trees.


10.2.4 Fix 2: group rare species as “other”
Instead of dropping the rare species, give them a new label. mutate() makes a new column, name, that keeps the nine most common species and calls everything else “other”:
top_nine <- c("oak", "willow oak", "pine", "crape myrtle", "hickory",
              "dogwood", "holly", "loblolly pine", "maple")

trees |>
  mutate(name = if_else(COMMONNAME %in% top_nine, COMMONNAME, "other")) |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_dots(fill = "name", size = 0.05) +
  tm_title("UNC Trees") +
  tm_layout(bg.color = "lightgray")






Figure 10.5: Nine species plus “other”. Every tree stays on the map, and the legend has ten entries.



if_else(condition, yes, no) checks each tree: if its species is in top_nine, it keeps the name; if not, it becomes “other”. The 498 trees with no name go to “other” too, because NA %in% top_nine is FALSE. Every tree stays on the map, and ten categories keep the legend readable (Figure 10.5).

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.3 Lines: mapping sidewalks with tm_lines()

10.3.1 Draw the sidewalk network
The sidewalk layer is a network of line segments. tm_lines() is the line version of tm_dots():
sidewalks |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_lines()






Figure 10.6: UNC sidewalk segments, one line each, with the default style.



With no arguments, every segment is the same thin black line (Figure 10.6). The gaps on the map are places with no sidewalk data, not places with no pavement: the layer only covers what has been surveyed.


10.3.2 Color sidewalks by surface
sidewalks |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_lines(col = "SURFACE_")






Figure 10.7: UNC sidewalks colored by surface material. Brick (pink) and concrete (blue) make up most of central campus.



A line has no inside to fill, so lines take col = rather than fill =. SURFACE_ is a text column, so tmap picks a qualitative palette. (The underscore at the end of the column name comes from the source data; you must type it exactly.) Brick and concrete make up most of central campus (Figure 10.7).

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.4 Polygons: mapping buildings with tm_polygons()

10.4.1 Draw the building footprints
Building footprints are areas, so tm_polygons() draws each one with a fill and an outline:
buildings |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons()






Figure 10.8: UNC building footprints, with the default gray fill.



With no arguments, every building gets the same gray fill (Figure 10.8). That already shows the shape of campus, before any attribute is mapped.


10.4.2 Shade buildings by year built
Map fill to a numeric column, and you have a choropleth map: areas shaded by a value.
buildings |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "YEARBUILT")






Figure 10.9: UNC buildings by year built. By default, tmap breaks the years into 50-year classes.



By default, tmap chooses “pretty” breaks, round numbers, here 50-year classes from 1750 to 2050 (Figure 10.9). Buildings with no year recorded are drawn gray and labeled Missing in the legend.






TipThink about it



Where are the oldest buildings on campus? The newest? What does the map suggest about how the campus grew?




10.4.3 Control the classes with n and style
How many classes the map uses, and where the breaks between them fall, change what the reader sees. This is called classification, and two settings control it:

n sets the number of classes.
style sets the method for choosing the breaks. "equal" makes equal intervals: every class covers the same range of values.

In tmap version 4, both go in a scale function, tm_scale_intervals(), given to the fill.scale argument:
buildings |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "YEARBUILT",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 4, style = "equal"))






Figure 10.10: Year built in four equal-interval classes. Each class covers about 57 years, from the oldest building (1795) to the newest (2024).



Equal intervals split the range from the oldest building to the newest into four equal parts (Figure 10.10). You can also write tm_polygons(fill = "YEARBUILT", n = 4, style = "equal"), the shorter form from version 3. It still works, but tmap prints a message suggesting fill.scale. Other styles include "quantile" (the same number of buildings in each class) and "jenks" (Jenks natural breaks, which puts the breaks in the biggest gaps between values). Later chapters return to classification, because the choice can change the story a map tells.

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.5 Putting a map together

10.5.1 Combine points, lines, and polygons
To draw several layers in one map, save each layer as its own object, then add them together with +:
# 1. Define independent layers
map_buildings <- buildings |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "FLOORS")

map_sidewalks <- sidewalks |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_lines()

map_trees <- trees |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_dots(fill = "HEIGHT", size = 0.02)

# 2. Add them together, placing buildings first to set the map extent
map_buildings + map_sidewalks + map_trees +
  tm_title("UNC Chapel Hill Campus Map") +
  tm_layout(bg.color = "#eeeeee")






Figure 10.11: Buildings shaded by number of floors, sidewalks, and trees colored by height, in one map.



Each layer draws on top of the ones before it, so put the polygons first, then the lines, then the points; otherwise the buildings would cover the trees. The first layer also sets the map’s extent, the area the map shows. tm_title() and tm_layout() style the whole map, so they go at the end, after all the layers.


10.5.2 Add a scale bar and north arrow
A reader expects a finished map to have a scale bar and a north arrow:
map_buildings + map_sidewalks + map_trees +
  tm_title("UNC Chapel Hill Campus Map") +
  tm_layout(bg.color = "#eeeeee") +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", position = c(0.7, 1))






Figure 10.12: The campus map with a scale bar at the bottom left and an eight-pointed north arrow at the top.



tm_scalebar() adds a scale bar, which shows how distances on the map relate to distances on the ground. tm_compass() adds a north arrow; type = "8star" is one of several styles. position places each one, either by name, such as c("left", "bottom"), or by numbers from 0 to 1 that give the share of the way across and up the map frame. Put them where they don’t cover any data.


10.5.3 Static or interactive: tmap_mode()
tmap has two modes, and the same code works in both:
tmap_mode("view")   # interactive web map
tmap_mode("plot")   # static map (the default)






Figure 10.13: The campus map in view mode, in RStudio’s Viewer pane. You can pan, zoom, and click a feature to see its attributes.



After tmap_mode("view"), every map becomes an interactive map on top of a basemap of streets and place names (Figure 10.13). You can pan, zoom, and click on any feature to see its attributes. It is the best way to explore your data. The basemap tiles load from the web, so view mode needs an internet connection. tmap_mode("plot") switches back to static maps, which are what you want for reports, slides, and anything printed.

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.6 Practice: map the world
These steps follow the in-class exercise. tmap comes with three world layers, so you don’t need to download anything.
Step 1: set up. Start a new R Markdown file, and load the packages and data:
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

data(World)
data(metro)
data(rivers)
Step 2: look at the data. Use glimpse() on World, rivers, and metro. Which is a point layer, which is a line layer, and which is a polygon layer? Which column of metro holds the projected population in 2030?
Step 3: make the map. Make one tmap that shows the countries, rivers, and metro areas. As a stretch, size the metro areas by their projected 2030 population.


Show one solution

# 1. Create individual maps
map_rivers <- rivers |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_lines(col = "lightblue", lwd = 0.7)

map_metro <- metro |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_bubbles(size = "pop2030", fill = "orange")

map_world <- World |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "name", fill.legend = tm_legend_hide())

# 2. Plot all the layers together
map_world + map_rivers + map_metro +
  tm_title("2030 Projected Metro Population") +
  tm_layout(bg.color = "lightblue")






Figure 10.14: Metro areas sized by projected 2030 population, over the world’s countries and rivers.



The layers go in order: countries first, then rivers, then the metro bubbles on top. tm_bubbles() draws circles sized by a column, here pop2030. Notice the difference between setting and mapping, just as in ggplot2: fill = "orange" is a color, so every bubble is orange, while size = "pop2030" is a column, so the size comes from the data. Filling the countries by name gives each one its own color, and fill.legend = tm_legend_hide() hides the legend, which would otherwise list 177 countries.

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.7 Check your understanding

In an sf object, each row is one: AttributeFeatureCoordinateLayer
Which tmap function names the data to draw, at the start of each layer? 
Which layer function draws polygons? tm_dots()tm_lines()tm_polygons()tm_shape()
To color sidewalk lines by a column, you use col = rather than fill =, because a line has no inside to fill. TRUEFALSE
For a numeric column such as HEIGHT, tmap’s default colors are a: Qualitative palette, one color per valueSequential palette, from light to darkSingle colorRandom set of colors
In tm_scale_intervals(n = 4, style = "equal"), what does n set? The size of the dotsThe number of classesThe number of layersThe number of the north arrow style
When you add layers together, the first layer sets the extent of the map. TRUEFALSE
Which function adds a north arrow? tm_scalebar()tm_compass()tm_title()tm_layout()
Which mode makes an interactive map that you can pan and zoom? tmap_mode(“plot”)tmap_mode(“view”)tmap_mode(“web”)tmap_mode(“static”)



Show hint for question 4

fill colors the inside of a dot or a polygon. A line is only an outline, so tmap colors it with col, the same name ggplot2 uses for the color of lines and outlines.

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.8 Summary

An sf object is a tidy data frame of spatial features, one per row, with their attributes in the columns and their shapes in a geometry column. Read a file into one with read_sf().
tmap builds a thematic map in layers: tm_shape() names the data, and tm_dots(), tm_lines(), or tm_polygons() draws it. Layers are joined with +.
Color features by an attribute with fill = "column" (dots and polygons) or col = "column" (lines). Numbers get a sequential palette; text gets a qualitative palette.
Too many categories make a map unreadable: filter() to the most common, or lump the rest together with mutate() and if_else().
Classification decides how many classes a map uses and where the breaks fall: fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 4, style = "equal").
Combine layers with +, with polygons first and points last. Finish with tm_title(), tm_scalebar(), tm_compass(), and tm_layout().
tmap_mode("view") makes interactive web maps for exploring; tmap_mode("plot") makes static maps for reports.

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.9 Exercises
Use the three campus layers for exercises 1 to 4, and tmap’s World data for 5 and 6.

Floors. Make a choropleth map of the buildings, shaded by FLOORS. Then try n = 3 and n = 7. Which do you find easiest to read?
Classification styles. Map YEARBUILT with style = "equal", "quantile", and "jenks", each with five classes. How do the breaks differ? Which map makes campus look oldest?
One species. Map only the willow oaks, as dots on top of the building footprints. Give the map a title, a scale bar, and a north arrow.
Sidewalk lengths. How many sidewalk segments are made of each surface? Use st_drop_geometry() and count(). Then try st_length() inside mutate() to find the total length of each surface. Is the answer different?
A world choropleth. World has a column called life_exp, life expectancy. Make a choropleth of it with five classes. Which regions stand out?
Explore. Switch to tmap_mode("view") and draw your map from exercise 5. Click on a few countries. Then switch back with tmap_mode("plot").

title: 10  Thematic Maps with tmap
text:
10.10 Further reading

The tmap website, https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap/, has a getting-started guide and many examples, all in version 4 syntax.
Geocomputation with R (2nd ed.), by Robin Lovelace, Jakub Nowosad, and Jannes Muenchow, free at https://r.geocompx.org. Its “Making maps with R” chapter covers tmap in depth, including faceted and animated maps.
The sf website, https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/, explains simple features and has a cheatsheet for its functions.




A closed shape that represents an area, such as a county, a lake, or a
census tract.
One piece of a plot or map, added with + and drawn on top
of the layers before it. In GIS, a layer holds one theme of features,
such as roads or soils.
“Simple features”: the R package for spatial vector data. An sf object
is a data frame with a geometry column holding each row’s point, line,
or polygon.
One spatial object in a layer of data, such as one tree, one sidewalk
segment, or one building. In an sf object, each row is a feature.
A non-spatial fact about a spatial feature, such as a tree’s species or
a building’s year built. Attributes are the columns of a layer’s
attribute table.
Dividing a numeric variable into a few classes for a map, by choosing
how many classes there are and where the breaks between them fall.
A bar on a map that shows how distances on the map relate to distances
on the ground.
A symbol on a map that shows which direction is north. In tmap,
tm_compass().
A web map you can pan, zoom, and click to see each feature’s attributes.
tmap makes one in view mode.
The tidyverse package for making plots and maps by adding layers.
A map that shows how one theme, such as income, tree height, or building
age, varies from place to place.
The use of data that have a location attached to answer questions about
the world. It combines what we study (the spatial), how we
handle it (data skills), and how we ask and answer questions
(science).
An R package for making thematic maps quickly, with sensible defaults.
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
Spatial data stored as points, lines, and polygons, each with a table of
attributes. In R, the sf package handles vector data.
A document format (.Rmd) that mixes formatted text with
chunks of R code. Knitting it runs the code and builds a finished
report.
The integrated development environment (IDE) where you write and run R.
R does the computing; RStudio is the workspace around it.
Data arranged so that each variable is a column, each observation is a
row, and each value has its own cell.
R’s table: rows are observations and columns are variables. A tibble is
the tidyverse’s version of a data frame.
The column of an sf object that holds each feature’s shape: a point, a
line, or a polygon.
A family of R packages (including dplyr,
ggplot2, and readr) for reading,
cleaning, reshaping, summarizing, and plotting data, all designed to
work together.
Code that takes inputs (arguments), does a job, and returns an output,
such as mean(temps).
An input to a function, written inside its parentheses.
A plain file of R code, ending in .R. Anything that isn’t
code must be written as a comment.
An open, plain-text format for vector features, written in JSON.
Coordinates are longitude first, then latitude, in WGS84.
The rules that tie coordinates to places on the Earth, including how the
round Earth is flattened onto a map (the projection). Layers must share
a coordinate system before you can combine them.
The angle east or west of the Prime Meridian, from 0° to 180°. Lines of
equal longitude are meridians.
The angle north or south of the Equator, from 0° to 90°. Lines of equal
latitude are parallels.
Colors that run from light to dark, used for numbers so that bigger
values look darker.
The key that explains what the colors, sizes, or shapes on a plot or map
mean. ggplot2 and tmap build one for every mapped aesthetic.
Distinct colors with no order, one per category, used for text columns
such as species names.
A map that shades areas, such as counties or buildings, by the value of
a variable.
A classification method that makes every class cover the same range of
values.
The rules that turn data values into visual values: which colors, which
classes, which axis breaks. Every mapped aesthetic has one, and
functions such as scale_fill_manual() or
tm_scale_intervals() change it.
A way of dividing values into map classes that puts the breaks where the
gaps between values are largest, so similar values share a color.
The area a map or a layer covers, from its westernmost to easternmost
and southernmost to northernmost points.
A background map of streets, places, or imagery, loaded from the web as
tiles, that your own data are drawn on top of.
A method for flattening the curved graticule onto a flat map. Every
projection distorts shape, area, distance, or direction.
Giving every mark the same fixed value, outside aes(), as
in geom_point(color = "blue"). It is a design choice, not a
data choice.
The exact rules for writing code: spelling, capitalization, commas,
quotation marks, and matching brackets.
A one-page summary of a package or tool. Posit publishes them for dplyr,
ggplot2, RStudio, and more.

title: 11  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
11.1 From the real world to the computer
In the last chapter you mapped campus trees, sidewalks, and buildings. But a map, or a layer of data in R, is never the world itself. A tree on the map is a dot; a building is a flat outline. Each is a model of reality, and every model makes choices about what to keep and what to leave out.
This chapter steps back from the code to ask how geographic information gets from the real world into a computer. It is organized around four questions:
The answers will help you choose the right data for a question, and understand what the data can and can’t tell you.

title: 11  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
11.1.1 Entities and features
Everything starts with the real world. Walk across campus and you pass trees, light poles, buildings, sidewalks, and lawns. Each of these real things is an entity. When we put them on a map or in a database, they become features: simplified representations of those entities.
Not every entity makes it onto the map. A typical campus map keeps the buildings and sidewalks, and leaves out the light poles and most of the trees. Choosing what to keep is the first step of abstraction.


11.1.2 Data abstraction
Data abstraction is the process of making the real world readable by a computer. It happens in steps, each further from what people see and closer to what a machine stores (Table 11.1).



Table 11.1: The levels of data abstraction, from the human end to the machine end.










Level
What it is
Example: a wetland




Real world
Too detailed to store as it is
The marsh itself, with its water, plants, and edges


Data model
We choose which objects and properties to keep
Wetland areas, each with an ID, an area, and a type


Data structure
Tables and lists of coordinates organize the model
A list of x, y coordinates for each outline, and a table of attributes


Machine code
Everything is stored as 0s and 1s
10011101 00110110 ...






The top of the table is meaningful to people, and the bottom to machines. Geographic information science works in the middle, with data models and data structures, where both can read it.


11.1.3 Continuous data and discrete objects
Geographic information comes in two broad types, and the type helps decide how to model it:

Continuous data exist everywhere on the map. Every location has a value, even if we only measured some of them, and the value changes from place to place. Examples: elevation, temperature, precipitation.
Discrete objects exist in one place and not in another. They are either present or absent, with clear edges. Examples: roads, houses, states.







TipThink about it



Is population density continuous or discrete? You could think of it as a value that exists everywhere and changes smoothly across a city. Or you could count the people in each census tract, which gives one number per area with sharp edges between them. Which is more realistic? Which is easier to work with?




11.1.4 Geographic data models
A geographic data model is “a formal (meaning mathematical) means of representing and manipulating spatially-referenced information.” People understand the world through ideas like river or neighborhood; computers understand numbers and rules. A data model lives in the overlap: precise enough for a computer, and meaningful enough for us. Every data model loses something, so it is always worth asking what was left out.
Geographic information reaches the computer in three main forms:

Vector data store discrete features as coordinates: points for fire hydrants, lines for streets, polygons for land parcels.
Raster data store a grid of cells, each holding a value, like the pixels of a satellite image or an elevation model.
Tabular data hold the attributes of features: for one house, its address, year built, square footage, and number of bedrooms. Attribute tables are usually joined to vector features.

The next two sections take vector and raster data in turn.

title: 11  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
11.2 Vector data

11.2.1 One object, three representations
The same real-world objects can be stored as different kinds of vector features. Take the buildings in an air photo (Figure 11.1):

As points, they record where each building is.
As lines, they record each building’s outline.
As areas (polygons), they record the outline and the space inside it.

What is the difference between the lines and the areas, when both trace the same outline? Enclosure. A line is just a boundary; a polygon knows it has an inside, so you can ask how big it is, color it in, or find out whether a point falls within it.






Figure 11.1: The same four buildings stored as points, as lines, and as areas.



The right choice depends on the map’s purpose and its scale.


11.2.2 Generalization and map scale
When a map shows a place at a smaller scale, detail has to go. This is called generalization. Imagine three maps of the same city:

A large-scale map, zoomed in on a neighborhood, draws the streets and buildings as areas.
An intermediate map, of the region around the city, draws the city as an area and the roads as lines.
A small-scale map, of the whole country, draws the city as a single point.

The names are easy to mix up. Map scale is a fraction: a large-scale map has a large fraction, such as 1:10,000, so it shows a small area in detail. A small-scale map has a small fraction, such as 1:10,000,000, so it shows a large area with little detail. The same feature can need a different geometry at a different scale, so a data model must be chosen with the map’s purpose in mind.


11.2.3 What makes something an entity?
To store an entity, we need to know five things about it:

A location: an address or a set of coordinates.
An extent: its size, boundary, or dimensions.
Non-spatial attributes: its name, number, qualities, or color.
Time: when it existed, or when the data were collected.
A geometry: its shape.

Think of a lake. Its location and extent come from an air photo, its geometry is a polygon traced around the shore, and its name, depth, and water quality are attributes.


11.2.4 Spatial data and attributes
Spatial data have a location: you could put a pin on a map for each campus building, each rain gauge in North Carolina, or each interstate highway. Non-spatial data have no location of their own: the parts of a bicycle, student ID numbers, or class grades.
The two meet in attributes. When we describe a spatial entity with non-spatial information, such as a building’s name or the year it was built, that information is called an attribute. Attribute data:

are always linked to a spatial feature;
are usually stored in tables, with one row per feature and one column per attribute;
have the same columns for every feature in a layer.

Follow a fire hydrant into a database. The hydrant becomes a point in a layer of hydrants, and everything we know about it goes into a row of the attribute table: its ID, its number of outlets, its color, its rating (Table 11.2). The ID is what ties each row back to its point. Because every hydrant has the same columns, we can query the layer, for example, “show all hydrants with a low rating”.



Table 11.2: An attribute table for a layer of fire hydrants. Each row is one hydrant (one point on the map), and each column is one attribute.





ID
Outlets
Color
Rating




1
3
red
high


2
3
red
high


3
2
green
low


4
3
red
mid






This is the same structure as the sf objects in the last chapter: each row is a feature, each column an attribute, and the geometry column holds the points.


11.2.5 The parts of vector data
These terms come up whenever you edit or analyze vector data (Figure 11.2):

A point is a single location that stands alone.
A node is the start or end point of a line.
A vertex is a point in between that gives the line its shape.
A line segment is the straight piece between two vertices.
A polygon is a closed ring of line segments.







Figure 11.2: The parts of vector data: points, a line that starts and ends at nodes and bends at vertices, and a polygon.



Nodes matter for networks. Roads connect at nodes, which is how routing software knows two streets meet. Vertices matter for accuracy: more vertices make a smoother, more accurate line, but a bigger file.


11.2.6 Thematic layers
Geographic data are organized into thematic layers. All the roads go in one layer, all the soils in another, and elevation in a third. Each layer holds one theme, and similar features go together.
Because every layer uses the same coordinate system, the layers stack exactly on top of each other, and a map is just a set of layers drawn together. That is exactly what you did in the last chapter, when you drew buildings, then sidewalks, then trees. Stacking layers is also the basis of overlay analysis: for example, finding the wetlands on a particular type of soil within a kilometer of a road.

title: 11  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
11.3 Raster data

11.3.1 Vector and raster compared
Rasters divide space into a regular grid of cells, and each cell stores one value. Figure 11.3 shows the same points, line, and area stored both ways. On the left, as vector data, the points are exact coordinates, the line is a chain of vertices, and the area is a polygon. On the right, as a raster, each feature is approximated by grid cells: the line becomes a staircase of cells, and the area a block of them.






Figure 11.3: The same points, line, and area stored as vector data (left) and as a raster (right).



How accurate the raster version is depends entirely on the size of the cells. Table 11.3 sums up the two models.



Table 11.3: The vector and raster data models compared.











Vector
Raster




Geometry
Points, lines, polygons
A regular grid of cells


Best for
Discrete objects
Continuous data


Location
Stored as coordinates
Set by the cell size and position in the grid


Values
Each feature has attributes
Each cell holds a value


Examples
Roads, parcels, wells
Elevation, satellite imagery, rainfall


Strengths
Precise and compact for features with clear edges
Simple to analyze; handles surfaces that vary everywhere


Weaknesses
Awkward for values that change continuously
Files grow quickly as cells get smaller; edges become staircases








11.3.2 A raster is a grid of cell values
Every cell in a raster holds exactly one value (Figure 11.4). The value can be a number, like an elevation in meters, or a code for a category, like 1 for forest and 2 for water. Places with no measurement are flagged as no data, here as N. Every raster format has a way to mark those cells, and in R they become NA.






Figure 11.4: A raster is a grid of cell values. Its location is fixed by the coordinates of the lower-left corner and the cell size.



A raster doesn’t store coordinates for every cell. It stores the coordinates of one corner, the origin, usually the lower-left corner, and the cell size: the length of one side of a cell in real-world units, such as meters. From those, the computer works out where any cell is from its row and column:
\[
N_{\text{cell}} = N_{\text{lower-left}} + \text{row} \times \text{cell size}
\]
\[
E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{lower-left}} + \text{column} \times \text{cell size}
\]
Here N is the northing (the y coordinate) and E the easting (the x coordinate), with rows counted up from 0 at the bottom and columns counted from 0 at the left. Try it: a raster of 30 m cells has its lower-left corner at easting 600,000 m and northing 3,950,000 m. Where is the corner of the cell in row 4, column 10?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Because a raster is just a grid of numbers, R can hold a small one in a matrix. This box makes the grid in Figure 11.4, with NA for the no-data cell, and draws it with base R’s image():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Real rasters are far bigger, with millions of cells, and in R you would use the terra package for them. But the idea is the same.


11.3.3 Cell size and resolution
The cell size is the raster’s resolution. Figure 11.5 shows the same 200 m square at three cell sizes. Going from 100 m to 50 m to 25 m cells takes it from 4 to 16 to 64 cells.






Figure 11.5: The same 200 m square at three cell sizes. Halving the cell size makes four times as many cells.



Smaller cells capture more detail, but the number of cells grows with the square of the resolution: halve the cell size and you have four times as many cells, and roughly four times as much data.






TipThink about it



A TV screen is a raster, and each pixel is a cell. If you were buying a new TV, which of the three grids in Figure 11.5 would give the sharpest picture? A 4K TV has about four times as many pixels as a 1080p TV of the same size. What does that say about the size of its pixels, and about how much data it needs?




11.3.4 Data structures
The data model is the idea; the data structure is how that idea is laid out in memory or on disk. A polygon, for example, can be stored as a set of arcs, each a list of coordinate pairs. A pointer at the end of one arc tells the computer where the next one begins. Neighboring polygons can share an arc, so their common boundary is stored once rather than twice. Data structures that record how features connect and share boundaries like this are called topological data structures.

title: 11  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
11.4 Geographic file formats
Data models and structures are stored in files, and you will meet several formats when you load spatial data into R (Table 11.4).



Table 11.4: Common geographic file formats.











Format
Extension
Data model
Notes




Shapefile
.shp, plus several others
Vector
Esri’s format, from the early 1990s; still very common


GeoJSON
.geojson
Vector
Open, plain-text standard; the default for web maps


KML
.kml, .kmz
Vector
The format behind Google Earth


GeoTIFF
.tif
Raster
An image with its location stored inside







11.4.1 Shapefiles
A shapefile is the most common way vector data are shared, and its name is misleading: it isn’t one file, but a group of files with the same name and different extensions (Table 11.5).



Table 11.5: The files that make up one shapefile, called roads.





File
What it holds




roads.shp
The geometry of each feature


roads.shx
A positional index, for faster access


roads.dbf
A database table of the attributes


roads.prj
The projection (coordinate system)


roads.sbn, roads.sbx
A spatial index of the features


roads.shp.xml
The metadata for the layer






Only .shp, .shx, and .dbf are required, but without the .prj file the software can’t place the data correctly on the Earth. Keep all the files together, in the same folder: a .shp on its own is not usable. When you email or download a shapefile, zip the whole set.
Shapefiles have limits worth knowing. Attribute column names can be at most 10 characters long, which is why you will see names like SURFACE_ or POP2020EST, and each file can be at most 2 GB. Newer formats, such as the GeoPackage (.gpkg), avoid these limits.


11.4.2 GeoJSON
GeoJSON is an open standard for simple geographic features, written in JSON, the plain-text format that web APIs use. You can open it in any text editor, read it, and edit it. It stores points, lines, polygons, or collections of features, and it has become the default format for web maps. The campus layers in the last chapter were GeoJSON files.
Here is a small GeoJSON file with one feature, a point at the Old Well:
{
  "type": "FeatureCollection",
  "features": [
    {
      "type": "Feature",
      "geometry": {
        "type": "Point",
        "coordinates": [-79.0512, 35.9121]
      },
      "properties": {
        "name": "Old Well"
      }
    }
  ]
}
A FeatureCollection holds a list of Features, and each feature has a geometry (its type and coordinates) and properties (its attributes). Notice that the coordinates are written longitude first, then latitude. GeoJSON always uses longitude and latitude on the WGS84 datum, the same system GPS uses. (Coordinate systems get a chapter of their own later in the course.) The free website https://geojson.io lets you draw features on a map and see their GeoJSON appear beside it.


11.4.3 KML
KML, Keyhole Markup Language, is the format behind Google Earth. It was created by Keyhole, the company whose Earth viewer Google bought in 2004, and it became an Open Geospatial Consortium standard in 2008. KML is written in XML, as nested tags, and stores points, paths, polygons, images, and even 3D models. Here is the same Old Well as a KML placemark:
<Placemark>
  <name>Old Well</name>
  <Point>
    <coordinates>-79.0512,35.9121,0</coordinates>
  </Point>
</Placemark>
Like GeoJSON, KML uses WGS84 longitude and latitude, plus an altitude. A .kmz file is a zipped KML file, usually bundled with its icons or images. KML is great for sharing and display, but less so for analysis, so it is usually converted to another format before you work with it in R.


11.4.4 GeoTIFF
GeoTIFF is the standard format for raster data: satellite images, air photos, and elevation models. It is an ordinary TIFF image with extra information inside the file saying where on Earth each pixel is, and which coordinate system it uses. It is a public-domain, open standard.
GeoTIFFs get big fast, often hundreds of megabytes. A newer variety, the Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG), arranges the cells in tiles with built-in zoomed-out copies, so that a web map or R can read only the area and the level of detail it needs, instead of downloading the whole file.


11.4.5 Metadata
Metadata are data about the data. The .shp.xml file in a shapefile is one example. Good metadata answer these questions:

Who created the data?
When were they created?
How were they created, and to what specifications?
Where can the data be found?
What coordinate system do they use, and how accurate are they?

In the US, federal agencies follow the FGDC metadata standard, from the Federal Geographic Data Committee; internationally, the standard is ISO 19115. Without metadata, you can’t judge whether data are fit for your purpose. A practical rule: if you can’t find out when and how a dataset was made, be very cautious about using it to make a decision.


11.4.6 Spatial data in R
How does R handle all of this? With data frames. In the last chapter, read_sf() read GeoJSON files into sf objects, which are data frames with an extra column that holds each feature’s geometry. The same function reads shapefiles (point it at the .shp file, with the other files beside it), KML, and GeoPackages. Rasters, such as GeoTIFFs, are read with the terra package. Later chapters put these to work.
