title: 11  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
11.6 Summary

A map or a GIS layer is a model of the world. Data abstraction turns real-world entities into features, through a data model and a data structure, down to machine code.
Continuous data, such as elevation, exist everywhere; discrete objects, such as roads, are either present or absent.
Vector data store discrete features as points, lines, and polygons, built from nodes, vertices, and line segments. The same entity can be a polygon at a large scale and a point at a small one (generalization).
Attributes are non-spatial information about features, stored in a table with one row per feature. Layers of one theme each stack into a map because they share a coordinate system.
Raster data store a grid of cells, each with one value. Its location comes from the origin and the cell size; smaller cells mean more detail, and more data.
Vector suits discrete objects; raster suits continuous surfaces. Common formats are the shapefile, GeoJSON, and KML for vector data, and GeoTIFF for rasters.
Metadata tell you who made the data, when, how, and how accurate they are. Without them you can’t judge whether data fit your purpose.

title: 11  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
11.7 Exercises

Entities on campus. List ten entities you pass on your way to class. For each, say whether you would store it as a point, a line, a polygon, or a raster, for a campus map at 1:5,000. Would any change for a map of all of Orange County?
Continuous or discrete? Classify each as continuous data or a discrete object, and explain your choice: air temperature, county boundaries, soil type, noise from an airport, bus stops, tree canopy cover.
Vector or raster? For each task, choose vector or raster data and explain why: (a) finding the shortest driving route between two addresses; (b) mapping the slope of the land across a county; (c) counting the trees within 10 m of a sidewalk; (d) mapping land cover from a satellite image.
Cell arithmetic. A raster covers an area 3 km wide and 2 km tall with 10 m cells. How many cells does it have? How many would it have with 30 m cells? Use R to check your answers.
Make a GeoJSON file. Go to https://geojson.io and draw a point at your favorite place on campus, a line along your route to class, and a polygon around a building. Look at the GeoJSON text. Which coordinates come first? Save the file and read it into R with sf::read_sf().
Read the metadata. Find a dataset on NC OneMap, https://www.nconemap.gov, and look at its metadata. Who made it, when, and in what coordinate system? Would you trust it to make a decision?

title: 11  What Is Geographic Data?
text:
11.8 Further reading

GIS Fundamentals: A First Text on Geographic Information Systems, by Paul Bolstad, covers data models, data structures, and file formats in more depth, with many diagrams.
Geocomputation with R (2nd ed.), by Robin Lovelace, Jakub Nowosad, and Jannes Muenchow, free at https://r.geocompx.org. Its “Geographic data in R” chapter explains how sf and terra store vector and raster data.
The GeoJSON standard, RFC 7946, at https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7946, is short and readable.

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
12.1 Where are we?
The last chapter showed that a map is a model of the world. This chapter takes on what I call the first central problem of spatial data in a computer: how do we represent the world in a computer?
Computers store numbers, not places. So every location has to become a pair of coordinates. Three building blocks make that possible:
We take them in that order.
How would you tell someone where you are right now? You might give:
All of these are valid ways to say where something is. But only coordinates are unambiguous, and easy for a computer to store, compare, and measure between. A landmark only helps people who know it, and “you are here” only works on that one map. Location always depends on what you measure from, and at what scale.

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
12  Location and Coordinate Systems
section: 12.2 Geodesy: the shape of the Earth
text:
12.2 Geodesy: the shape of the Earth

12.2.1 Measuring the Earth
Geodesy is the science of measuring the Earth’s size, shape, orientation, and gravity. Every coordinate you will ever use rests on a geodetic model of the Earth.
People have measured the Earth for a long time. Around 240 BCE, the Greek scholar Eratosthenes noticed that at noon on the summer solstice, the sun shone straight down a well in Syene, in southern Egypt. At the same moment in Alexandria, to the north, a vertical stick cast a shadow at an angle of about 7.2°. That is one-fiftieth of a circle, so he multiplied the distance between the cities by 50 to estimate the Earth’s circumference. His answer was close to the modern value of about 40,000 km. Just how close depends on the length of the stadion, the unit he used, which historians still argue about.


12.2.2 Sphere or ellipsoid?
Is the Earth a sphere? Close, but not quite. Because it spins, the Earth bulges at the Equator and is flattened at the poles. Its shape is an ellipsoid (also called a spheroid): a sphere squashed a little along its axis.

The semi-major axis, a, runs from the center to the Equator: about 6,378 km.
The semi-minor axis, b, runs from the center to a pole: about 6,357 km.

The difference is only 21 km, but it matters for precise mapping. We describe it with the flattening:
\[
f = \frac{a - b}{a} \approx \frac{1}{298}
\]
A sphere is fine for a small-scale map of the world. For anything precise, we use an ellipsoid. Different ellipsoids were fitted at different times and for different places. Clarke 1866 was fitted for North America; GRS80 and WGS84 fit the whole globe, and are almost identical to each other.
The real Earth is lumpier still. The surface that gravity defines, roughly where mean sea level would be if the oceans flowed under the continents, is called the geoid. The ellipsoid is the simplest smooth shape that comes close to it.
You can work out the flattening yourself from the WGS84 axes:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


12.2.3 Datums
An ellipsoid is a shape floating in space. A datum pins it to the real Earth. A geodetic datum says which ellipsoid to use and exactly where it sits relative to the Earth, so that a latitude and longitude point to one place on the ground.
On the ground, a datum is made real by thousands of surveyed control points. The brass disks you can find set into bridges, sidewalks, and mountain tops are benchmarks placed by the National Geodetic Survey. A witness post nearby often warns people not to disturb them.
Three datums show up again and again in North American data:



Table 12.1: Common datums in North America.










Datum
Ellipsoid
Notes




NAD27 (North American Datum of 1927)
Clarke 1866
Surveyed from one origin point, at Meades Ranch, Kansas


NAD83 (North American Datum of 1983)
GRS80
Centered on the Earth’s mass; readjusted several times; now maintained through CORS, a network of Continuously Operating Reference Stations


WGS84 (World Geodetic System 1984)
WGS84
The global datum that GPS uses






In North America, NAD83 and WGS84 differ by only a meter or two. But moving from NAD27 to NAD83 can shift a point by tens of meters or more. Change the datum and the same coordinates point to a different place on the ground, so always check which datum your data use.

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
12.3 Building a coordinate system
With a model of the Earth in hand, we can lay a grid on it. Building a coordinate system takes two anchors, and both come from the Earth’s rotation:

The poles. The North and South Poles are where the Earth’s spin axis meets the surface.
The Equator. The circle halfway between the poles. It is 0° latitude, and it divides the Northern Hemisphere from the Southern.

Then we draw the grid (Figure 12.1):

Parallels are lines of latitude. They run east–west, parallel to the Equator, and measure from 0° at the Equator to 90° north or south at the poles.
Meridians are lines of longitude. They run from pole to pole, meet at the poles, and measure from 0° to 180° east or west.

Unlike the Equator, the starting line for longitude has no natural place. It had to be agreed on. In 1884, an international conference chose the meridian through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, England, as the Prime Meridian, 0° longitude. (So the Prime Meridian is 0° W, or 0° E. And the Equator is 0° N, or 0° S. Zero is zero.)






Figure 12.1: The graticule on a globe. The Equator is in red and the Prime Meridian in blue. Parallels and meridians are drawn every 15°.



A full circle of longitude around the Earth is 360°. Latitude only covers 180°, from pole to pole.

12.3.1 The graticule
The graticule is the network of parallels and meridians drawn on a map. It is a reference grid, not data. Which lines should you show? Match the interval to the scale: every 30° on a world map, every 1° or less on a map of a state. Keep the lines thin and light so they don’t compete with the data. On many thematic maps you can leave them off.


12.3.2 A degree isn’t a fixed distance
Meridians meet at the poles, so the parallels get shorter as you move away from the Equator. One degree of latitude is always about 111 km. But one degree of longitude is about 111 km at the Equator, and shrinks to zero at the poles. It is roughly 111.32 km times the cosine of the latitude:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
At Chapel Hill’s latitude, a degree of longitude is about 90 km. This is why you can’t treat degrees as if they were meters. We’ll come back to it in Section 12.7.

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
12.4 Writing coordinates
There are two common ways to write the same angle:

Decimal degrees (DD) are a single signed number, such as −104.54°. Negative means south latitude or west longitude. This is the format GIS software and GPS units store.
Degrees, minutes, and seconds (DMS) split the angle into whole degrees, minutes (′), and seconds (″), such as 104° 32′ 24″ W. A letter, N, S, E, or W, replaces the sign.

There are 60 minutes in a degree and 60 seconds in a minute, so 3,600 seconds in a degree.
DD to DMS. Take the whole number of degrees. Multiply the decimal part by 60 to get minutes. Multiply the decimal part of that by 60 to get seconds. For −104.54°: 0.54 × 60 = 32.4′, and 0.4 × 60 = 24″. So −104.54° is 104° 32′ 24″ W.
DMS to DD. Add the parts back up: degrees + minutes / 60 + seconds / 3600, then add the sign.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
GIS software almost always wants decimal degrees, so this conversion comes up when you type in coordinates from older maps or documents.

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
12.5 Map projections
A grid on a globe is still not a flat map. Before we flatten it, it helps to see how the pieces stack up. Read Table 12.2 from the bottom up: each layer rests on the one below it.



Table 12.2: Building a projection, from the Earth up.









Layer
What it adds




Map projection
Flattens the curved grid onto a plane, in meters or feet


Geographic coordinate system
Latitude and longitude, in degrees


Datum
Pins the ellipsoid to the real Earth


Ellipsoid
A smooth mathematical model of the Earth’s shape


The Earth
Lumpy and irregular






If you change a lower layer, everything above it shifts. That is why two datasets must share a datum and a projection before they will line up.

12.5.1 Projecting the globe
A map projection is a method for moving the graticule from the globe to a flat surface. Picture a clear globe with a light bulb inside it. The bulb throws the shadow of the grid onto a sheet of paper. Wrap the paper into a cylinder around the globe, roll it into a cone, or hold it flat against one point, and you get the three classic projection surfaces: cylindrical, conic, and planar (or azimuthal).


12.5.2 Distortion
You can’t flatten an orange peel without stretching or tearing it, and you can’t flatten the globe without distortion. Every projection distorts at least one of four properties:

Shape
Area
Distance
Direction

The Mercator projection, for example, keeps local shapes and angles true, which made it ideal for navigation. But it badly inflates areas near the poles. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks about as big as Africa. In fact Africa is about 14 times larger. Greenland is about the same size as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, roughly 2.2 million km² against 2.3 million km². Compare the two red countries in Figure 12.2.






Figure 12.2: The world in four projections. Greenland and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in red, have almost the same area.



The first map in Figure 12.2 is not really a projection at all. It plots longitude as x and latitude as y, as if degrees were a flat grid. Many programs draw unprojected data this way, which is why a map of raw latitude and longitude looks stretched east–west away from the Equator.


12.5.3 Why distance distorts
Imagine a flat map surface that cuts through the ellipsoid along two lines, like a knife slicing an orange. A surface that cuts the globe this way is called secant. Along the two lines where the surfaces meet, called standard lines, the scale is exactly true. Between them, distances on the map shrink. Outside them, distances stretch. The farther you go from a standard line, the bigger the distortion. This is why projections designed for small areas, with standard lines close by, distort so little.


12.5.4 Projection families
Every projection is designed to keep some properties at the cost of others (Table 12.3).



Table 12.3: The four projection families and what each preserves.










Property
Preserves
Examples




Conformal
Local shape and angles
Mercator, Lambert Conformal Conic


Equal-area
Area
Albers Equal-Area Conic, Mollweide


Equidistant
Distance from one point, or along chosen lines
Azimuthal Equidistant, Equidistant Conic


Azimuthal
Direction from a center point
Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area, Gnomonic






The key trade-off: no projection can be both conformal and equal-area. Some compromise projections, such as Robinson, preserve nothing exactly but keep every distortion moderate, which is why they are popular for world maps.






TipThink about it



If you had to pick one projection for every map you will ever make, which would you choose, and why? What would go wrong with your choice for a map of the whole world? For a map of Chapel Hill?




12.5.5 The State Plane Coordinate System
For local work in the United States, surveyors and governments use the State Plane Coordinate System: a set of local projections, with one or more zones per state. Each zone is small enough to keep scale error under 1 part in 10,000. Zones that run long north–south use Transverse Mercator; zones that run long east–west use Lambert Conformal Conic. Coordinates are in feet or meters, not degrees.
North Carolina is wide from east to west, so it has a single Lambert Conformal Conic zone. That is the projection we use in this book: NAD83 / North Carolina, EPSG code 32119, in meters.

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
12.6 Choosing a projection
There is no single best projection. Two rules of thumb help you choose:
Fit your area. The smaller the area, the less distortion.

Working in Chapel Hill or Raleigh? The North Carolina State Plane zone (EPSG:32119).
Working across the Southeast? A UTM zone, such as UTM Zone 17N, or an Albers projection for the region.
Working across the lower 48 states? Albers Equal-Area Conic (EPSG:5070) is the standard.

Preserve what you measure.

Comparing areas or densities? Use an equal-area projection. Over a small area, such as a city, a conformal projection is close enough.
Measuring distances? Use an equidistant projection, or an azimuthal equidistant one centered on your starting point.
Measuring directions from a point? Use an azimuthal projection centered on that point.
Keeping shapes? Use a conformal projection.

And if you work with elevation data, make sure the horizontal units match the vertical ones. Mixing feet and meters wrecks slope and hillshade calculations.

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
12.7 Coordinate reference systems in R
In R, the datum, the coordinate system, and the projection travel together as a coordinate reference system (CRS). Every sf object carries one. Most are identified by an EPSG code, a number from a public registry: 4326 is WGS84 latitude and longitude, and 32119 is NC State Plane in meters.
Check a layer’s CRS with st_crs(), and change it with st_transform():
library(sf)

nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"))

st_crs(nc)$epsg          # 4267: NAD27, in degrees
st_crs(nc)$units         # NULL: a geographic CRS has no linear units

nc_sp <- nc |> st_transform(32119)
st_crs(nc_sp)$units      # "m"
st_transform() recalculates every coordinate. It is different from st_set_crs(), which only changes the label and leaves the numbers alone. Use st_set_crs() only when a layer has no CRS and you know what it should be.






Figure 12.3: North Carolina in WGS84 latitude and longitude (top) and in NC State Plane (bottom). The shape changes, and so do the units on the axes.




12.7.1 Degrees are not meters
Why does it matter? Chapel Hill and Raleigh are about 0.44 degrees apart. That number is not a distance you can use: a degree of longitude here is about 90 km, but a degree of latitude is about 111 km, so there’s no single factor to convert it. Measured properly, the two cities are about 40.5 km apart:
towns <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-79.0558, 35.9132)),   # Chapel Hill
                st_point(c(-78.6382, 35.7796)),   # Raleigh
                crs = 4326)

st_distance(towns)                       # about 40,465 m, on the ellipsoid
st_distance(st_transform(towns, 32119))  # about 40,530 m, in State Plane
For latitude and longitude, sf measures distance on the curved Earth, so st_distance() still returns meters. But many other operations, and many other programs, treat coordinates as if they were flat. Before you measure, buffer, or join by distance, check the CRS with st_crs() and project your data with st_transform(). And before you combine two layers, make sure they share the same CRS.

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
12.9 Summary

To store a location, a computer needs a datum (a model of the Earth tied to the ground), a coordinate system (a grid on that model), and a map projection (a way to flatten it).
Geodesy measures the Earth. Its shape is an ellipsoid, flattened at the poles by about 1/298. Common North American datums are NAD27, NAD83, and WGS84.
Latitude runs from 0° at the Equator to 90° at the poles along parallels; longitude runs 0° to 180° east or west of the Prime Meridian along meridians. The grid of both is the graticule.
Coordinates can be written in decimal degrees or degrees, minutes, and seconds. A degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles, so degrees are not a distance.
Every projection distorts shape, area, distance, or direction. Conformal, equal-area, equidistant, and azimuthal projections each protect one property, and none is both conformal and equal-area.
Choose a projection that fits your area and preserves what you measure. For North Carolina, use State Plane (EPSG:32119).
In R, check a layer’s CRS with st_crs() and change it with st_transform().

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
12.10 Exercises

Your own coordinates. Find the latitude and longitude of the building you’re in, using a phone or an online map. Write them in decimal degrees and in degrees, minutes, and seconds.
Eratosthenes. The distance from Syene to Alexandria was about 5,000 stadia, and the shadow angle was 7.2°. What circumference did Eratosthenes get, in stadia? If a stadion was 157.5 m, how far off was he from 40,075 km?
The true size. Use https://www.thetruesize.com to drag Greenland, Alaska, and North Carolina toward the Equator. What happens to their size on the Mercator map, and why?
Pick a projection. Choose a projection, and say why, for (a) a map comparing forest area in every country; (b) a map showing flight distances from RDU airport; (c) a map of parcels in Orange County.
Check the CRS. Load the nc data from the sf package (see Section 12.7). What datum is it in? Transform it to EPSG:32119 and to EPSG:5070, and plot all three. What changes?
Degrees and distance. Pick two towns in North Carolina, one north of the other, and two at the same latitude, about the same number of degrees apart. Use st_distance() to compare the distances. Explain the difference.

title: 12  Location and Coordinate Systems
text:
12.11 Further reading

GIS Fundamentals: A First Text on Geographic Information Systems, by Paul Bolstad, has a full chapter on geodesy, datums, map projections, and State Plane coordinates.
Geocomputation with R (2nd ed.), by Robin Lovelace, Jakub Nowosad, and Jannes Muenchow, free at https://r.geocompx.org. See the chapter “Reprojecting geographic data”.
Map Projections: A Working Manual, by John P. Snyder (U.S. Geological Survey, 1987), is the classic reference, free from the USGS.
The EPSG registry at https://epsg.io lets you search for any coordinate reference system by name or code.

title: 13  Census Data and APIs
text:
13.1 A brief history of the US Census
Most of the spatial data science you will do about people in the United States starts with Census data. Population, income, housing, commuting, education: if a question involves who lives where, the Census Bureau has probably measured it, for small areas, across the whole country, for free.
This chapter has two halves. The first covers what the data are: where they come from, how Census geography is organized, and which variables you will use most. The second covers how to get them: what an API is, how to make a request by hand, and how the tidycensus package turns that request into one line of R that returns a map-ready data frame.
Article I of the Constitution requires a count of the population every ten years so that seats in the House of Representatives can be apportioned among the states. The first census, in 1790, was carried out by U.S. marshals on horseback and counted 3.9 million people. The count has run every decade since.
The Census Bureau has repeatedly pushed new technology into being because the job of counting a growing country kept outgrowing the old tools (Table 13.1). Herman Hollerith’s punch-card tabulating machines, built for the 1890 census, led to the company that became IBM. A century later, the 1990 census introduced TIGER, one of the first national digital map databases. The boundary files you will download later in this chapter descend directly from it.
For our purposes the most important change is the one from 2005. Before then, detailed social and economic questions (income, education, commuting) were asked on a “long form” sent to a sample of households once a decade. Since 2005 those questions have moved to the American Community Survey, which samples households every year. That gives two distinct sources of Census data, and you will choose between them constantly:

text:
Table 13.1: Milestones in the history of the US Census.










Year
Milestone
What changed

The decennial census is a full count of everyone, every ten years. It asks only a few questions (age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, household relationship, housing tenure), but it covers every person.
The American Community Survey (ACS) is a continuous sample survey. It asks many more questions, but every number it publishes is an estimate, with a margin of error (Section 13.7.1).


13.1.1 The moving center of population
Each census, the Bureau calculates the mean center of population: the point where a flat map of the United States would balance if every resident weighed the same. In 1790 it sat in Kent County, Maryland, on the Eastern Shore. By 2020 it had moved about 884 miles, in a straight line, to Wright County, Missouri (Figure 13.1) (U.S. Census Bureau, n.d.).

lower48 <- states(cb = TRUE, resolution = "20m", year = 2020) |>
  filter(!STUSPS %in% c("AK", "HI", "PR")) |>
  st_transform(5070)

# Draw each series as its own path, plus a dashed link between the two 1950 points
paths <- centers |>
  group_by(extent) |>
  summarize(do_union = FALSE) |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING")

link_1950 <- centers |>
  filter(year == 1950) |>
  summarize(do_union = FALSE) |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING")

labeled <- centers |>
  filter(year %in% c(1790, 1850, 1900, 1950, 2020), extent == "Lower 48" | year == 2020)

# Zoom to the eastern two-thirds of the country, where the path lies
zoom <- st_bbox(st_buffer(centers, 600000))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = lower48, fill = "#f6efe0", color = "#b9ad97", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = link_1950, color = "#3b5b7a", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = paths, color = "#3b5b7a", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = centers, aes(fill = year), shape = 21, size = 2.6, color = "white", stroke = 0.4) +
  geom_sf_label(
    data = labeled, aes(label = year), nudge_y = 75000,
    size = 3.2, label.size = 0, fill = alpha("white", 0.8)
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#9fb7cc", high = "#1d3550", name = "Census year") +
  coord_sf(xlim = zoom[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = zoom[c("ymin", "ymax")], expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"))







Figure 13.1: Mean center of US population at each census, 1790–2020. Centers through 1950 are for the lower 48 states; from 1950 on they include Alaska and Hawaii, which pulls the 1950 point slightly west and south (dashed link). Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Centers of Population, 1790–2020.





The path tells the story of American settlement. Through the 1800s the center moved almost straight west as settlement pushed across the continent, fastest before 1900. After 1950 it bent southwest as the Sun Belt grew, and it has been in Missouri since 1980.






TipThink about it



Which direction do you expect the center of population to move by 2030? What trends in migration, birth rates, or immigration would push it further west, further south, or back east?

title: 13  Census Data and APIs
text:
13.2 Census geography
Census data are always published for areas, never for individual people or addresses. Understanding how those areas are defined, and how they fit together, is the first step in using the data well.






Figure 13.2: The standard hierarchy of Census geographic entities. The central spine, from the nation down to blocks, nests completely. The entities branching off it do not. Source: U.S. Census Bureau.



Figure 13.2 shows the standard hierarchy. The central spine runs from the nation to regions, divisions, states, counties, census tracts, block groups, and finally blocks. Every unit on the spine nests perfectly: each block lies inside exactly one block group, which lies inside exactly one tract, one county, and one state. That nesting is what makes the spine so useful. You can add blocks up to block groups, block groups to tracts, and so on, and never double-count anyone.
The geographies that branch off the spine, such as ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, places (cities and towns), and congressional districts, are built from blocks too, but they do not nest neatly inside counties or tracts. A ZIP code can cross county lines, and a city can include parts of several tracts. When you have a choice, work on the spine.
The three smallest units on the spine are the ones you will use most for local analysis. Figure 13.3 shows all three for Orange County, North Carolina.

orange_tracts <- tracts("NC", "Orange", year = 2020)
orange_bgs    <- block_groups("NC", "Orange", year = 2020)
orange_blocks <- blocks("NC", "Orange", year = 2020)

geo_levels <- bind_rows(
  orange_tracts |> transmute(level = "Tracts"),
  orange_bgs    |> transmute(level = "Block groups"),
  orange_blocks |> transmute(level = "Blocks")
) |>
  mutate(level = fct_inorder(level))

ggplot(geo_levels) +
  geom_sf(fill = "#f6efe0", color = "#3b5b7a", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~level) +
  theme_void()







Figure 13.3: Census tracts, block groups, and blocks in Orange County, North Carolina (2020 boundaries). Each level subdivides the one above it.





Census blocks are the smallest unit. A block is often a single city block bounded by streets, but blocks are bounded by any visible feature (railroads, streams, shorelines) and in rural areas can be large. Only the decennial census is published for blocks, and in 2020 block-level data carry the most differential-privacy noise (Section 13.7.3), so use them with care.
Block groups combine several blocks and usually hold 600 to 3,000 people. They are the smallest geography for which ACS 5-year estimates are published, which makes them the finest level available for most social and economic variables. That detail comes at a cost: block group estimates have large margins of error.
Census tracts combine block groups and typically hold 1,200 to 8,000 people, about 4,000 on average. They are drawn to be fairly similar in population and stable over time, which makes them the workhorse unit for neighborhood analysis. Their boundaries are still revised each decade, though, so comparisons across censuses take care (Section 13.7.4).

13.2.1 FIPS codes and GEOIDs
Every Census area has a unique identifier called a GEOID, built by stringing together FIPS codes (Federal Information Processing Standards codes) for each level of the hierarchy. FIPS codes are standard numeric IDs for states and counties: North Carolina is 37 and Orange County is 135.

WarningKeep GEOIDs as text



GEOIDs look like numbers, but treat them as text. Alabama’s state FIPS code is 01. Read it as a number and it becomes 1, every Alabama GEOID loses a digit, and your joins quietly fail. When you read a CSV, set the column type explicitly, for example read_csv(file, col_types = cols(GEOID = col_character())).


The GEOID is also the key you will join on. Census tables and Census boundary files both carry a GEOID column, so attaching data to shapes is a single left_join() on that field. (Chapter 15 covers joins in detail.)

Not every table is published for every geography. As areas get smaller, the Bureau publishes fewer tables and adds more noise to protect privacy. Table 13.3 summarizes the 2020 decennial products.

title: 13  Census Data and APIs
text:
13.4 What is an API?
You could get any of the variables above by clicking through data.census.gov and downloading a CSV. For a one-off table that works. For anything you want to repeat, share, or scale up, it is far better to ask for the data from code, through an API.
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules for how one program asks another for data or services. Your R script is one program; the Census Bureau’s server is the other. Your script sends a request, and the server sends back data (Figure 13.4).







flowchart LR
  A["Your code<br/>(R script)"] -- "request" --> B{{"API"}}
  B -- "request" --> C["Their server<br/>(Census Bureau)"]
  C -- "data" --> B
  B -- "data" --> A




Figure 13.4: An API sits between your code and someone else’s server. Your code sends a request in an agreed format, and the server returns data.





A restaurant menu is a useful analogy. The menu lists what you can order and how to ask for it. You never see the kitchen, and you get back exactly what you ordered, as long as you ordered something on the menu.

13.4.1 Web APIs: URLs in, JSON out
Most data APIs on the web follow a style called REST. Three ideas cover almost everything you need:

Every dataset or service has its own web address, called an endpoint. The 2022 ACS 5-year data live at https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs5.
Requests are ordinary HTTP requests, the same thing your browser sends when it loads a page. A GET request reads data; a POST request sends data. Data APIs mostly use GET.
Responses usually come back as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), structured text that R can turn into lists or data frames.



13.4.2 Anatomy of a request
A REST request is just a URL with two parts: the endpoint, which says which service to call, and the parameters, which say what you want from it. A ? separates the two, each parameter is written name=value, and an & separates parameters.
Here is a request to Esri’s geocoding service that looks up one address:
https://geocode.arcgis.com/arcgis/rest/services/World/GeocodeServer/findAddressCandidates?singleLine=380%20new%20york%20st%20redlands%20ca&f=pjson
Everything before the ? is the endpoint. singleLine is the address to look up (%20 is how a space is written inside a URL), and f=pjson asks for pretty-printed JSON. Paste that URL into a browser and you will see the JSON response.
Here is a Census API request with the same structure. It asks for median household income for every county in North Carolina:
https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs5?get=NAME,B19013_001E&for=county:*&in=state:37
get lists the variables, for picks the geography (county:* means every county), and in limits the request to state 37, North Carolina.


13.4.3 Why use an API?
APIs take a little more setup than a download button. They pay that back in four ways:

Reproducible. Your script is an exact record of what you downloaded, so you, a classmate, or a reviewer can rerun it and get the same data.
Targeted. Parameters return only the variables and places you need.
Current. You pull fresh data each time you run the script, instead of keeping stale files around.
Scalable. One loop can request every state, or every year.

These benefits might not seem like much the first time you download a table. They matter the second time you need the same data, or when someone asks exactly how you got it.

title: 13  Census Data and APIs
text:
13.5 Calling an API from R
There are two ways to call an API from R: build the request yourself, or use a package that wraps the API for you. It is worth seeing both, because a wrapper package won’t always exist.

13.5.1 Step 0: get and store a key
The Census API asks you to identify yourself with a free key. Request one at https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html; it arrives by email within a few minutes. Then store it once:

tidycensus::census_api_key("YOUR KEY HERE", install = TRUE)

install = TRUE writes the key to your .Renviron file as CENSUS_API_KEY, so R loads it at the start of every session. Restart R after you run this. From then on, your code reads the key with Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY").






WarningKeep keys out of your scripts



Never paste an API key directly into a script or Quarto document you might share or push to GitHub. Anyone who has your key can use it as you. Store it in .Renviron, which stays on your computer.




13.5.2 By hand, with httr2
Every manual API call follows the same steps, whatever the service (Table 13.5).



Table 13.5: The steps of a manual API call.











Step
Task
R functions
What happens




0
Get a key
Sys.setenv() or .Renviron
Sign up once; keep the key out of your script


1
Build the request
request(), req_url_query()
Endpoint URL plus parameters


2
Send it
req_perform()
R sends an HTTP GET and waits for the reply


3
Parse the response
resp_body_json()
Turn JSON text into a list or matrix


4
Analyze
dplyr, sf, tmap
Clean, join to geometry, and map






Here are steps 1 to 3 for the North Carolina income request, using httr2:

library(httr2)

resp <- request("https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs5") |>
  req_url_query(
    get   = "NAME,B19013_001E",
    `for` = "county:*",
    `in`  = "state:37",
    key   = Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")
  ) |>
  req_perform()

nc_raw <- resp_body_json(resp, simplifyVector = TRUE)
head(nc_raw)

for and in are reserved words in R, so they need backticks when used as argument names. Look at what comes back: a matrix of text, with the column names in the first row and every value, including income, stored as a string. Step 4 starts with cleaning it:

colnames(nc_raw) <- nc_raw[1, ]

nc_manual <- as_tibble(nc_raw[-1, ]) |>
  transmute(
    GEOID  = paste0(state, county),
    NAME,
    income = as.numeric(B19013_001E)
  )

nc_manual



13.5.3 With a package: tidycensus
tidycensus (Walker and Herman, n.d.) does steps 1 through 3, and most of step 4, for you. This single call builds the same URL behind the scenes, sends it, and returns a tidy data frame:

nc_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B19013_001",
  state     = "NC",
  year      = 2022
)

nc_income

The result has one row per county with GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate, and moe (margin of error) columns. The rest of this chapter uses tidycensus. Similar wrapper packages exist for other services: tigris for Census boundary files and arcpullr for Esri REST services, for example. When there is no package for the API you need, the httr2 pattern above will always work.

title: 13  Census Data and APIs
section: 13.6 Worked example: mapping young children in North Carolina
text:
13.6 Worked example: mapping young children in North Carolina
This section puts the pieces together. The goal is to map the share of each North Carolina census tract’s population that is under 5 years old.

13.6.1 Find the variables
load_variables() downloads the full list of variables for a dataset and year:

vars_acs5 <- load_variables(2022, "acs5", cache = TRUE)

vars_acs5 |>
  filter(str_detect(name, "^B01001_")) |>
  head(5)

The result has a name column (the code), a label describing the line, a concept naming the table, and the smallest geography it is published for. In RStudio, View(vars_acs5) opens it in a searchable viewer. You can also filter it in code, for example filter(vars_acs5, str_detect(concept, "SEX BY AGE")). cache = TRUE saves the list so it loads instantly next time.
Searching the labels shows that table B01001, Sex by Age, has what we need: the total (_001), males under 5 (_003), and females under 5 (_027).






WarningCheck the concept, not just the label



Many ACS tables come in lettered versions for single race groups. B01001A is Sex by Age (White Alone) and B01001B is Sex by Age (Black or African American Alone). Their lines have the same labels as B01001, so it is easy to grab the wrong one. Always check the concept column.




13.6.2 Download data with geometry
get_acs() with geometry = TRUE downloads the tract boundaries along with the data and joins them on GEOID, so the result is an sf object, ready to map:

nc_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(total    = "B01001_001",
                male_u5  = "B01001_003",
                female_u5 = "B01001_027"),
  state     = "NC",
  year      = 2022,
  output    = "wide",
  geometry  = TRUE
)

nc_tracts

Naming the variables (total = "B01001_001") gives the output columns readable names. output = "wide" puts each variable in its own pair of columns: totalE and totalM for the estimate and margin of error, and so on.


13.6.3 Calculate and map
Now add the two under-5 counts, divide by the total, and map the result. moe_sum() and moe_prop() carry the margins of error through the calculation (Section 13.7.1):

nc_under5 <- nc_tracts |>
  mutate(
    under5E   = male_u5E + female_u5E,
    under5M   = map2_dbl(male_u5M, female_u5M, \(a, b) moe_sum(c(a, b))),
    pct_u5    = under5E / totalE * 100,
    pct_u5_moe = moe_prop(under5E, totalE, under5M, totalM) * 100
  )

tm_shape(nc_under5) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill       = "pct_u5",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "% under 5"),
    lwd        = 0.2
  )

A handful of tracts have no value. These are tracts where no one lives, such as national forests, military training areas, or open water, so the percentage would mean dividing by zero. Before you interpret the map, remember that each tract’s value is an estimate. Small tracts can have margins of error nearly as large as the estimate itself, so a single dark tract may reflect sampling noise as much as a real pattern.






NoteTry it



Change the code above to map the share of each county’s population that is 65 or older. You will need several lines of B01001 for each sex. Use load_variables() to find them.

title: 13  Census Data and APIs
text:
13.7 Going further with tidycensus
The worked example covers the most common case. This section covers what you need to know once you are past your first download.

13.7.1 Margins of error
Every ACS value is an estimate from a sample, and tidycensus returns a margin of error (moe) alongside each estimate. ACS margins of error use a 90% confidence level: there is a 90% chance that the true value lies within estimate ± moe.
The smaller the area, the smaller the sample behind it, and the larger the margin of error relative to the estimate. A useful way to judge reliability is the coefficient of variation (CV): the standard error as a percentage of the estimate. Divide the MOE by 1.645 to get the standard error, then divide by the estimate:
\[
CV = \frac{MOE / 1.645}{\text{estimate}} \times 100
\]

nc_income |>
  mutate(cv = (moe / 1.645) / estimate * 100) |>
  arrange(desc(cv)) |>
  head()

There is no single official cutoff, but a common rule of thumb treats estimates with a CV above about 30% as unreliable: report them with caution, or combine areas or years to get a larger sample (U.S. Census Bureau 2020).
When you combine estimates you must also combine their margins of error, and you can’t just add them. tidycensus provides functions for the standard formulas: moe_sum() for sums, moe_prop() for proportions, moe_ratio() for ratios, and moe_product() for products.


13.7.2 Calculating percentages
Raw counts mostly tell you where people live. A map of the number of renters looks a lot like a map of population. To compare places, convert counts to shares.
The summary_var argument adds a second variable, usually the table total, to every row as summary_est and summary_moe. That puts the numerator and denominator side by side, so the share is a single division:

nc_white <- get_acs(
  geography   = "county",
  variables   = "B02001_002",
  summary_var = "B02001_001",
  state       = "NC",
  year        = 2022
) |>
  mutate(
    pct     = estimate / summary_est * 100,
    pct_moe = moe_prop(estimate, summary_est, moe, summary_moe) * 100
  )

nc_white |> select(NAME, estimate, summary_est, pct, pct_moe)



13.7.3 Decennial Census data
get_decennial() works like get_acs() but pulls from the full-count decennial census. Because these are counts rather than sample estimates, there is no moe column. For 2020, choose the summary file with sumfile: "pl" for the redistricting counts (available down to blocks) or "dhc" for more detailed age, sex, household, and housing tables.

nc_pop <- get_decennial(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = "P1_001N",
  state     = "NC",
  year      = 2020,
  sumfile   = "dhc"
)

nc_pop

“Full count” does not mean “exact.” To protect respondents’ privacy, the 2020 census applied differential privacy: carefully calibrated statistical noise added to published tables. The noise is negligible for states and counties but can be substantial for blocks, especially for small population groups. Treat individual block counts with caution, and aggregate blocks where you can.


13.7.4 Comparing across years
Change over time is one of the most interesting things to measure with Census data, and one of the easiest to get wrong. Four traps to watch for:

Boundaries change. Tract and block group boundaries are redrawn every ten years. A GEOID from 2010 and the same GEOID in 2020 may not describe the same place. ACS releases from 2020 on use 2020 boundaries.
5-year periods overlap. The 2017–2021 and 2018–2022 estimates share four years of responses, so differences between them are muted. Compare non-overlapping periods, such as 2013–2017 and 2018–2022.
Dollars are nominal. Income, rent, and home values are reported in dollars of their own period. Adjust for inflation before comparing.
Codes change. Tables and lines are occasionally renumbered or redefined. Check load_variables() for every year you use.

get_acs() returns one year per call. To pull several, loop over the years with purrr and stack the results:

years <- c(2012, 2017, 2022)  # non-overlapping 5-year periods

nc_income_years <- map(years, \(y) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = "B19013_001",
    state     = "NC",
    year      = y
  ) |>
    mutate(year = y)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

nc_income_years |> filter(NAME == "Orange County, North Carolina")

The 2012, 2017, and 2022 releases cover 2008–2012, 2013–2017, and 2018–2022, so they do not overlap. The income values are still in nominal dollars.


13.7.5 More tidycensus functions
tidycensus can do much more than get_acs() and get_decennial(). Table 13.6 lists some of the most useful extras.



Table 13.6: Other tidycensus functions and arguments.










Function or argument
What it returns
Example use




get_estimates()
Annual population estimates and components of change
County population growth since 2020


get_pums()
Individual and household ACS microdata
Custom tabulations not in published tables


get_flows()
County-to-county migration flows
Where people moving into a county came from


table = "B19001"
Every variable in one ACS table
Full household income distribution in one call


survey = "acs1"
1-year ACS estimates
Recent data for large counties and metros


tigris::erase_water()
Geometry with water areas removed
Cleaner maps along coasts and lakes

title: 13  Census Data and APIs
text:
13.8 Summary

US Census data come from two main sources: the decennial census, a full count every ten years with few questions, and the American Community Survey, a continuous sample with many questions and a margin of error on every estimate.
Census geography nests from the nation down to tracts, block groups, and blocks. Every area has a GEOID built from FIPS codes. Keep GEOIDs as text and join on them.
Smaller areas mean more detail but fewer published tables, more privacy noise, and larger margins of error. ACS 5-year estimates are the only ACS product for tracts and block groups.
An API lets your code request data from a server. A REST request is an endpoint URL plus parameters, and the response is usually JSON.
tidycensus wraps the Census API: get_acs() and get_decennial() return tidy data frames, and geometry = TRUE makes them map-ready.
Convert counts to shares with summary_var, carry margins of error through calculations with the moe_*() functions, and compare across years only with non-overlapping periods, consistent boundaries, and inflation-adjusted dollars.

title: 13  Census Data and APIs
text:
13.9 Exercises

Reading GEOIDs. The GEOID 370630020271003 identifies a Census block. Which state, county, tract, and block group does it belong to? How many digits does each part have?
Choosing a source. For each question, name the survey (decennial, ACS 1-year, or ACS 5-year) and the smallest geography you could use. (a) How many housing units are in each block in Durham? (b) What was median household income in Wake County last year? (c) What share of residents in each Chapel Hill neighborhood rent their home?
Build a URL. Write by hand the Census API URL that requests total population (B01003_001E) for every county in Virginia (state FIPS 51) from the 2022 ACS 5-year data. Paste it into a browser to check it. Then reproduce the same request with httr2.
Reliability. Download median household income for every block group in Orange County, NC. What share of block groups have a CV above 30%? Repeat for tracts and compare.
A rate map. Map the share of households with no vehicle available for tracts in your home county, or in Mecklenburg County, NC. Use B25044 and include the margin of error of the share.
Change over time. Compare median gross rent (B25064_001) for North Carolina counties in the 2013–2017 and 2018–2022 ACS. Which counties saw the largest increase? Explain why you should adjust for inflation, and what else could make your comparison misleading.
Your own question. Return to the question you wrote down in Section 13.3. Download the data you need, make a map, and write one paragraph interpreting it, including what the margins of error tell you about your confidence.

title: 13  Census Data and APIs
text:
13.10 Further reading

Kyle Walker, the author of tidycensus, has written a free online book, Analyzing US Census Data: Methods, Maps, and Models in R (Walker 2023). It covers everything in this chapter in more depth and is the best next step for any project that uses Census data.
The tidycensus documentation, at https://walker-data.com/tidycensus, has vignettes on spatial data, margins of error, and microdata.
The Census Bureau’s ACS handbooks explain how the survey works and how to handle margins of error (U.S. Census Bureau 2020).
To browse tables without code, use data.census.gov, then bring the variable codes you find back to load_variables() and tidycensus.




The full count of everyone in the US, every ten years. It asks only a
few questions but covers every person.
The Census Bureau’s continuous survey of a sample of households every
year. It asks many more questions than the decennial census, but every
value is an estimate with a margin of error.
The unique ID of a Census area, made by stringing together the FIPS
codes of each level, such as 37135 for Orange County, NC.
Keep GEOIDs as text, and join tables on them.
In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as
months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic,
such as median income; each Census variable has a code.
The specific, answerable question a project sets out to answer, usually
with a place and a time.
Application Programming Interface: a set of rules for how one program
asks another for data or services, such as your R script asking the
Census Bureau’s server for a table.
An R package that downloads US Census data through the Census API and
returns it as a tidy data frame, with boundaries attached if you ask.
How far a sample estimate might be from the true value. ACS margins of
error use a 90% confidence level: there is a 90% chance the true value
lies within the estimate plus or minus the MOE.
The use of data that have a location attached to answer questions about
the world. It combines what we study (the spatial), how we
handle it (data skills), and how we ask and answer questions
(science).
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
R’s table: rows are observations and columns are variables. A tibble is
the tidyverse’s version of a data frame.
Dividing the seats in the House of Representatives among the states by
population, the reason the Constitution requires a census.
The Census Bureau’s national digital map database of streets and
boundaries, first used for the 1990 census. Census boundary files come
from it.
A subset of a population that is surveyed to estimate something about
the whole population. Smaller samples give less certain estimates.
Carefully calibrated random noise added to published 2020 census tables
to protect respondents’ privacy. It matters most for small areas such as
blocks.
The point where a flat map of the country would balance if every
resident weighed the same.
The average x coordinate and average y coordinate of a set of features.
Like the mean, outliers pull it.
The smallest Census geography, often a single city block bounded by
streets or other visible features. Only decennial census data are
published for blocks.
When every smaller area lies entirely inside exactly one larger area, as
blocks do inside block groups, tracts, and counties. Nested areas can be
added up without double-counting anyone.
A small area of about 1,200 to 8,000 people (4,000 on average), drawn to
be fairly stable over time. The workhorse unit for neighborhood
analysis.
A group of census blocks, usually holding 600 to 3,000 people. It is the
smallest geography with ACS 5-year estimates.
The Census Bureau’s approximation of a ZIP code’s area, built from
census blocks. ZCTAs do not nest inside counties or tracts.
ACS estimates that pool 60 months of responses. They are the most
reliable ACS product and the only one for tracts and block groups. An
estimate labeled 2022 describes 2018 to 2022.
A standard numeric code for a state or county (Federal Information
Processing Standards). North Carolina is 37.
Combining two tables by matching rows on a shared key column, such as
attaching Census data to boundaries by GEOID with
left_join().
A plain-text table in which each line is a row and commas separate the
values. Read one into R with read.csv() or
read_csv().
The first 2020 census product: basic population, race, voting-age, and
housing counts down to the block, used to redraw voting districts.
The 2020 census product with more detailed tables on age, sex,
households, and housing than the redistricting data.
ACS estimates from 12 months of responses. They are the most current but
are only published for areas of 65,000 people or more.
An input to a function, written inside its parentheses.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
The number you divide by to turn a count into a share, usually the total
of the same table, such as total population.
A set of lines and blocks of code that work together to do a whole job.
R runs a program from top to bottom, so order matters.
A plain file of R code, ending in .R. Anything that isn’t
code must be written as a comment.
The most common style of web API: each dataset has its own URL, you ask
for data with ordinary web requests, and the answer usually comes back
as JSON.
The web address of one dataset or service in an API, such as
https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs5.
The protocol web browsers and servers use to talk. A GET
request reads data; a POST request sends data.
JavaScript Object Notation: structured text that most web APIs send
back, which R can turn into lists or data frames.
A name=value setting added to an API request after the
?, such as for=county:*, that says what you
want.
Turning an address or place name into coordinates that can be mapped.
The ability for anyone to rerun an analysis from its code and data and
get the same result.
An R package that hides the details of calling an API behind simple
functions, such as tidycensus for the Census API.
A private code that identifies you to an API. Store it in
.Renviron, never in a script you share.
The newer successor to R Markdown, from the same developers. Quarto
files end in .qmd. This book is written in Quarto.
Code that takes inputs (arguments), does a job, and returns an output,
such as mean(temps).
The tidyverse package for transforming data frames: filtering rows,
choosing columns, adding new columns, joining tables, and summarizing.
“Simple features”: the R package for spatial vector data. An sf object
is a data frame with a geometry column holding each row’s point, line,
or polygon.
An R package for making thematic maps quickly, with sensible defaults.
An R package for building, sending, and reading web (HTTP) requests,
used to call an API by hand.
An R package that downloads Census boundary files (TIGER/Line
shapefiles) as sf objects.
An R package that downloads layers from ArcGIS REST services as sf
objects, with get_spatial_layer().
The integrated development environment (IDE) where you write and run R.
R does the computing; RStudio is the workspace around it.
How sure you can be that the true value lies within a range. The ACS
uses a 90% confidence level for its margins of error.
The standard error as a percentage of the estimate. A CV above about 30%
is a common sign that an estimate is unreliable.
A measure of how much a sample estimate would vary from sample to
sample. For the ACS, it is the margin of error divided by 1.645.
Dollar amounts as reported in their own year, not adjusted for
inflation. Adjust them before comparing across years.
The tidyverse package for repeating a task over many inputs, such as
downloading data for several years.
Records for individual people or households (with identifying details
removed), rather than totals for areas. The ACS publishes microdata as
PUMS.



U.S. Census Bureau. 2020. Understanding and Using American Community Survey Data: What All Data Users Need to Know. U.S. Government Publishing Office. https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/library/handbooks/general.html.


U.S. Census Bureau. n.d. Centers of Population, 1790–2020. https://www.census.gov/geographies/reference-files/time-series/geo/centers-population.html.


Walker, Kyle. 2023. Analyzing US Census Data: Methods, Maps, and Models in R. CRC Press. https://walker-data.com/census-r.


Walker, Kyle, and Matt Herman. n.d. Tidycensus: Load US Census Boundary and Attribute Data as ’Tidyverse’ and ’Sf’-Ready Data Frames. https://walker-data.com/tidycensus.

title: 14  ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
text:
14.1 Recap: APIs
Chapter 13 showed how an API lets your code ask another program’s server for data, using the Census Bureau’s API and the tidycensus package. This chapter uses the same idea for a different, and very common, source of GIS data: layers published with Esri’s ArcGIS software. By the end of it you’ll load a layer from North Carolina’s statewide GIS portal, NC OneMap, straight into R and map it.
An API is a set of rules that lets your code request data from another program’s server. The pattern is always the same: request, then response. Your code sends an endpoint URL, often with parameters that say what you want, and the server sends data back, usually as JSON.
Why bother, when you could click a Download button? Two reasons from Chapter 13 still apply:
tidycensus is a wrapper package for the Census API. Today’s wrapper package is arcpullr, for ArcGIS servers.

title: 14  ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
text:
Reproducibility. Your script is the record of exactly where the data came from and how you got them. Anyone can rerun it.
Efficiency. You download only the data you need, not a whole statewide file.

title: 14  ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
text:
14.2 ArcGIS portals and feature services
Thousands of government agencies, universities, and companies publish their GIS data online through ArcGIS Online or ArcGIS Enterprise, Esri’s systems for sharing maps and data on the web. Many run a public portal: a website where you can search, preview, and download their layers. North Carolina’s is NC OneMap, https://www.nconemap.gov/, which gathers layers from state agencies, counties, and cities: roads, parcels, schools, hospitals, flood zones, and much more.
Behind the website, each published layer lives on an ArcGIS server. A layer published as a feature service (or as one layer of a map service) has its own REST endpoint: a URL that returns the layer’s features and attributes when your code asks for them. arcpullr is an R package that sends a request to that endpoint and returns the layer as an sf object, ready for the dplyr, sf, and tmap tools you already know.
When you search a portal, look at the type of each result. “Feature Service” or “Feature Layer” marks a layer arcpullr can read (Figure 14.1). Other items, such as documents, web maps, and apps, are not.






Figure 14.1: Searching NC OneMap for health data. Each result’s Type line says what kind of item it is; “Feature Service” marks a layer arcpullr can read.

title: 14  ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
text:
14.3 Finding a layer’s REST URL
arcpullr needs one thing from you: the layer’s REST URL. Here is how to find it on NC OneMap, using the Medical Facilities layer. The same steps work on most ArcGIS Online and ArcGIS Enterprise portals.

Search NC OneMap for a dataset, such as “medical facilities”.
Open its item page. Check that the details panel on the left says it is a feature layer.
Click “I want to use this” at the bottom of the details panel (Figure 14.2).
Choose “View Data Source” from the list that opens (Figure 14.3). It opens the layer’s REST service page in a new tab.
Copy that page’s URL from the address bar. That URL is what arcpullr needs.







Figure 14.2: The Medical Facilities item page on NC OneMap. The details panel on the left describes the layer; “I want to use this” is at its bottom.









Figure 14.3: The “I want to…” menu. “View Data Source” opens the layer’s REST service page.




14.3.1 Reading the REST Services Directory page
The page that opens is the layer’s page in the ArcGIS REST Services Directory (Figure 14.4). It is plain, but it holds everything you need to know before you write any code:






Figure 14.4: The ArcGIS REST Services Directory page for the Medical Facilities layer. Its URL is the layer’s REST endpoint.




The URL. https://services.nconemap.gov/secure/rest/services/NC1Map_Health/MapServer/2. The number at the end, 2, is the layer ID: this service holds several layers, and Medical Facilities is number 2. If you copy a URL without the number, you have the whole service, not one layer.
Geometry Type. esriGeometryPoint, so each feature is a point. Others are polylines and polygons.
MaxRecordCount. 2,000: the most features the server returns for one request.
Fields. Further down the page, a list of the attribute columns and their types. You need these names to filter the layer.

The item page reports 6,814 records, more than the 2,000 the server returns at once. You don’t need to worry about that: arcpullr asks for the features in batches and puts them back together. Still, check that the number of rows you get matches what the portal reports.

title: 14  ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
text:
14.4 Anatomy of an arcpullr request
Install arcpullr once, in the Console, with install.packages("arcpullr"). Then:
library(arcpullr)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

url <- "https://services.nconemap.gov/secure/rest/services/NC1Map_Health/MapServer/2"
medical.centers <- get_spatial_layer(url, where = "fcounty = 'Orange'")
Line by line:

url stores the REST endpoint you copied from the service page.
get_spatial_layer() sends the request and returns the layer as an sf object.
where = is a filter, written in SQL, that runs on the server. Here fcounty = 'Orange' returns only the facilities in Orange County. Without a where argument, you get every feature in the layer.


14.4.1 Writing a where clause
The where argument is a small piece of SQL, the language of databases, that the server applies before it sends anything back. It uses the field names from the REST page, not the ones you might rename later in R. A few rules cover most needs:



Table 14.1: Common where clauses. The field names are examples; use the fields listed on your layer’s REST page.





You want
where =




Text equal to a value
"fcounty = 'Orange'"


One of several values
"fcounty IN ('Orange', 'Durham', 'Wake')"


A number above a value
"beds > 100"


Two conditions
"fcounty = 'Orange' AND beds > 100"


Text that starts with something
"fcounty LIKE 'Ch%'"






Note the quotes: the whole clause is an R string in double quotes, and text values inside it go in single quotes. SQL uses =, not ==, and AND and OR, not & and |.
Why filter on the server instead of downloading everything and using filter() in R? For a statewide layer of a few thousand points, either works. But many layers are far bigger: every parcel or building in the state. Filtering on the server means less data crosses the internet, the request is faster, and you never hit the server’s limits. It also makes your script say exactly which part of the data you used.






TipThink about it



The REST page says the Medical Facilities layer was “geocoded from the facilities database”. What could go wrong with locations made that way (Chapter 13)? How might you check a few of them?

title: 14  ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
text:
14.5 Two requests, one map
Here are two requests to the same layer: one for every medical facility, and one for Orange County only. tmap draws all of them in black, then the Orange County facilities in red on top (Figure 14.5):
url <- "https://services.nconemap.gov/secure/rest/services/NC1Map_Health/MapServer/2"
all.medical.centers    <- get_spatial_layer(url)
orange.medical.centers <- get_spatial_layer(url, where = "fcounty = 'Orange'")

tm_shape(all.medical.centers) +
  tm_dots() +
  tm_shape(orange.medical.centers) +
  tm_dots(fill = "red")






Figure 14.5: Medical facilities from NC OneMap: every facility in black, and those in Orange County, from a second, filtered request, in red.



The dots alone trace the shape of the state, with dense clusters around Charlotte, the Triad (Greensboro, Winston-Salem, and High Point), and the Triangle (Raleigh, Durham, and Chapel Hill), where most people live.

14.5.1 Before you analyze
The result is an ordinary sf object, so everything from earlier chapters applies:

Check it. nrow(), names(), and glimpse() show how many features came back and what the columns are called.
Check the coordinate system. Run st_crs() on the result. Before measuring distances or areas, project it to North Carolina State Plane with st_transform(32119) (Chapter 12).
Note the date. Portal layers are dynamic: agencies update them, sometimes daily. Rerunning your script next month may give different data. Record the date you downloaded it, and save a copy with st_write() if your results must be exactly reproducible.



14.5.2 More arcpullr functions
get_spatial_layer() is the one you’ll use most. arcpullr has others for other jobs:

get_table_layer() downloads a table that has no geometry.
get_layer_by_poly() downloads only the features that fall inside a polygon you give it, such as one county’s boundary. Like where, it filters on the server, but by location instead of by attribute.
get_image_layer() and get_map_layer() download raster images and map services.

title: 14  ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
text:
14.6 Try it

Go to https://www.nconemap.gov/ and browse the data by theme, or search for a topic you care about.
Find a dataset that is a feature service.
Track down its REST URL: “I want to use this”, then “View Data Source”.
Paste the URL into get_spatial_layer() and map the result with tmap.
Bonus: add a where filter for your own county. Which field holds the county name in your layer?

In .../NC1Map_Health/MapServer/2, what is the 2? The version of the serviceThe layer IDThe number of fieldsThe page of results

title: 14  ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
text:
14.8 Summary

Agencies publish GIS layers on ArcGIS Online and ArcGIS Enterprise portals. NC OneMap is North Carolina’s.
Each published layer has a REST endpoint URL. On NC OneMap, find it with “I want to use this” and then “View Data Source”.
The REST Services Directory page shows the layer ID (the number at the end of the URL), the geometry type, the MaxRecordCount, and the field names.
arcpullr’s get_spatial_layer(url) downloads a layer as an sf object.
A where clause, written in SQL, filters the layer on the server: where = "fcounty = 'Orange'". Filtering on the server is faster and sends less data.
Portal layers change over time. Check what you got, project it before measuring, and record the download date.

title: 14  ArcGIS Data with arcpullr
text:
14.9 Exercises

Your county. Download the NC OneMap Medical Facilities layer for your home county (or Orange County) with a where clause. How many facilities are there? Compare your count with the full layer filtered in R with filter().
Two counties. Use IN to download the facilities for Orange and Durham counties in one request. Map them, colored by county.
A new layer. Find a different feature service on NC OneMap, such as schools, parks, or fire stations. Record its REST URL, geometry type, MaxRecordCount, and three of its field names, then download and map it.
Polygons. Find a polygon layer on NC OneMap. Download it, project it with st_transform(32119), and calculate the area of each feature with st_area().
Join it up. Count the medical facilities in each county, then join the counts to a county boundary layer (Chapter 15) and make a choropleth map of facilities per 10,000 people, using county populations from tidycensus (Chapter 13).

text:
14.10 Further reading

The arcpullr page on CRAN, https://cran.r-project.org/package=arcpullr, links to the package manual and vignettes, which list every function with examples.
NC OneMap, https://www.nconemap.gov/, North Carolina’s portal for state and local GIS data.
Esri’s ArcGIS REST APIs documentation, https://developers.arcgis.com/rest/, explains what a feature service is and every parameter a query can use, including where.

of the layers before it. In GIS, a layer holds one theme of features,
such as roads or soils.

preview, and download, such as NC OneMap.

local agencies.

be requested through its REST endpoint.

for data with ordinary web requests, and the answer usually comes back
as JSON.

https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs5.

listing its layer ID, geometry type, MaxRecordCount, and fields.

is a data frame with a geometry column holding each row’s point, line,
or polygon.

objects, with get_spatial_layer().
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().

asks another for data or services, such as your R script asking the
Census Bureau’s server for a table.

An R package that downloads US Census data through the Census API and

web. Many agencies’ data portals run on them.

segment, or one building. In an sf object, each row is a feature.

2 in .../MapServer/2, that picks one layer out
