title: Unit 4: Spatial Analysis
text:
Chapter 15: Joins: Attribute and Spatial
This unit puts data together and starts to analyze it. It joins tables by a shared column and by location, then explores data the way an analyst first meets a new dataset: describing each variable’s center and spread, plotting its distribution, and mapping it. It ends with statistics that describe where features are, and puts your own R functions to work calculating them.
A join combines tables by matching rows. This chapter covers dplyr’s inner, left, right, and full joins, naming the key with join_by(), and chaining joins across several tables. It explains cardinality, and why you should know it before you join. It then joins by location with sf’s st_join(), compares simple and summarized, inside and distance spatial joins, and shows why distances need a projected coordinate system.

title: Unit 4: Spatial Analysis
text:
Chapter 16: Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
Before modeling data, get to know it. This chapter places exploratory data analysis in the data science workflow and adds the spatial question: how do values vary across space? It covers checking a data table, measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and dispersion (range, IQR, standard deviation), histograms, boxplots, and density plots, distribution shapes and outliers, and mapping rates rather than counts.

title: Unit 4: Spatial Analysis
text:
Chapter 17: Spatial Descriptive Statistics
Spatial descriptive statistics describe where features are. This chapter covers the mean center, the weighted mean center (including the U.S. center of population), the central feature, and the standard distance, each matched to the familiar statistic it extends. It then reviews writing functions in R, from a one-line addSeven() to a meanCenter() function for any layer of polygons.



Combining two tables by matching rows on a shared key column, such as
attaching Census data to boundaries by GEOID with
left_join().
In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as
months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic,
such as median income; each Census variable has a code.
Code that takes inputs (arguments), does a job, and returns an output,
such as mean(temps).
The tidyverse package for transforming data frames: filtering rows,
choosing columns, adding new columns, joining tables, and summarizing.
A join that keeps every row of both tables, with NA wherever there is no
match. full_join() in dplyr.
How many rows in one table can match a row in another: one-to-one,
one-to-many, many-to-one, or many-to-many.
“Simple features”: the R package for spatial vector data. An sf object
is a data frame with a geometry column holding each row’s point, line,
or polygon.
A join that matches features by their location, such as attaching to
each point the polygon it falls inside. st_join() in R.
A method for flattening the curved graticule onto a flat map. Every
projection distorts shape, area, distance, or direction.
The rules that tie coordinates to places on the Earth, including how the
round Earth is flattened onto a map (the projection). Layers must share
a coordinate system before you can combine them.
Learning what is in a dataset, with summaries and plots, before trying
to explain or predict anything with it.
The steps of a data analysis: import, tidy, then a loop of transform,
visualize, and model, and finally communicate.
One value that describes the center of a set of values: the mean,
median, or mode.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
How spread out values are around their center, measured by the range,
interquartile range, or standard deviation.
Q3 minus Q1: the spread of the middle half of the data. Outliers barely
affect it. IQR() in R.
A measure of how spread out values are around their mean, in the same
units as the values. sd() in R.
A chart that divides a variable’s range into bins and draws a bar for
how many values fall in each. geom_histogram() in ggplot2.
A smoothed histogram whose total area is 1. geom_density()
in ggplot2.
A value far from all the others. It may be real or an error, so check it
before you report it.
Statistics that describe the center and spread of a set of locations,
such as the mean center and standard distance.
The average x coordinate and average y coordinate of a set of features.
Like the mean, outliers pull it.
A mean center in which each feature counts in proportion to an
attribute, such as population.
The point where a flat map of the country would balance if every
resident weighed the same.
The existing feature with the smallest total distance to all the others:
the spatial counterpart of the median.
The typical distance of features from their mean center: the spatial
counterpart of the standard deviation, drawn as a circle.
A closed shape that represents an area, such as a county, a lake, or a
census tract.

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
text:
15.1 What is a join?
Data rarely arrive in one table. Student names live in one table and the courses they take in another. Census counts live in a spreadsheet and county boundaries in a shapefile. EMS calls are points and neighborhoods are polygons. To answer most questions, you have to put two tables together.
A join combines two or more tables by matching rows. This chapter covers two kinds:
Recall that a data table has one row per observation and one column per variable. A join lines up the rows of two tables wherever a shared column has the same value. That shared column is the key.
Here are two small tables. students has one row per student. takes has one row for each course a student took. Both have an id column. Run the box to make them:
Look closely before you join. Zhang took two courses. Parr and McKeon took none. And two rows of takes belong to IDs, 33456 and 45678, that aren’t in students at all. Each type of join treats these unmatched rows differently.

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
text: Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
text:
15.2 Types of joins
It helps to think of each table as a collection of rows, drawn as a circle. Where the circles overlap are the rows whose key appears in both tables. A table with no duplicate rows is a set; one that may have duplicates is a bag, and R data frames behave like bags.






Figure 15.1: The four main joins. The blue part of each diagram is the rows the join keeps.




15.2.1 Inner join
An inner join keeps only the rows whose key appears in both tables:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Parr and McKeon are dropped because they took no courses, and the two GEOG-215 rows are dropped because no student matches them. Zhang appears twice, because Zhang took two courses.
The by = join_by(id) part names the key. You could leave it out and dplyr would guess, but naming it is the habit to build.


15.2.2 Left join
A left join keeps every row of the left table, the first one, and adds the matching columns from the right table:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Parr and McKeon now appear, with NA in the course columns. This is the join you will use most, because it never drops a row from the table you care about. But check the row count afterwards: it can grow when a key has several matches. students has 4 rows, and the result has 5.


15.2.3 Right join
A right join is the mirror image. It keeps every row of the right table:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now the GEOG-215 rows appear, with NA for name and department. Any right join can be written as a left join by swapping the order of the tables, and most people find the left join easier to read.


15.2.4 Full join
A full join keeps every row from both tables. It matches rows where it can and fills in NA where it can’t, so nothing is dropped:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


15.2.5 Natural joins and cross joins
Two more joins are worth knowing about, mostly so you can avoid them by accident.
A natural join is an inner join on every column the two tables share by name. In dplyr, if you leave out by, inner_join() does exactly this and prints a message, such as Joining with `by = join_by(id)`, to tell you which columns it used. It’s convenient but fragile. If both tables also had a column called name or year, it would silently join on that too. In your own code, spell out the key.
A cross join pairs every row of one table with every row of the other: the cartesian product. In dplyr it is cross_join(). Our 4 students and 5 course rows give 20 rows. It grows fast: two tables of 1,000 rows give a million.
You may also meet a self join, which joins a table to itself, such as a table of employees joined to their managers in the same table.






TipThink about it



Suppose the keys were stored differently in the two tables: "00128" as text in one and 128 as a number in the other. Would they match? How would you find out, and how would you fix it?




15.2.6 Joining more than two tables
Joins chain. Pipe the result of one join into the next to combine three or more tables. Here we add an instructor table, keyed by course_id:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Notice that the key changes from step to step: id for the first join and course_id for the second. Each inner join can only drop rows, so if records go missing, check the row count after each step to see where.

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
text:
15.3 Cardinality
Before you run a join, ask how many rows on each side can match. Cardinality is the relationship between the rows of two tables, and it tells you how big the result will be.



Table 15.1: The four kinds of cardinality.










Cardinality
Meaning
Examples




One-to-one
Each row matches at most one row in the other table
Governor and state; person and passport


One-to-many
One row matches many rows in the other table
Book and pages; state and cities


Many-to-one
The same relationship, seen from the other side
Cities and state; students and advisor


Many-to-many
Rows on both sides can match many rows
Students and classes






students to takes is one-to-many: one student can take many courses. That is why Zhang’s row was copied in the result. A many-to-many join multiplies rows on both sides, and can make a result far bigger than either table. dplyr warns you when it finds one.
So here is the rule of joining: know the cardinality before you join. It tells you how many rows to expect, and if the result has a different number, something about your keys isn’t what you thought. Cardinality will matter again when we design databases later in the course.

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
text:
15.4 Why join by location?
So far the key has been a shared column. But often two tables share no ID at all, only location. Consider three questions:

How many EMS calls fall in each neighborhood? The calls are points and the neighborhoods are polygons.
How many students attend school in each district? The schools are points with an enrollment, and the districts are polygons.
What is a coffee chain’s revenue in each sales region? The stores are points with revenue, and the regions are polygons.

All three have the same shape. Join each point to the polygon it falls inside, then summarize by polygon. The key is location.

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
text:
15.5 Spatial joins

15.5.1 From attribute joins to spatial joins
In GIS terms, an attribute join has a destination table that receives new columns, a source table that supplies them, and a common field that links the two. The output is the destination table with the source’s columns added.
A spatial join has the same structure, but the link is a spatial relationship instead of a common field. Two relationships cover most needs:

Inside: one feature falls inside, or intersects, another. Each school gets the attributes of the county it is in.
Distance: one feature is closest to another. Each city gets the attributes of the nearest airport.



15.5.2 Spatial joins in R
In R, the sf package does spatial joins with st_join():
st_join(x, y, join = st_intersects)
x is the destination and y the source. The join argument sets the relationship:

st_intersects (the default) or st_within for one feature inside another;
st_nearest_feature for the closest feature.

By default st_join() keeps every row of x, like a left join. Set left = FALSE to get an inner join, which drops the features of x that matched nothing.
Here is a real example, using two datasets from the spData package: the 742 bicycle hire stations in London, as points, and London’s 33 boroughs, as polygons. Which borough is each station in?
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(spData)

# Project both layers to the British National Grid, in meters
stations <- cycle_hire |> st_transform(27700)
boroughs <- lnd |> st_transform(27700)

stations_joined <- st_join(stations, boroughs["NAME"])
nrow(stations_joined)    # 742: one row per station
Each station now carries a NAME column: the borough it falls inside. One station sits just outside every borough polygon, so its NAME is NA; left = FALSE would drop it.


15.5.3 Four kinds of spatial join
Two decisions define a spatial join: the relationship (inside, or distance), and whether you attach one match per feature or summarize all of them (Table 15.2).



Table 15.2: Four kinds of spatial join. The arrow points from the source layer to the destination layer that receives its attributes.











Simple: attach one matching record
Summarized: aggregate all matches




Inside
Which county is each school in? (schools ← counties)
How many schools are in each county? (counties ← schools)


Distance
Which attraction is closest to each hotel, and how far is it? (hotels ← attractions)
How many attractions are closest to each hotel? (hotels ← attractions)






A simple join attaches the attributes of one matching feature. Each septic system gets the geology formation underneath it; each city gets its nearest airport and the distance to it. In both cases, every destination feature has exactly one match, and one source feature can match many destination features, so the cardinality is many-to-one. There is no ambiguity about which fields to attach.
A summarized join handles one-to-many and many-to-many relationships. When one county contains many schools, a simple join can’t pick just one. Instead, a summarized join counts or aggregates the matching features, such as the number of schools in each county, or their total enrollment, and attaches that.
The rule of joining applies to spatial joins too. Simple joins are one-to-one or many-to-one. Summarized joins handle one-to-many and many-to-many by aggregating.


15.5.4 Summarized joins in R
In R, a summarized join is st_join() followed by group_by() and summarize(), or count(). To count the stations in each borough:
station_counts <- stations_joined |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(NAME, name = "n_stations")

boroughs <- boroughs |>
  left_join(station_counts, by = join_by(NAME))
The last step is an attribute join. Dropping the geometry first turns the joined stations into a plain table, and left_join() keeps all 33 boroughs, with NA for the 22 that have no hire stations. Westminster has the most, with 171 (Figure 15.2).






Figure 15.2: London’s bicycle hire stations (black points) and the number in each borough, from a summarized spatial join. Gray boroughs have none.



For a distance join, use st_nearest_feature, then measure how far away the match is with st_distance():
cities_airports <- st_join(cities, airports, join = st_nearest_feature)

nearest <- st_nearest_feature(cities, airports)
cities_airports$dist <- st_distance(cities, airports[nearest, ],
                                    by_element = TRUE)

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
section: 15.6 Spatial joins and the coordinate system
text:
15.6 Spatial joins and the coordinate system
What units is a distance in? Software reports distances in the units of the data’s coordinate system. If the data are in a geographic coordinate system, those units are decimal degrees, and a distance of 0.47 means 0.47 degrees. As Section 12.7 showed, degrees can’t simply be converted to miles or kilometers, because a degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles.
Worse, the match itself can change. Degrees stretch unevenly, so the feature that is nearest in degrees isn’t always the one that is nearest on the ground. A distance join run on latitude and longitude can attach a different feature than the same join run in a projected coordinate system.
So, before any spatial join:

Check each layer’s coordinate system with st_crs().
Make sure both layers use the same one. st_join() stops with an error if they don’t.
For distance joins, project both layers with st_transform() to a projection that preserves distance in your study area, such as State Plane for North Carolina (EPSG:32119).

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
text:
15.7 Check your understanding

Which join keeps only the rows whose key appears in both tables? inner_join()left_join()full_join()cross_join()
You left-join students (4 rows) to takes. One student took two courses and the others took none or one. Can the result have more than 4 rows? Yes, keys with several matches are repeatedNo, a left join never changes the row countNo, it always has fewer rows
Any right join can be rewritten as a left join by swapping the order of the tables. TRUEFALSE
A cross join of a 10-row table and a 30-row table has how many rows? 
What is the cardinality between students and their academic advisor, if each student has one advisor? One-to-oneOne-to-manyMany-to-oneMany-to-many
In st_join(x, y), which layer receives the new attributes? x, the destinationy, the sourceNeither; it makes a new layer with only y’s columns
Which join argument attaches the closest feature? st_intersectsst_withinst_nearest_featurest_distance
Counting the schools in each county is an example of a: Simple inside joinSummarized inside joinSimple distance joinNatural join
A distance join on data in latitude and longitude gives the same matches as the same join on projected data. TRUEFALSE

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
text:
15.8 Summary

A join combines tables by matching rows. An attribute join matches a shared key column; a spatial join matches by location.
dplyr’s inner join keeps matches only; a left join keeps every row of the first table; a right join keeps every row of the second; a full join keeps everything. Name the key with join_by(), and chain joins with the pipe.
A natural join matches on every shared column name, which is fragile. A cross join pairs every row with every row.
Cardinality (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many) tells you how many rows a join will return. Know it before you join.
st_join(x, y, join = ...) attaches the attributes of y to x using a spatial relationship: st_intersects or st_within for inside, st_nearest_feature for distance. It keeps every row of x unless left = FALSE.
Simple spatial joins attach one match; summarized joins aggregate many, with group_by() and summarize() or count().
Distances come out in the data’s units. Check the CRS with st_crs() and project with st_transform() before joining by distance.

title: 15  Joins: Attribute and Spatial
text:
15.9 Exercises

Predict, then run. Before running each join in Section 15.2, write down how many rows you expect and which names will have NA. Then check.
Find the unmatched rows. dplyr has two filtering joins: semi_join() keeps the rows of x that have a match in y, and anti_join() keeps the rows that don’t. Use anti_join() to list the students who took no courses, and the course rows with no matching student.
Cardinality. Give the cardinality of each relationship, and explain: (a) capital city and state; (b) students and phone numbers; (c) counties and ZIP codes; (d) census tracts and counties.
Base R. Base R’s merge() also joins tables. Find the arguments to merge() that give an inner, a left, and a full join of students and takes.
London bikes. Reproduce the station counts in Figure 15.2. Then make a map of stations per square kilometer of each borough. Does the ranking change?
NC schools. Find a point layer of North Carolina public schools on NC OneMap, https://www.nconemap.gov. Join it to NC counties and count the schools in each county. Which county has the most schools? The most per 10,000 people?

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.1 From EDA to ESDA
Someone hands you a data table: a hundred rows, a dozen columns. Now what?
The answer is not to jump straight to a model. First, get to know the data: how big it is, what each column holds, what is missing, and how each variable is spread out. That process of getting to know your data is exploratory data analysis, or EDA. When the data are spatial, we add one more question, about where values occur, and it becomes exploratory spatial data analysis, or ESDA.
Most examples in this chapter use the nc data that come with the sf package: North Carolina’s 100 counties, with the number of births in each from 1974 to 1978 (BIR74) and from 1979 to 1984 (BIR79). The live code boxes use the flights data from Chapter 9.

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.1.1 The “understand” loop
Recall the data science workflow from R for Data Science. We import data and tidy it. Then we spend most of our time in a loop to understand it: transform, visualize, model, and back again. Only then do we communicate the results. EDA lives in that loop. It is iterative: each plot or summary raises a new question, which sends you back to transform the data again.
EDA is not one technique. It is everything we do to learn what is in a dataset before we try to explain or predict anything with it:

cleaning and wrangling the data;
finding duplicates and missing data (NA);
calculating and transforming variables;
making graphs, plots, charts, and maps;
calculating descriptive statistics.

The payoff is better questions. Good data, known well, lead to good questions, and good questions guide the analysis that follows.


16.1.2 Two questions guide the investigation
EDA can feel open-ended, so use two questions to keep it focused:

What type of variation occurs within my variables? Answer it with central tendency, dispersion, and plots of one variable, such as histograms and boxplots. Most of this chapter answers this question.
What type of variation occurs between my variables? Answer it with plots of two or more variables, such as scatterplots and grouped boxplots, and with correlation.



16.1.3 ESDA adds a geographic question
Spatial data let us ask one more: what type of geographic variation occurs within my variables? Three tools answer it:

Maps: where are the high and low values?
Spatial autocorrelation: are similar values located near each other? This is Tobler’s first law in action.
Clustering: are there hot spots or cold spots?

This chapter covers maps and descriptive statistics. Chapter 17 covers spatial descriptive statistics, and Chapter 22 covers spatial autocorrelation.

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
section: 16.2 Step one: get to know the data table
text:
16.2 Step one: get to know the data table
Before you look at any one variable, check the basics of the whole table:

The number of observations (rows, or features).
The number of complete observations. How many have NA?
The number of fields (variables, or columns).
The data type of each field. Does it match what the field means?

Useful R functions are nrow(), ncol(), glimpse(), and summary(). Try them on flights:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Missing values change what you can calculate: mean() returns NA unless you set na.rm = TRUE. Types matter too. A FIPS code stored as a number loses its leading zero, and a count stored as text can’t be averaged.
For nc, the same checks show 100 rows and 15 columns, including the geometry, and no missing values in BIR74:
library(sf)
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf")) |>
  st_transform(32119)

nrow(nc)              # 100
sum(is.na(nc$BIR74))  # 0
These answers decide which approaches make sense: numeric fields get means and histograms, and categorical fields get counts and modes.

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.3 Describing a variable’s center
Central tendency is one value that describes the central position of a set of values.



Table 16.1: Three measures of central tendency.










Measure
What it tells you
Use it for




Mean
The average: the sum of the values divided by the count
Numeric data


Median
The middle value once the values are sorted
Numeric data, especially skewed data


Mode
The most common value
Categorical (nominal) data, or any data






We’ll work through each on the same ten values:
\[
\{3, 8, 12, 6, 5, 10, 2, 3, 6, 3\}
\]
Sorted, they are {2, 3, 3, 3, 5, 6, 6, 8, 10, 12}.

16.3.1 Mean
The mean is what most people call the average. Add the values and divide by how many there are:
\[
\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n} = \frac{58}{10} = 5.8
\]
Here \(\bar{x}\) (“x-bar”) is the mean, \(\sum\) means “add up”, \(x_i\) is each value, and \(n\) is the count. Because every value enters the sum, one extreme value can pull the mean a long way.


16.3.2 Median
The median is the middle of the sorted values, so the first step is always to sort. With an odd number of values, the median is the single middle one. With an even number, it is the mean of the two middle values. We have 10 values, so we average the 5th and 6th: (5 + 6) / 2 = 5.5.
Half the values are below the median and half above, so extreme values barely move it.


16.3.3 Mode
The mode is the most frequent value. In the sorted list, 3 appears three times, more than any other value, so the mode is 3. A variable can have no mode, one, or several.
The mode is the only measure of center that works for categorical data. You can find the most common land-cover class, but you can’t average land-cover classes. Base R has no function for the statistical mode: mode() returns how R stores an object. Use table() or count() and take the most frequent value instead.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.4 Describing a variable’s spread
The mean describes the center. Dispersion describes the spread, or variability, around it. Here are two sets of values with exactly the same mean:

A: {3, 8, 12, 6, 5, 10, 2, 3, 6, 3}. Mean 5.8, from 2 to 12.
B: {−56, 8, −1, 64, −34, 84, −5, 38, 6, −46}. Mean 5.8, from −56 to 84.

If you only reported the mean, these would look identical. They are not. That is why you should always pair a measure of center with a measure of spread.

16.4.1 Range and interquartile range
The range is the largest value minus the smallest. It is quick to calculate and easy to explain, but it uses only the two most extreme values, so one outlier changes it.
Quartiles split the sorted values into four groups of equal size. The first quartile, Q1, is the 25th percentile; the third, Q3, is the 75th; and the median is the second. The interquartile range (IQR) is Q3 − Q1: the spread of the middle half of the data. It ignores the extremes, so outliers barely affect it.
Take these 12 values: {3, 1, 2, 8, 12, 6, 5, 10, 2, 3, 6, 3}. Sorted and split in half, they are
\[
\{1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3 \mid 5, 6, 6, 8, 10, 12\}
\]

Range = 12 − 1 = 11.
Q1 is the median of the lower half, between 2 and 3: 2.5.
Q3 is the median of the upper half, between 6 and 8: 7.
IQR = 7 − 2.5 = 4.5.

Software uses slightly different rules for percentiles. R’s default rule interpolates between values, so it gives Q1 = 2.75 and Q3 = 6.5, and IQR() returns 3.75. With a small sample the difference is visible; with hundreds of values the methods agree closely. When you work by hand, show your method.


16.4.2 Standard deviation
The standard deviation is the most common measure of spread. It is roughly the typical distance between a value and the mean. To calculate it:

Subtract the mean from each value. This is the deviation.
Square each deviation, so negative ones don’t cancel positive ones.
Add them up and divide by n − 1. This is the variance.
Take the square root, to return to the original units.

\[
s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}
\]
For set A the standard deviation is 3.3; for set B it is 45.7. Same mean, about 14 times the spread. Like the mean, the standard deviation uses every value, so it is sensitive to outliers. Check the numbers in R:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


16.4.3 All together
summarize() puts the whole toolkit in one call. Here it is for births in North Carolina’s counties:
nc |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarize(min    = min(BIR74),
            q1     = quantile(BIR74, 0.25),
            median = median(BIR74),
            mean   = mean(BIR74),
            q3     = quantile(BIR74, 0.75),
            max    = max(BIR74),
            sd     = sd(BIR74),
            IQR    = IQR(BIR74))



Table 16.2: Summary statistics for births per county, 1974–78.





min
Q1
median
mean
Q3
max
sd
IQR




248
1,077
2,180.5
3,299.6
3,936
21,588
3,848.2

The key comparison is the mean against the median. The mean is about 1.5 times the median, and the standard deviation is larger than the mean. Both are signs of right skew: most counties have few births, and a few large urban counties, led by Mecklenburg with 21,588, pull the mean up. For skewed variables like this one, the median and the IQR describe a typical county better than the mean and the standard deviation.

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.5 Visualizing distributions
Summary statistics compress a variable into a few numbers. Plots show the whole distribution.

16.5.1 Histograms and boxplots
A histogram divides the range of a variable into bins, and draws a bar for the number of values in each. A boxplot draws the box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median. The whiskers reach to the furthest values within 1.5 times the IQR of the box, and points beyond them are drawn one by one as potential outliers.
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(nc, aes(x = BIR74)) + geom_histogram()
ggplot(nc, aes(y = BIR74)) + geom_boxplot()









Figure 16.1: Histogram











Figure 16.2: Boxplot






Both tell the same story as Table 16.2: births per county are strongly right-skewed.


16.5.2 Choosing a bin width
A histogram depends on one choice you make: the bin width. In ggplot, set binwidth or bins inside geom_histogram(). The default of 30 bins prints a message telling you to pick a better value.






Figure 16.3: The same births data with three bin widths.



Too narrow, and every small fluctuation becomes its own spike; the shape is lost in noise. Too wide, and the bins swallow the detail. Try a few widths, and choose one that shows the structure without the noise.


16.5.3 Shape decides whether the mean is typical
Always look at the shape of a distribution before you trust its mean (Figure 16.4).






Figure 16.4: Six distribution shapes. The red line is the mean and the dashed line the median.




Symmetric: the mean and the median are about the same.
Skewed: the long tail pulls the mean toward it. Births per county are skewed right.
Uniform: there’s no peak at all.
Bimodal or multimodal: the mean can land in a dip where few values are. Two or more peaks often mean that different groups are mixed together, such as urban and rural counties.

So ask: does the mean describe a typical value here? Or should I report the median, or split the data into groups?


16.5.4 Outliers
An outlier is a value far from the rest. Plots make outliers easy to spot. In a histogram, it is a lone bar far to the right, separated from the others by empty bins. In a boxplot, it is a point beyond the whisker. Seven counties are beyond the upper whisker in Figure 16.2, and Mecklenburg is the highest.
Ask what explains an outlier before deciding what to do. A large urban county is a real value and stays in. A typo or a wrong unit is an error to fix. Either way, outliers are why the mean and standard deviation can be so much larger than the median and IQR. Whatever you decide, say so in your write-up.


16.5.5 Density plots
A density plot is a smoothed histogram. Instead of counting values in bins, it estimates a smooth curve. The total area under the curve is 1, so the y-axis is a density, not a count. With a variable measured in thousands, the densities are tiny numbers. Peaks show where values concentrate.
ggplot(nc, aes(x = BIR74)) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.6)






Figure 16.5: Density plot of births per county, 1974–78.



Density plots shine when you compare groups, because several curves can share one set of axes. To compare two columns, first stack them into one column with pivot_longer(). Then map the column names to fill:
library(tidyr)

nc |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(BIR74, BIR79) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = name)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)






Figure 16.6: Births in 1974–78 and 1979–84, on one set of axes.



The alpha argument makes the curves see-through, so the overlap stays visible.


16.5.6 Your turn
Recreate a density plot of air_time for two airlines, American (AA) and United (UA). The code filters the flights, drops missing air times, and maps carrier to fill. Fill in the missing geom:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Show answer

Replace geom_histogram() with geom_density(alpha = 0.6). Why does air_time have several peaks? Each peak is a group of common routes with similar distances: a multimodal distribution.

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.6 Maps add the spatial dimension
Everything so far ignores location. A map adds it back, and this is where EDA becomes ESDA.
Map a rate, a density, or a percentage, not a raw count. Big counties have more of almost everything, so a map of raw counts mostly shows which counties are big. Here we divide births by each county’s area, from st_area():
library(tmap)

nc |>
  mutate(area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6,
         births_per_km2 = BIR74 / area_km2) |>
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "births_per_km2",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.oranges"))






Figure 16.7: Births per square kilometer in each county, 1974–78.



Most of the state is pale, with low density, and a handful of urban counties stand out: Mecklenburg, New Hanover, Cumberland, Forsyth, and Durham, then Gaston and Guilford. Now ask the ESDA question. Are the high values scattered, or do they cluster together?

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.7 Spatial statistics describe location
The statistics in this chapter describe values. Spatial descriptive statistics describe locations:

The mean center is the average x coordinate and the average y coordinate of all the features.
The weighted mean center does the same, but weights each feature by an attribute, such as births or population.
The standard distance is how far features typically sit from the mean center: the spatial version of the standard deviation.

And the question of whether nearby values are similar is measured with spatial autocorrelation statistics, such as Moran’s I (Chapter 22). Chapter 17 covers the spatial descriptive statistics.

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.8 Check your understanding

What is the mean of {2, 4, 4, 10}? 
What is the median of {2, 4, 4, 10}? 
Which measure of center is the only one that works for categorical data, such as land-cover class? MeanMedianModeStandard deviation
Which measure of spread is least affected by one extreme value? RangeStandard deviationInterquartile rangeVariance
A variable’s mean is much larger than its median. Its distribution is probably: Skewed rightSkewed leftSymmetricUniform
In a boxplot, the box spans: The minimum to the maximumQ1 to Q3The mean plus and minus one standard deviationThe 5th to the 95th percentile
The area under a density curve is equal to 1. TRUEFALSE
A choropleth map should usually show raw counts rather than rates or densities. TRUEFALSE

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.9 Summary

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is how we learn what’s in a dataset before explaining or predicting anything. ESDA adds the question of how values vary across space.
Start with the table: rows, complete rows, columns, and data types.
Describe each variable’s center with the mean, median, or mode, and its spread with the range, interquartile range, or standard deviation. For skewed data, prefer the median and IQR.
Histograms, boxplots, and density plots show a whole distribution. Choose the bin width with care, and read the shape: symmetric, skewed, uniform, or multimodal.
Plots make outliers easy to spot. Find out what explains them before deciding what to do.
Maps add location. Map rates or densities, not raw counts, and ask whether high values cluster.
Spatial descriptive statistics, such as the mean center and standard distance, describe where features are.

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.10 Exercises

By hand, then in R. For {7, 1, 4, 9, 4, 12, 3}, calculate the mean, median, mode, range, and standard deviation by hand. Check each with R.
Same mean, different spread. Make two sets of 8 numbers with a mean of 10: one with a standard deviation under 2, and one with a standard deviation over 20.
Explore BIR79. Repeat Table 16.2 for BIR79. Did births become more or less skewed? Which counties are outliers?
Bin widths. Make histograms of distance in flights with three bin widths. Which shows the structure best? Describe the shape.
Rates. Make a map of SID74 / BIR74, the rate of sudden infant deaths per birth. Compare it with a map of raw SID74. Which counties change most?
Two variables. Make a scatterplot of BIR74 against BIR79. What does it tell you about variation between the two variables?

title: 16  Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis
text:
16.11 Further reading

R for Data Science (2nd ed.), by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund, free at https://r4ds.hadley.nz. The “Exploratory data analysis” chapter is the source of the two guiding questions.
Spatial Analysis Methods and Practice, by George Grekousis (Cambridge University Press, 2020), covers exploratory spatial data analysis and spatial descriptive statistics.
Geographic Data Science with Python, by Sergio Rey, Dani Arribas-Bel, and Levi John Wolf, free at https://geographicdata.science/book. Its chapters on choropleth mapping and spatial autocorrelation preview what comes next.




Learning what is in a dataset, with summaries and plots, before trying
to explain or predict anything with it.
The steps of a data analysis: import, tidy, then a loop of transform,
visualize, and model, and finally communicate.
EDA that also asks how values vary across space, using maps, spatial
autocorrelation, and clustering.
A value that is unknown, written NA (“not available”) in R.
Most calculations with NA give NA; test for it
with is.na().
One value that describes the center of a set of values: the mean,
median, or mode.
The average: the sum of the values divided by how many there are. A few
very large or small values can pull it a long way.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
The most common value. The only measure of center that works for
categorical data.
How spread out values are around their center, measured by the range,
interquartile range, or standard deviation.
The largest value minus the smallest. range() in R returns
both.

title: 17  Spatial Descriptive Statistics
text:
17.1 Many statistics have a spatial counterpart
Chapter 16 described the values of a variable: where its center is and how spread out it is. This chapter does the same for locations. Where is the middle of a set of features? Which feature is most central? And how spread out are they?
The answers are spatial descriptive statistics. In the second half of the chapter, you will also write your own functions in R, and read one that calculates a weighted mean center.
Most descriptive statistics you already know have a spatial version (Table 17.1).
A quick refresher on the last row. The standard deviation measures how spread out values are around their mean. In a normal, bell-shaped distribution, about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, and about 95% within two. Keep that picture in mind: the standard distance draws the same idea on a map, as a circle.
Throughout the chapter we’ll use six points, with x and y in kilometers and a weight, such as population in thousands:

title: 17  Spatial Descriptive Statistics
text:
Table 17.1: Descriptive statistics and their spatial counterparts.










Statistic
Spatial counterpart
Question it answers




Mean
Mean center; weighted mean center
Where is the average location?


Median
Central feature
Which real feature is most central?


Standard deviation
Standard distance
How spread out are the locations?









Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 17  Spatial Descriptive Statistics
text:
17.2 Mean center
The mean center is the simplest spatial statistic. Average all the x coordinates, average all the y coordinates, and that pair is the mean center:
\[
\bar{X} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}, \qquad \bar{Y} = \frac{\sum y_i}{n}
\]

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
For our six points the mean center is at (6.33, 5). It doesn’t have to be one of the points, and here it isn’t.
Like the ordinary mean, the mean center is sensitive to outliers. In Figure 17.1, adding one distant point drags the center toward it.






Figure 17.1: The mean center (red) of nine points (A), and of the same points with one outlier added (B). The open circle in B marks where the center was before.




17.2.1 The mean center of North Carolina
Figure 17.2 shows the mean center of North Carolina’s counties, calculated from the centroid of each of the 100 counties. It falls in the Piedmont, in Chatham County. Every county counts the same here, so tiny Chowan County pulls as hard as Wake or Mecklenburg.

title: 17  Spatial Descriptive Statistics
text:
17.3 Weighted mean center
Often some locations matter more than others. A county with a million people should count for more than one with 4,000. The weighted mean center multiplies each coordinate by its weight, w, adds them up, and divides by the sum of the weights:
\[
\bar{X}_w = \frac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i}, \qquad \bar{Y}_w = \frac{\sum w_i y_i}{\sum w_i}
\]
Base R’s weighted.mean() does exactly this:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Point 2 carries half the total weight, so it pulls the center from (6.33, 5) to (5.45, 5.75), toward itself.
The best-known weighted mean center is the U.S. center of population. After every census, the Census Bureau calculates the mean center of the country’s population, weighting each location by the number of people who live there. As Figure 13.1 shows, it has moved from Maryland in 1790 to Missouri in 2020: west with settlement, and since about 1950 south as well, with the growth of the Sun Belt.
Now the same for North Carolina, with each county weighted by its births from 1974 to 1978 (Figure 17.2).






Figure 17.2: The mean center of North Carolina’s 100 county centroids (green), and the mean center weighted by births, 1974–78 (black).



The weighted center moves about 12 km, almost due south. Several of the counties with the most births, such as Mecklenburg, Cumberland, Onslow, and New Hanover, lie south of the state’s middle, while many counties along the Virginia line had few. East to west, Mecklenburg and the Triangle roughly balance each other. With recent population data, the Triangle’s fast growth pulls the weighted center east instead. The weights you choose change the answer, so say which you used.






TipThink about it



What would the center of North Carolina look like if you weighted each county by its land area instead? By its number of hog farms? What question would each center answer?

title: 17  Spatial Descriptive Statistics
text:
17.4 Central feature
The central feature is the existing feature that is closest to all the others. To find it, measure the distance from each feature to every other feature, add them up, and pick the feature with the smallest total.
It is the spatial cousin of the median. Instead of averaging, it picks a real feature from the data. That matters when the answer must be a real place: say, choosing which of your existing offices should host a regional meeting.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Point 4, at (7, 5), has the smallest total distance, 21.8 km, so it is the central feature. The mean center, (6.33, 5), is close by, but it isn’t a point in the data.
For North Carolina, the central feature of the county centroids is Chatham County (Figure 17.3).






Figure 17.3: The central feature (large blue dot) of North Carolina’s county centroids: Chatham County.

title: 17  Spatial Descriptive Statistics
text:
17.5 Standard distance
The standard distance is the spatial version of the standard deviation: the typical distance between features and their mean center.
\[
SD = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{X})^2}{n} + \frac{\sum (y_i - \bar{Y})^2}{n}}
\]
Take each point’s distance from the mean center in x and in y, square them, average, add, and take the square root.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We draw it as a circle centered on the mean center, with the standard distance as its radius. A large circle means the features are spread out; a small one means they cluster tightly.
Comparing circles is how we compare dispersion: between two weightings, two time periods, or two kinds of features. In Figure 17.4, the solid circle uses every county equally, and has a radius of about 203 km. The dashed circle is weighted by births. It is smaller, about 158 km, because most births happened in a few urban Piedmont counties.






Figure 17.4: Standard distance circles for North Carolina’s counties: unweighted (green, solid) and weighted by births (black, dashed). Counties are shaded by births, 1974–78.

title: 17  Spatial Descriptive Statistics
text:
17.6 Functions in R
So far we have calculated these statistics one line at a time. A function wraps code up so you can run it on any data with one line.

17.6.1 What is a function?
You have used functions all along: mean(), st_read(), ggplot(), and Chapter 5 showed how to write your own. Here is a quick review before we put them to work on spatial statistics. A function is a named, reusable block of code. Every function has:

a name;
inputs, called arguments;
an output, called the return value.

You call a function by its name, with its inputs in parentheses.


17.6.2 Writing your own
Here is a function named addSeven. Its one input is numbers, and it returns those numbers plus 7:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The name goes on the left of the assignment arrow. The word function is followed by the inputs in parentheses, and the code goes inside the braces. The value of the last line is what the function returns. addSeven(c(1, 2, 3)) returns 8, 9, 10, because R adds 7 to every element of the vector.
Your turn. Write timesTwo(), which doubles its input. Then write addAny(), with a second input, amount, so that it adds any number you choose:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Show answer

timesTwo <- function(numbers) {
  numbers * 2
}

addAny <- function(numbers, amount) {
  numbers + amount
}

addAny(c(1, 2, 3), 10)   # 11 12 13

A function can also bundle up a whole calculation. This one returns the standard distance of any set of points:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


17.6.3 A function for the weighted mean center
Here is a function, meanCenter(), that finds the weighted mean center of any layer of polygons. Its inputs are a spatial layer and a vector of weights. Its output is a point:
library(sf)

meanCenter <- function(layer, weights) {
  # convert the polygons into points
  points <- st_centroid(layer)
  # calculate the weighted mean x and y coordinates
  mc_x <- weighted.mean(st_coordinates(points)[, 1], weights)
  mc_y <- weighted.mean(st_coordinates(points)[, 2], weights)
  # create a point
  mean_center <- st_sfc(st_point(c(mc_x, mc_y)))
  # give it the same coordinate reference system as the layer
  mean_center <- st_set_crs(mean_center, st_crs(layer))
  # return the point
  mean_center
}
Walk through it from top to bottom. st_centroid() turns each polygon into a point. st_coordinates() returns a matrix of those points’ coordinates, with x in the first column and y in the second, and weighted.mean() averages each one using the weights. st_point() and st_sfc() turn the two numbers into a point geometry, and st_set_crs() gives it the same coordinate reference system as the input layer. The last line, mean_center, is what the function returns.
Notice that weights works just like amount in addAny(): it’s a second input that changes the result. Pass a column of 1s, or any constant, and you get the unweighted mean center. Use it like this:
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf")) |>
  st_transform(32119)

mc_births <- meanCenter(nc, nc$BIR74)
mc_plain  <- meanCenter(nc, rep(1, nrow(nc)))

st_distance(mc_plain, mc_births)   # about 12,200 m
Why project to State Plane first? The mean of latitudes and longitudes isn’t a true center, for the same reasons degrees aren’t a distance (Section 12.7). Calculate spatial statistics in a projected coordinate system.

title: 17  Spatial Descriptive Statistics
text:
17.8 Summary

Spatial descriptive statistics describe the center and spread of a set of locations.
The mean center is the average x and the average y. Like the mean, it is pulled by outliers.
The weighted mean center weights each feature by an attribute, such as population. The U.S. center of population is the best-known example.
The central feature is the real feature with the smallest total distance to all the others: the spatial cousin of the median.
The standard distance is the typical distance from the mean center: the spatial standard deviation, drawn as a circle.
A function packages code you’ll reuse. It has a name, arguments (inputs), and a return value (the last line). meanCenter() combines sf functions to find the weighted mean center of any layer.
Calculate spatial statistics on projected data.

title: 17  Spatial Descriptive Statistics
text:
17.9 Exercises

By hand. Five stores are at (1, 1), (3, 2), (2, 5), (6, 4), and (8, 8), in km. Find the mean center, the central feature, and the standard distance by hand, then check them in R.
Weights. Give the five stores weights of 100, 20, 20, 20, and 500 (their sales). Find the weighted mean center. Which way did it move, and why?
Your own function. Write a function, centralFeature(x, y), that returns the number of the central feature. Test it on the six points in this chapter.
Weighted standard distance. Extend standardDistance() to take a third input, w, and return the weighted standard distance. (Replace each mean with weighted.mean(), and each division by n with a division by the sum of the weights.)
Two periods. Use meanCenter() to find the weighted mean center of births in North Carolina for BIR74 and for BIR79. Did it move? How far, and in which direction?
Population. Once you have read Chapter 13, download the population of each North Carolina county from the American Community Survey with tidycensus, and find the population-weighted mean center. How does it compare with the center for 1970s births?

title: Unit 5: Statistics and Science
text:
Chapter 18: Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA
This unit turns data into evidence. It tests whether groups of places differ, models how one variable changes with others, and puts the pieces together into a reproducible spatial data science project, from the research question to the conclusion. It ends by testing Tobler’s first law of geography, that near things are more related than distant things: first deciding what “near” means, with distances and neighbors, and then measuring whether values on a map are clustered, random, or dispersed.
This chapter places statistical tests in the cycle of data analysis. It explains what a p-value does and doesn’t tell you, and why the replication crisis changed how scientists report them. It then compares group means with analysis of variance, from a small worked example to median male age across North Carolina’s regions, with follow-up tests and alternatives for when ANOVA’s assumptions fail.

title: Unit 5: Statistics and Science
text:
Chapter 19: Linear Regression
Regression asks how one variable changes as another changes. This chapter covers correlation, fitting a line with lm(), slopes, intercepts, residuals, and predictions, and how to read R’s model summary, including R² and adjusted R². It models median house value in North Carolina’s counties, then maps the residuals to see where the model fails.

title: Unit 5: Statistics and Science
section: Chapter 20: Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
Chapter 20: Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
This chapter steps back to ask how data become knowledge. It covers the data, information, knowledge, wisdom pyramid, big data, choosing sources, and why reproducibility and replicability matter. It then walks through the parts of a project, from the research question and background to methods, results, and conclusions, and ends with what makes a project spatial data science.

title: Unit 5: Statistics and Science
text:
Chapter 21: Distance and Neighborhoods
This chapter covers what distance means and the main ways to measure it: Euclidean, great circle, Manhattan, and network distance. It then uses distance and shared borders to decide which features are neighbors, with distance bands, k nearest neighbors, and rook and queen contiguity, and stores those relationships in a neighborhood weight matrix, built in R with spdep.

title: Unit 5: Statistics and Science
section: Chapter 22: Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Chapter 22: Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
This chapter tests objectively whether things on a map are clustered. It measures point patterns with the Average Nearest Neighbor ratio, global spatial autocorrelation with Moran’s I and a permutation test, and local hot spots and cold spots with Getis-Ord Gi*, using births in North Carolina’s counties.

title: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA
text:
18.1 What is data analysis?
Western North Carolina’s mountain counties are known as a retirement destination. The Piedmont has the big cities, universities, and their young workers. So do men in the west really tend to be older than men in the Piedmont? Or could the difference we see in the numbers be due to chance?
That is the question behind this chapter: do groups of places really differ, or could the difference be chance? We’ll build up the tools in order. First, what data analysis is, and what a statistic and a p-value are. Then variance, the measure of spread that the method is built on. Then analysis of variance (ANOVA), applied to median male age in North Carolina’s 100 counties. We finish with what changes when the observations are places on a map.
Data analysis turns raw observations into evidence. We summarize what the data show, and we test whether the patterns are real or could be due to chance. It is a cycle, not a single test:
Chapter 16 covered step 3, describing data. This chapter is about step 4, testing, and about the measure of spread, variance, that connects the two.

Step

title: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA
text:
18.2 Statistics and p-values
A statistic is a number calculated from a sample that summarizes the data. There are two broad kinds:

Descriptive statistics summarize: the mean, the median, the standard deviation.
Test statistics weigh evidence: t, F, chi-square.

Because a statistic comes from a sample, it estimates a value for the whole population, and it would change if you drew a different sample. A test asks whether the pattern in this sample is bigger than that sample-to-sample wobble would produce by chance.
Every test starts from a null hypothesis, written H₀: the boring claim that there is no difference, no relationship, nothing going on. The alternative hypothesis, H₁, is that there is something. The test then works out how surprising your data would be if the null hypothesis were true.

18.2.1 Reading a test result
Read the output of any statistical test in three steps:

The test statistic. How large the pattern is compared with random variation, for example F.
The p-value. The probability of a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true, that is, if the groups truly did not differ.
The decision. By convention, if p < 0.05, reject the null hypothesis: the result is called statistically significant. If p ≥ 0.05, you have no evidence of a difference. That is not the same as evidence of no difference.

Suppose an ANOVA gives p = 0.03. That means: if the groups truly didn’t differ, a result this extreme would happen about 3% of the time. It does not mean there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true, or that the difference between the groups is large.






WarningSignificant is not the same as important



A tiny difference can be statistically significant if you have lots of data, and a large one can miss p < 0.05 if you have little. A p-value says nothing about the size of a difference. Always report the size of the difference too.




18.2.2 p-values and the replication crisis
p-values matter because they are the shared test of “could this be chance?”, and for decades journals have used p < 0.05 as the bar for publication. That bar created bad incentives:

p-hacking: re-running an analysis in different ways until something crosses 0.05.
The file drawer: results that don’t reach 0.05 go unpublished, so the published record overstates how often effects are found.
The bright line: treating 0.049 as “real” and 0.051 as “nothing”, as if they were different worlds.




Table 18.2: A century of the p-value. Sources: Ioannidis (2005), PLOS Medicine; Open Science Collaboration (2015), Science; Wasserstein and Lazar (2016), The American Statistician; Amrhein, Greenland, and McShane (2019), Nature.









Year
Event




1925
R. A. Fisher suggests p < 0.05 as a convenient guide, not a fixed rule.


1933
Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson add fixed error rates. Textbooks later blend the two ideas.


2005
John Ioannidis argues that most published research findings are false.


2015
The Open Science Collaboration repeats 100 psychology studies: 97% of the originals had reported p < 0.05, but only 36% of the repeats did.


2016
The American Statistical Association warns that p-values are widely misread.


2019
More than 800 scientists sign a call to retire “statistical significance”.






The failure of so many published findings to hold up when other researchers repeated them is called the replication crisis. The lesson for your own work: report the p-value with the size of the effect and a confidence interval, never on its own. And treat p = 0.051 and p = 0.049 as what they are: almost exactly the same amount of evidence.
crumbs: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA

title: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA
text:
18.3 Variance: measuring spread
ANOVA is built on variance, which you met in Chapter 16. Variance is the average squared distance of each value from the mean:
\[
s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}
\]
For a sample we divide by n − 1 rather than n. Small variance means values cluster near the mean; large variance means they spread widely. The standard deviation, s, is the square root of the variance, back in the data’s own units.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

18.3.1 Two kinds of variation
Now suppose we have three groups, A, B, and C, of six values each (Figure 18.1). There are two kinds of variation:

Within-group variation: the spread of the values around their own group’s mean.
Between-group variation: how far the group means sit from the overall mean.







Figure 18.1: Three groups of six values. Each colored dot is one value, the black bar is that group’s mean, and the dashed line is the overall mean of all 18 values.



ANOVA compares the two:
\[
F = \frac{\text{between-group variance}}{\text{within-group variance}}
\]
If the group means sit far apart relative to the noise inside each group, F is large, and the groups differ more than chance alone would produce. If the groups are really just random draws from one population, F hovers around 1.
crumbs: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA

title: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA
section: 18.4 ANOVA: are the group means different?
text:
18.4 ANOVA: are the group means different?
Analysis of variance, or ANOVA, tests whether the means of three or more groups differ. (With only two groups, you would use a t-test. ANOVA extends the idea to more groups without the extra false positives you’d get from running many t-tests.)
The two hypotheses are:

H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃. All the group means are equal.
H₁: At least one group mean differs.

ANOVA builds F from sums of squares (SS), the summed squared distances from the means, each divided by its degrees of freedom (df) to give a mean square (MS). With k groups and N observations in all:



Table 18.3: How ANOVA builds the F statistic.





Source
df
Mean square (MS)




Between groups
k − 1
SS between ÷ (k − 1)


Within groups (residuals)
N − k
SS within ÷ (N − k)


F statistic

MS between ÷ MS within






For the three groups in Figure 18.1, k = 3 and N = 18. The overall mean is 6.33. Work it through:

SS between = 6 × (5 − 6.33)² + 6 × (8 − 6.33)² + 6 × (6 − 6.33)² = 28. With 3 − 1 = 2 df, MS between = 14.
SS within: each group’s values are spread around its own mean with a variance of 2, so its squared distances add up to 5 × 2 = 10. Three groups give 30. With 18 − 3 = 15 df, MS within = 2.
F = 14 ÷ 2 = 7.

aov() fits the model, and summary() prints the ANOVA table. The formula value ~ group reads “value, by group”:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
F = 7, with 2 and 15 degrees of freedom, and p = 0.0071. If all three groups came from one population, an F this large would turn up less than 1% of the time, so we reject H₀: at least one group mean differs.
Where does the p-value come from? If H₀ is true, F follows a known shape, the F distribution, which depends on the two degrees of freedom. The p-value is the share of that distribution beyond your F. In R, pf() gives it directly:

section: 18.5 Example: median male age by North Carolina region
text:
18.5 Example: median male age by North Carolina region
Back to the question we started with: is the median age of males different between western, central, and eastern North Carolina?

Data: American Community Survey 5-year estimates of median age for males (table B01002) for all 100 North Carolina counties, downloaded with tidycensus (Chapter 13).
Groups: the west (the mountains), the center (the Piedmont), and the east (the coastal plain). Each county belongs to one region (Figure 18.2).
Unit of analysis: the county, not the person or the census tract.







Figure 18.2: North Carolina’s counties grouped into three regions (top), and the median age of males in each county from the ACS 5-year estimates (bottom).



Before testing anything, look at the data. Each dot in Figure 18.3 is one county, and each box holds the middle half of the counties in its region:
nc_df <- st_drop_geometry(nc)

ggplot(nc_df, aes(region, estimate, fill = region)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 1.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3")) +
  labs(title = "Male Median Age by Region, North Carolina Counties",
       x = NULL, y = "Median age (male, years)",
       caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates, table B01002") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")






Figure 18.3: Median male age by region. Each dot is one county.



The table puts numbers on the picture:
nc_df |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            mean   = mean(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd     = sd(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
            median = median(estimate, na.rm = TRUE))



Table 18.4: Median male age, in years, by region.

The West is oldest, with a mean of 44.5 years, and the Piedmont youngest, at 39.2. The East sits between, at 41.8, with the widest spread. But the boxes overlap a lot. Is the gap between the regional means large compared with the spread inside each region? That is exactly what ANOVA tests.

18.5.1 The ANOVA
One line fits the model: estimate is the variable we compare, and region defines the groups.
fit <- aov(estimate ~ region, data = nc_df)
summary(fit)
            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)
region       2  420.8  210.41   8.439 0.000418 ***
Residuals   97 2418.5   24.93
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
Read it in three steps:

Test statistic. F = 210.41 ÷ 24.93 = 8.44. The variation between regions is about eight times the variation within them. With k = 3 regions and N = 100 counties, the degrees of freedom are 2 and 97.
p-value. 0.000418, far below 0.05. If the three regions really had the same mean, an F this large would almost never happen (Figure 18.4).
Decision. Reject the null hypothesis. At least two of the regions differ in median male age.







Figure 18.4: The F distribution with 2 and 97 degrees of freedom: the values of F you’d expect if the regions didn’t differ. The shaded tail is the top 5%; the NC example’s F = 8.44 lies far beyond it.



Notice what the result does not say. It doesn’t say all three regions differ, only that some do. And it doesn’t say why: region doesn’t cause age. Retirement migration, college towns, and military bases are all possible explanations that the test can’t tell apart.






TipThink about it



Before you saw the data, which region would you have guessed has the oldest men? What features of a county (a university, a military base, a retirement community) would pull its median age down or up?

title: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA
text:
18.6 After ANOVA: which groups differ?
ANOVA tells us that at least two groups differ, not which ones. To find out, run a post-hoc test. Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) test compares every pair of groups and adjusts the p-values, so that making three comparisons doesn’t inflate the chance of a false positive:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
For the three groups, only B and A differ significantly: B’s mean is 3 higher, with an adjusted p-value of 0.006. C and A (p = 0.46) and C and B (p = 0.066) do not. In the North Carolina example, TukeyHSD(fit) on the regional model shows which pairs of regions differ; try it in Exercise 2.

18.6.1 Check the assumptions
ANOVA’s p-value is only trustworthy if three assumptions hold:

Independence: each observation tells you nothing about the others.
Normality: the values in each group, or more exactly the model’s residuals, are roughly normal.
Equal variances: the groups have similar spreads.

The Shapiro-Wilk test checks normality. Its null hypothesis is that the residuals are normal, so a large p-value is good news. For the North Carolina model, shapiro.test(residuals(fit)) gives W = 0.98 and p = 0.18: no evidence that the residuals aren’t normal.
If the assumptions fail, there are standard fallbacks:

Welch’s ANOVA, oneway.test(), does not assume equal variances.
The Kruskal-Wallis test, kruskal.test(), compares the groups by rank, so it does not need normal data.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
All three tests agree here: the groups differ (p < 0.05).

title: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA
section: 18.7 What makes it spatial data science?
text:
18.7 What makes it spatial data science?
The first assumption, independence, is where spatial data cause trouble. The observations in our example are places, and places are connected.

Nearby places are alike. By the first law of geography, near things are more related than distant things. Neighboring counties share age profiles, so the 100 counties are not 100 independent pieces of evidence. Treating them as independent tends to make ANOVA’s p-value look smaller than it should.
Boundaries shape the answer. Drawing the three regions differently, or analyzing census tracts instead of counties, could change the result. That is the modifiable areal unit problem.
Spatial tools account for neighbors. Moran’s I (Chapter 22) tests whether a model’s residuals cluster on the map, and spatial regression and permutation tests build neighbors into the model to give more honest p-values.

The bottom line: before you trust a p-value from map data, map the residuals and check them for spatial autocorrelation. Our ANOVA says median male age differs across North Carolina’s regions (F = 8.44, p < 0.001), with the West oldest. Because the counties are neighbors on a map, treat that p-value with some caution.

text:
18.8 Check your understanding

An ANOVA gives p = 0.03. This means: If the groups truly didn’t differ, a result this extreme would happen about 3% of the timeThere is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is trueThe difference between the groups is large97% of the data support the hypothesis
The null hypothesis of an ANOVA is that: All the group means are equalAll the group means are differentAt least one group mean differsThe groups have different variances
A statistically significant result is always a large or important one. TRUEFALSE
The F statistic is between-group variance divided by: Within-group varianceThe overall meanThe number of groupsThe p-value
An ANOVA compares 4 groups with 40 observations in all. How many degrees of freedom does the between-groups row have? 
ANOVA gives F = 8.44 and p = 0.0004 for three regions. What can you conclude? All three regions differ from each otherThe West is older than the EastRegion causes differences in ageAt least two regions differ in median male age
Which test compares every pair of groups after an ANOVA? Shapiro-WilkTukey’s HSDKruskal-WallisMoran’s I

title: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA
text:
18.9 Summary

Data analysis is a cycle: ask, collect, describe, test, and communicate.
A statistic summarizes a sample. A test starts from a null hypothesis of no difference, and the p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. By convention, p < 0.05 is statistically significant.
p-values are easy to misuse. Report them with the size of the effect and a confidence interval, and don’t treat 0.05 as a bright line.
Variance is the average squared distance from the mean. ANOVA compares between-group with within-group variance: F = MS between ÷ MS within. A large F and small p mean at least one group mean differs.
In R: fit <- aov(value ~ group, data = d), then summary(fit). Follow it with TukeyHSD(fit) to find which groups differ. Use oneway.test() or kruskal.test() if the assumptions fail.
In North Carolina, median male age differs by region (F = 8.44, p = 0.0004), with the West oldest. Because neighboring counties are alike, check spatial data for spatial autocorrelation before trusting a p-value.

title: 18  Comparing Groups: p-values and ANOVA
text:
18.10 Exercises

By hand. Three groups have the values (2, 4, 6), (5, 7, 9), and (8, 10, 12). Calculate the group means, SS between, SS within, and F by hand, then check your answer with aov().
Which regions? Run TukeyHSD() on the North Carolina regional model. Which pairs of regions differ significantly? Does that match what you see in Figure 18.3?
Female age. Download the median age for females (variable B01002_003) for North Carolina’s counties with tidycensus, assign each county to the same regions, and run an ANOVA. Do the regions differ for women too?
Draw the lines differently. Move the boundary between the central and eastern regions one tier of counties east or west, and rerun the ANOVA. How much does F change? What does that tell you about the modifiable areal unit problem?
Births. Using the nc data from the sf package (Chapter 16), make a variable for births per square kilometer, group the counties into three regions by the longitude of their centroids, and test whether births per square kilometer differ by region. Check the assumptions, and use kruskal.test() if they fail.
