text:
18.11 Further reading

Wasserstein, R. L., and Lazar, N. A. (2016). “The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose.” The American Statistician 70(2): 129–133. Six short principles for using p-values well.
Amrhein, V., Greenland, S., and McShane, B. (2019). “Scientists Rise Up Against Statistical Significance.” Nature 567: 305–307.
Open Science Collaboration (2015). “Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science.” Science 349(6251): aac4716.
OpenIntro Statistics (4th ed.), by David Diez, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Christopher Barr, free at https://www.openintro.org/book/os/. Chapter 7 covers ANOVA.




A number calculated from a sample that summarizes the data, such as a
mean. It would change if you drew a different sample.
The claim a test starts from: that there is no difference or no
relationship. A small p-value is evidence against it.
The probability of a result at least as extreme as yours if the null
hypothesis were true. It is not the chance the null hypothesis is true.
Analysis of variance: a statistical test of whether the averages of
three or more groups differ, such as median age in three regions. It
compares variation between groups with variation within them.
ANOVA’s test statistic: the variance between groups divided by the
variance within groups. Near 1 if the groups don’t differ.
Tukey’s honestly significant difference test: compares every pair of
groups after an ANOVA, with p-values adjusted for the number of
comparisons.
One thing that was measured or recorded, such as a student, a county, or
a flight. In a data frame, each row is an observation.
A measure of spread: the standard deviation squared, so its units are
squared too. var() in R.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
A subset of a population that is surveyed to estimate something about
the whole population. Smaller samples give less certain estimates.
A measure of how spread out values are around their mean, in the same
units as the values. sd() in R.
A statistic that weighs evidence in a hypothesis test, such as
t or F: how large a pattern is compared with random
variation.
The claim that there is a difference or relationship, such as “at least
one group mean differs”.
By convention, a result with p < 0.05. Significant doesn’t
mean large or important.
Re-running an analysis in different ways until a p-value falls below
0.05, which produces false findings.
Doing research so others can check and reuse it: open access papers,
open data, open methods, and open-source software.
The discovery, in the 2010s, that many published findings fail to hold
up when other researchers repeat the studies.
A range that is likely to contain the true value of something estimated
from data. geom_smooth() shades a 95% confidence interval
around its trend line.
The squared distances of values from a mean, added up. ANOVA splits it
into between-group and within-group parts.
The number of values free to vary in a calculation. In ANOVA, k
− 1 between groups and N − k within them.
A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom: a variance.
F is the ratio of two mean squares.
An observation’s actual value minus the value a model predicts for it.
Map them to see where a model fits poorly.
The Census Bureau’s continuous survey of a sample of households every
year. It asks many more questions than the decennial census, but every
value is an estimate with a margin of error.
ACS estimates that pool 60 months of responses. They are the most
reliable ACS product and the only one for tracts and block groups. An
estimate labeled 2022 describes 2018 to 2022.
An R package that downloads US Census data through the Census API and
returns it as a tidy data frame, with boundaries attached if you ask.
A small area of about 1,200 to 8,000 people (4,000 on average), drawn to
be fairly stable over time. The workhorse unit for neighborhood
analysis.
In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as
months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic,
such as median income; each Census variable has a code.
The values of F you’d expect if the null hypothesis were true.
Its shape depends on two degrees of freedom. pf() in R.
A test run after an ANOVA to find which pairs of groups differ, such as
Tukey’s HSD.
The assumption, built into most standard statistics, that knowing one
observation tells you nothing about another. Data about places usually
break it, because nearby places tend to be alike.
A test of whether values, such as a model’s residuals, are normally
distributed. A large p-value means no evidence against normality.
A version of ANOVA that doesn’t assume the groups have equal variances.
oneway.test() in R.
A test of whether three or more groups differ, using ranks instead of
values, so it doesn’t need normal data. kruskal.test() in
R.
Waldo Tobler’s statement that “everything is related to everything else,
but near things are more related than distant things.” It is the idea
behind spatial autocorrelation.
The way results can change when the same individual data are grouped
into different areas, either larger or smaller ones or the same size
with different boundaries.
A global measure of spatial autocorrelation, from −1 (dispersed) through
0 (random) to +1 (clustered), with a p-value.
A statistical model of how one variable (such as home price) changes
with one or more others (such as distance to downtown).
A test that shuffles values across locations many times and asks how
often the shuffles beat the observed statistic.
The tendency for things that are close together to be more alike than
things that are far apart, such as neighboring counties having similar
incomes.
“Simple features”: the R package for spatial vector data. An sf object
is a data frame with a geometry column holding each row’s point, line,
or polygon.
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
The angle east or west of the Prime Meridian, from 0° to 180°. Lines of
equal longitude are meridians.
The geometric center of a polygon. st_centroid() in R.
The ability for anyone to rerun an analysis from its code and data and
get the same result.

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
19.1 From data to knowledge
Chapter 18 asked whether groups of places differ. This chapter asks a different question: how does one variable change as another changes? Do counties where more people work from home have higher house values? By how much? And how well does that explain the differences between counties?
The tool is regression. We’ll start with where regression fits in turning data into knowledge, build it up on a small example you can run, and then follow a North Carolina project on median house values from research question to residual map.
Data science is using data to gain information or knowledge about the world. Data become knowledge in steps, each adding context:
Regression is one of the main ways we take that last step: from a pattern on a map to a tested explanation.

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
Table 19.1: Each step adds context, ending in a tested explanation.










Step
What it is
North Carolina example




Data
Raw values without context
Median house value and the share of people working from home in each county


Information
Data organized and summarized
A map showing which counties have the highest house values


Knowledge
Information explained and tested
A regression showing that counties with more remote workers have higher house values








19.1.1 Spatial data are special
Spatial data need their own methods, for four reasons:

Location is a core attribute, and location is messy: projections, geocoding errors, and boundaries that change.
Nearby things are more alike. This spatial autocorrelation breaks the independence assumption behind standard statistics, including the regression in this chapter.
Spatial data are visual, so they call for maps and other visualizations.
Spatial data often change over time, which adds a temporal side to the analysis.

Spatial data science draws on many fields to deal with these: environmental and sociodemographic data with location and time attached; remote sensing, geostatistics, spatial databases, and geographic information science; cloud platforms and APIs; and programming in R, Python, and SQL.

title: 19  Linear Regression
section: 19.2 Regression explains how one variable changes with others
text:
19.2 Regression explains how one variable changes with others
Regression analysis fits a model that estimates one variable from one or more others.

The dependent variable, y, is the outcome you want to explain: here, median house value.
The independent variables, x, are the variables you think explain it: the percent working from home, median income, median age.

A regression estimates three things about each independent variable:

Direction: does y rise or fall as x rises?
Strength: how much of the variation in y does x explain?
Size: how much does y change for each one-unit change in x?


19.2.1 Correlation and regression
Correlation shows whether two variables move together. The correlation coefficient, r, runs from −1 (a perfect negative straight-line relationship) through 0 (none) to 1 (a perfect positive one) (Figure 19.1).






Figure 19.1: Four sets of points and their correlation coefficients.



Regression goes further. It estimates how much y changes for each unit of x, and it draws the line of best fit: the straight line that comes closest to the points, in the sense that the squared vertical distances from the points to the line add up to as little as possible. That’s why it is called ordinary least squares.
The line has the familiar form
\[
y = b_0 + b_1 x
\]
where b₀ is the intercept (the value of y when x is 0) and b₁ is the slope: how much y changes when x goes up by one. The intercept and slope are the model’s coefficients.

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
19.3 Writing a regression formula
In R, a regression formula puts the dependent variable on the left of the tilde, ~, and the independent variables on the right, joined by +:
dependent ~ independent1 + independent2 + ... + independentN
For example:
ice_cream_sales ~ temperature
weight ~ height + sex + cheeseburgers_per_day + steps_per_day + phone_number
The second formula makes a point: every variable needs a reason to be there. Height, sex, diet, and exercise all plausibly affect weight. A phone number has no plausible link at all, even if, by chance, it happened to correlate with weight in your data. Choose variables from what you know about the process, not by trying everything.
lm(), for linear model, fits the regression:
lm(median.house.value ~ works.from.home.percent, data = ncCounties)

19.3.1 A small example to try
An ice cream stand records its high temperature and the number of cones sold on 12 days:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The correlation is 0.98: temperature and sales move together very closely. The regression says
\[
\text{cones} = -245.7 + 6.77 \times \text{temperature}
\]
so each extra degree goes with about 6.8 more cones sold. The intercept, −245.7, is the predicted sales at 0 °F. It’s needed to place the line, but it means nothing on its own: no one buys ice cream at 0 °F, and the stand never opened on a day that cold.
Use the model to predict with predict():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
At 77 °F the model predicts about 275 cones. At 100 °F it predicts 431, but be careful: that is extrapolation, a prediction outside the range of the data (62 to 91 °F). The straight line may not hold there.

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
19.4 Anatomy of a regression
Figure 19.2 shows the parts of a fitted regression:






Figure 19.2: The ice cream regression. The blue line is the line of best fit and the shaded band its 95% confidence band. Dotted orange lines are the residuals: each day’s distance from the line.




The line of best fit is the best estimate of y for any value of x.
R² (R-squared) is the share of the variance in y that the model explains, from 0 to 1. Here R² = 0.96: temperature explains 96% of the day-to-day variation in sales. As a rough guide, below about 0.3 the two variables are barely connected.
The 95% confidence band shows how uncertain the line itself is. It’s narrowest near the middle of the data and widens toward the ends.
Residuals are the vertical distances from each point to the line: observed minus predicted. Points far from the line are outliers worth understanding, not deleting. On the 68 °F day, the stand sold about 25 fewer cones than predicted. Was it raining?


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
19.5 Reading the model summary
summary() reports the statistical results:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Work down the output:

Call: the model you fitted.
Residuals: a five-number summary of the residuals. Roughly symmetric around 0 is good.
Coefficients: one row per coefficient.

Estimate: the intercept, and the slope for each independent variable. Here 6.77 cones per degree.
Std. Error: how uncertain each estimate is.
t value: the estimate divided by its standard error.
Pr(>|t|): the p-value for the null hypothesis that the true coefficient is 0, that is, that x has no relationship with y. Stars flag small p-values: *** means p < 0.001. For temperature, p = 4.5 × 10⁻⁸ (R writes 4.51e-08), so the relationship is very unlikely to be chance.

Residual standard error: the typical size of a residual, about 14 cones.
Multiple R-squared and Adjusted R-squared: the share of variation explained. Adjusted R² lowers R² a little for each independent variable in the model, so that adding useless variables can’t make a model look better. Use it to compare models with different numbers of variables.
F-statistic: a test of whether the model as a whole explains anything, with its p-value.

title: 19  Linear Regression
section: 19.6 Example: house values in North Carolina
text:
19.6 Example: house values in North Carolina
Now a real project, written up as an R Markdown report. Its research question: what demographic variables may influence median house value in North Carolina counties in 2020? In particular, is the share of people working from home related to house values, and by how much?
The data are Census Bureau estimates for North Carolina’s 100 counties for 2020, loaded as an sf object called ncCounties. (Names ending in E, such as median.house.valueE, are estimates from the American Community Survey, as tidycensus names them.) Before modeling, map each independent variable (Figure 19.3):






Figure 19.3: The independent variables: median income, the percent working from home, median age, and the percent who are white alone, for North Carolina’s counties in 2020.



Higher incomes and more remote work stand out around the Triangle and Charlotte. Older populations are in the mountains and along parts of the coast.






TipThink about it



Why might counties where more people work from home have higher house values? Think of at least two explanations. Does working from home push prices up, or do the jobs that allow remote work simply pay more?



19.6.1 The first model
first.model <- lm(median.house.valueE ~ works.from.home.percent, data = ncCounties)
summary(first.model)
Call:
lm(formula = median.house.valueE ~ works.from.home.percent, data = ncCounties)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max
-60097 -19670  -5395  13763 102485

Coefficients:
                        Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)                73974       5839   12.67   <2e-16 ***
works.from.home.percent    36564       2185   16.73   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 29220 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7408,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7381
F-statistic:   280 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
Read the three key numbers:

The coefficient. Each additional percentage point of people working from home goes with a median house value about $36,564 higher.
The p-value. Below 2 × 10⁻¹⁶, effectively zero. Three stars: p < 0.001.
Adjusted R². 0.7381: the share working from home alone accounts for about 74% of the variation in median house value between counties.



19.6.2 Adding variables: a multivariate model
A model with more than one independent variable is a multivariate (or multiple) regression. The second model adds median age, median income, and the percent white:
second.model <- lm(median.house.valueE ~ works.from.home.percent +
                     median.ageE + median.incomeE + white.percent,
                   data = ncCounties)
summary(second.model)
Coefficients:
                          Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)             -7.949e+04  2.596e+04  -3.062  0.00286 **
works.from.home.percent  2.434e+04  2.324e+03  10.476  < 2e-16 ***
median.ageE              1.839e+02  4.794e+02   0.384  0.70218
median.incomeE           4.313e+00  7.233e-01   5.964 4.19e-08 ***
white.percent            8.154e+02  1.432e+02   5.695 1.37e-07 ***
---
Residual standard error: 21620 on 95 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.8624,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.8567
F-statistic: 148.9 on 4 and 95 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
R writes large and small numbers in scientific notation: 2.434e+04 means 2.434 × 10⁴, or 24,340. What changed?

Adjusted R² rose from 0.74 to 0.86. Together the four variables explain about 86% of the variation.
Median age is not significant (p = 0.70). Once the other variables are in the model, age adds little.
The other three are significant. Holding the others constant, each extra dollar of median income goes with $4.31 more house value (so $4,313 per $1,000 of income), and each extra percentage point white goes with about $815.
The work-from-home coefficient shrank, from $36,564 to about $24,340. Part of what the first model credited to remote work really went with income: counties where more people work from home also tend to have higher incomes. A coefficient in a multivariate model is the change in y for one unit of x with the other variables held constant.







WarningCorrelation is not causation



Even a strong, significant coefficient doesn’t show that x causes y. Here it isn’t clear which way the relationship runs: working from home could drive up house prices, or people whose jobs allow remote work may earn more and so buy more expensive houses. A good write-up says so.

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
19.7 Mapping residuals
A regression isn’t finished until you check its residuals, and with spatial data that means mapping them. A residual is a county’s observed house value minus the model’s prediction. Residuals near 0 mean the model fits that county well; large positive or negative residuals mean a poor fit.
ncCounties$resids <- second.model$residuals

tm_shape(ncCounties) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "resids",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(midpoint = 0),
              fill.legend = tm_legend("Residuals 2020",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right"))) +
  tm_title("Model Residuals, NC Counties 2020")






Figure 19.4: Residuals from the second model, by county. Purple counties have lower house values than the model predicts; green counties have higher values.



Look for clusters. If counties with large positive residuals sit next to each other, the model is missing something spatial: here, perhaps second homes and vacation markets in the mountains and on the beach, which raise house values beyond what local incomes predict. Clustered residuals also mean the observations aren’t independent, so the model’s standard errors and p-values are too small.
The fix is a cycle:

Fit the model.
Map the residuals.
Test them with Moran’s I (Chapter 22), which measures whether the residuals cluster more than chance would produce.
Revise the model: add the missing variables, or move to a spatial regression model, such as a spatial lag model or a spatial error model, that builds neighbors into the model.

Repeat steps 2 to 4 until the residuals no longer cluster.

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
19.8 Check your understanding

In lm(house_value ~ income, data = d), the dependent variable is: house_valueincomedlm
Correlation tells you how much y changes for each unit of x. TRUEFALSE
A slope of 36,564 for works.from.home.percent means each extra percentage point working from home goes with a median house value that is: $36,564 higher$36,564 lower36,564% higher36,564 times higher
An adjusted R² of 0.74 means the model explains about what percent of the variation in y? 
Which number should you use to compare models with different numbers of independent variables? Multiple R-squaredAdjusted R-squaredThe interceptThe residual standard error
In the second model, median age has p = 0.70. This means: Median age adds little once the other variables are in the modelMedian age explains 70% of house valueMedian age is the most important variableThe model is wrong
A residual is: The observed value minus the predicted valueThe predicted value minus the meanThe slope of the lineThe p-value of a coefficient
Clusters of similar residuals on a map suggest the model is missing something spatial. TRUEFALSE

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
19.9 Summary

Data become information when organized and knowledge when explained and tested. Regression is a main tool for the last step.
Spatial data need their own methods: location is messy, nearby things are alike (spatial autocorrelation), and the data are visual and change over time.
Regression models a dependent variable (y) from one or more independent variables (x). Correlation says whether two variables move together; regression says by how much, and draws the line of best fit.
In R: lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d), then summary(). Read each coefficient, its p-value, and the adjusted R². Every variable needs a reason to be in the model.
In North Carolina in 2020, each percentage point working from home went with about $36,564 higher median house value (adjusted R² = 0.74). Adding income and percent white raised adjusted R² to 0.86 and shrank that coefficient to about $24,340.
Regression shows association, not causation.
Map the residuals. Clusters of similar residuals mean the model misses something spatial; test them with Moran’s I, then revise the model.

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
19.10 Exercises

Ice cream by hand. Using the ice cream model, predict sales at 70 °F and at 85 °F from the equation, then check with predict(). Which of the 12 days has the largest positive residual?
Fahrenheit to Celsius. Convert temp to degrees Celsius and refit the model. What happens to the slope, the intercept, and R²? Why?
Your own variables. Download median house value (B25077_001), median household income (B19013_001), and one variable of your choice for North Carolina’s counties with tidycensus (Chapter 13). Fit a model with income, then with both variables. Did adjusted R² go up?
Map the residuals. Map the residuals from your model in Exercise 3. Where does the model over-predict and under-predict? Do the residuals look clustered?
Births. With the sf package’s nc data, regress BIR79 on BIR74. Interpret the slope and R². Why is this a less interesting model than it looks?

title: 19  Linear Regression
text:
19.11 Further reading

OpenIntro Statistics (4th ed.), by David Diez, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Christopher Barr, free at https://www.openintro.org/book/os/. Chapters 8 and 9 cover linear and multiple regression.
Geocomputation with R (2nd ed.), by Robin Lovelace, Jakub Nowosad, and Jannes Muenchow, free at https://r.geocompx.org. Its chapter on statistical learning applies models to spatial data.
Spatial Regression Models (2nd ed.), by Michael D. Ward and Kristian Skrede Gleditsch (SAGE, 2018), introduces the spatial lag and spatial error models.




The outcome a model explains, y. It goes on the left of the
~ in an R formula.
A variable used to explain the dependent variable, x. It goes
on the right of the ~.
Whether two variables move together. It doesn’t say how much one changes
with the other, or which causes which.
A statistical model of how one variable (such as home price) changes
with one or more others (such as distance to downtown).
A number a regression estimates: the intercept, or the slope for each
independent variable.
The probability of a result at least as extreme as yours if the null
hypothesis were true. It is not the chance the null hypothesis is true.
The share of the variation in y that a model explains, from 0
to 1.
R-squared lowered a little for each independent variable, so adding
useless variables can’t make a model look better. Use it to compare
models.
A regression with more than one independent variable. Each coefficient
is the change in y with the others held constant.
An observation’s actual value minus the value a model predicts for it.
Map them to see where a model fits poorly.
In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as
months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic,
such as median income; each Census variable has a code.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
The specific, answerable question a project sets out to answer, usually
with a place and a time.
A method for flattening the curved graticule onto a flat map. Every
projection distorts shape, area, distance, or direction.
Turning an address or place name into coordinates that can be mapped.
The tendency for things that are close together to be more alike than
things that are far apart, such as neighboring counties having similar
incomes.
The assumption, built into most standard statistics, that knowing one
observation tells you nothing about another. Data about places usually
break it, because nearby places tend to be alike.
The use of data that have a location attached to answer questions about
the world. It combines what we study (the spatial), how we
handle it (data skills), and how we ask and answer questions
(science).
Collecting information about Earth without touching it, from sensors on
satellites, aircraft, or drones. It produces most of the world’s raster
data.
Application Programming Interface: a set of rules for how one program
asks another for data or services, such as your R script asking the
Census Bureau’s server for a table.
Structured Query Language, the language of databases. ArcGIS
where clauses use it: fcounty = 'Orange'.
r, from −1 to 1: how closely two variables follow a straight
line, and in which direction. cor() in R.
The straight line that comes closest to the points in a scatterplot: a
regression’s estimate of y for each x.
The usual way to fit a regression line: choose the line that makes the
sum of squared residuals as small as possible.
The predicted value of y when every x is 0: where the
regression line crosses the y axis.
How much y changes when x goes up by one unit: the
coefficient of an independent variable.
Combining two tables by matching rows on a shared key column, such as
attaching Census data to boundaries by GEOID with
left_join().
A model in which y is a straight-line function of the
x variables. lm() in R.
Using a model to predict outside the range of the data it was fitted to.
The relationship may not hold there.
A range that is likely to contain the true value of something estimated
from data. geom_smooth() shades a 95% confidence interval
around its trend line.
A measure of spread: the standard deviation squared, so its units are
squared too. var() in R.
A value far from all the others. It may be real or an error, so check it
before you report it.
A measure of how much a sample estimate would vary from sample to
sample. For the ACS, it is the margin of error divided by 1.645.
The claim a test starts from: that there is no difference or no
relationship. A small p-value is evidence against it.
ANOVA’s test statistic: the variance between groups divided by the
variance within groups. Near 1 if the groups don’t differ.
A document format (.Rmd) that mixes formatted text with
chunks of R code. Knitting it runs the code and builds a finished
report.
“Simple features”: the R package for spatial vector data. An sf object
is a data frame with a geometry column holding each row’s point, line,
or polygon.
The Census Bureau’s continuous survey of a sample of households every
year. It asks many more questions than the decennial census, but every
value is an estimate with a margin of error.
An R package that downloads US Census data through the Census API and
returns it as a tidy data frame, with boundaries attached if you ask.
By convention, a result with p < 0.05. Significant doesn’t
mean large or important.
One thing that was measured or recorded, such as a student, a county, or
a flight. In a data frame, each row is an observation.
A global measure of spatial autocorrelation, from −1 (dispersed) through
0 (random) to +1 (clustered), with a p-value.
A spatial regression model that includes the neighbors’ values of
y as an extra explanatory variable.
A spatial regression model that allows the errors of neighboring
observations to be correlated.
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
The weighted average of an observation’s neighbors’ values, calculated
with row-standardized weights. lag.listw() in spdep.

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
20.1 No information without data
You have now learned to get data, tidy it, map it, describe it, and test it. This chapter is about putting those pieces together into a project that someone else can read, trust, and rerun. We start with the ideas underneath: what data, information, and knowledge are, where data come from, and what makes an analysis science. Then we walk through a real project, on house values in North Carolina, section by section.
The writer and programmer Daniel Keys Moran put the first idea briefly: you can have data without information, but you can’t have information without data. Raw data become information only after they are processed, organized, and interpreted.
A list of hourly temperatures is data. A forecast that says “bring an umbrella this afternoon” is information.
crumbs: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
Table 20.1: Data and information.











Data
Information




What it is
Raw and unprocessed
Processed, organized data with meaning


What it’s for
The basis for analysis
Supporting decisions and giving insight


Value
Little on its own
Directly valuable and actionable


Examples
Numbers, dates, measurements, text
Reports, summaries, insights, conclusions








20.1.1 The DIKW pyramid
The DIKW pyramid takes the idea further, in four levels (Figure 20.1). Each builds on the one below:

Data: facts and figures.
Information: data organized to be useful.
Knowledge: information built up and tested over time and across many situations.
Wisdom: principles, reasoning, and knowledge applied to judge what is true and right.







Figure 20.1: The DIKW pyramid, with an example of each level from this chapter’s project on North Carolina house values.



Data science is using data to gain information or knowledge about the world. It mostly works on the bottom levels of the pyramid, and helps people climb toward the top.
crumbs: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
20.2 The data science process
Chapter 6 introduced the data science workflow from R for Data Science: import the data, tidy it, then cycle through transform, visualize, and model until you understand it, and finally communicate the results. The middle loop repeats, and programming runs through every step. A project write-up is the “communicate” step, but a good one shows all the others too.

20.2.1 Big data
Big data is often described by three Vs:

Volume: the sheer amount, from terabytes of records, transactions, and files up.
Velocity: how fast it arrives, from batches to near-real-time feeds and live streams.
Variety: the mix of structured tables, semi-structured JSON, and unstructured text and images.

Many spatial datasets, such as satellite imagery or the GPS traces from phones, score high on all three.


20.2.2 Where data come from



Table 20.2: Where data come from, and the formats they arrive in.









Sources
Formats




Authoritative: federal, state, county, and local government
Files: GeoJSON, shapefiles, CSV


Web scraping: social media, live feeds, news
API calls: data on demand (Chapters 13 and 14)


The Internet of Things: sensors streaming readings
Images, text, and 3D formats


Real-time analytics feeds







Government agencies are usually the most authoritative sources. Also note whether a dataset is static, a fixed snapshot, or dynamic, continually updated, because a dynamic source may give different data the next time you run your code.
crumbs: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
20.3 Science: reproducibility and replicability
Spatial data science is still science. It builds on a body of knowledge, follows the scientific method, and rests on empirical evidence. Two words describe whether others can trust and build on a result:

Reproducible: the same data and methods give the same results. Anyone can rerun your analysis and get your numbers.
Replicable: a new study, with different data, answering the same question, gets consistent results.

Open science makes both possible: open access (papers anyone can read), open data, open methods, open-source software such as R and RStudio, open peer review, and open educational resources (like this book).
R Markdown, from Chapter 2, is a reproducibility tool. It keeps data loading, code, results, and write-up in one document, so anyone with the file and the data can knit it and get the same report.
crumbs: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
20.4 Why spatial data are special
Location links observations together, so spatial data need their own methods.
What makes them special:

The first law of geography: near things are more related than distant things.
Spatial autocorrelation: values cluster, so observations are not independent. Neighboring counties tend to have similar house values.
Spatial heterogeneity: relationships change from place to place. Remote work may matter more for house values near cities than in rural counties.

What it means for your analysis:

Clustered residuals make standard tests overconfident. Map your model’s residuals and test them with Moran’s I (Chapter 22).
Scale and zoning matter. County and tract results can differ: the modifiable areal unit problem.
Projection matters. Distances and areas depend on the coordinate system (Chapter 12).
crumbs: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
20.5 Building blocks of a project
Every project has the same building blocks:



Table 20.3: The building blocks of a spatial data science project.









Section
What goes in it




Introduction
Your research question and why it matters


Background
What earlier work found, and how it relates to your question


Data and methods
Your data, cited and described; the code that tidies them; maps and descriptive statistics


Results
Maps, graphs, and statistics that help answer the question


Conclusion
Your answer, as well as you can give it; limitations; what you’d do differently


References
Every source you used






We’ll go through each one using an example project, written in R Markdown, titled What Demographic Variables May Influence Median House Value for North Carolina in 2020? You met its models in Chapter 19.

20.5.1 Introduction: the research question
The research question drives everything else. A good one is:

Specific and focused. Include the place and time where they matter.
Answerable, even if you end up not able to answer it fully.
Worth asking. Explain why it matters.

It doesn’t have to be phrased as a question, but that often helps.
The example’s introduction says that the project examines which demographic factors might relate to median home value in North Carolina’s counties in 2020: in particular, whether the percentage of people working from home is related to home value, and by how much it raises or lowers it. It names the other variables it will bring in (percent white alone, median age, and median income) and says the project will explore the data, build a model, and discuss how well the model fits, statistically and spatially, using residuals. A reader knows the place, the time, the variables, and the plan by the end of the second paragraph.






TipThink about it



Which is the better research question, and why? (a) “What affects house prices?” (b) “Is the share of residents who work from home related to median house value in North Carolina’s counties in 2020?” How would you make (b) more spatial?




20.5.2 Background: build on earlier research
The background shows you’ve read what came before. What have others found? How does it shape your question, your data, or your methods?
The example’s background notes that house prices and cost of living have clear geographic patterns, but are not a common topic for geographers. It summarizes a study by Campbell and James that built a housing cost index for North Carolina’s counties, the ratio of median home value to median household income, and tested whether second homes in the mountains and at the beach push costs up. That earlier work suggests variables to include and a spatial pattern to look for.


20.5.3 Data and methods: show your work
In data and methods, you show your work:

Cite the source of your data: which agency, which survey, which year, and how you got it.
Include the code that loads and tidies the data.
Describe the data with summary statistics and maps.

# Load the libraries used in this research
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

# Load the 2020 NC counties data
ncCounties <- read_sf("...")
glimpse(ncCounties)
glimpse() shows 100 rows, one per county, and the columns. Then a summary and a map of the dependent variable, median home value, and a map of each independent variable (Figure 19.3). Mapping each variable before modeling it is how you notice patterns, such as higher incomes and more remote work around the Triangle and Charlotte, and problems, such as a county with a missing value.


20.5.4 Results: model your question
A model is a simplified representation of a real-world process. The results section fits models that test your question, and reports them with maps, graphs, and statistics.
The example’s first model tests whether the share of people working from home is related to median house value. Each additional percentage point working from home goes with about $36,564 higher median house value, with an adjusted R² of 0.74. A second model adds median income, median age, and percent white, and raises the adjusted R² to 0.86 (Chapter 19).


20.5.5 Check the model: map the residuals
A spatial results section doesn’t end with the model summary. Check the model by mapping its residuals, each county’s observed value minus the model’s prediction:

Fit the model.
Map the residuals. Where does the model over- or under-predict?
Test them with Moran’s I (Chapter 22). Do the residuals cluster more than chance would produce?
Revise the model. If they cluster, add explanatory variables or fit a spatial lag or spatial error model.

Repeat steps 2 to 4 until the residuals no longer cluster.


20.5.6 A second method: comparing regions with ANOVA
Regression asks how one variable changes with another. ANOVA (Chapter 18) asks whether a variable’s mean differs across three or more groups. In a project on North Carolina, the groups can be regions, such as the mountains, the Piedmont, and the coastal plain, and the variable median male age by county. aov(age ~ region) tests whether the regions differ, and TukeyHSD() shows which ones. Because the groups are places, map them, so the reader can see the regional pattern.


20.5.7 Conclusion: answer the question
The conclusion should:

Answer your question, or explain honestly why you couldn’t.
Discuss limitations. What could make the results misleading?
Say what you’d do differently next time, and what future work should try.

The example’s conclusion does all three. It answers the question: three variables (percent working from home, percent white, and median income) are related to median house value, and each extra percentage point working from home adds potentially over $20,000. It is honest about the spatial fit: the residuals vary a lot across the state, with some mountain, coastal, and rural counties not following the model, which suggests missing variables. It names limitations: medians hide the range within each county, and the direction of the relationship is unclear (does remote work raise prices, or do people who can work from home simply earn more?). And it proposes future work: smaller units such as census tracts, more variables such as job type and education, and comparisons over time or with similar states.


20.5.8 References
List every source you used, in a consistent style, and cite them in the text. That includes data sources, such as “U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates”, and R packages, which you can cite with citation("tidycensus").
crumbs: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
section: 20.6 So, what is spatial data science?
text:
20.6 So, what is spatial data science?
Spatial data science combines three things:

spatial data,
maps and visualizations, and
spatial analysis.

Done well, it is also open, reproducible, and replicable, and it is often built on big data.
One caution. Using spatial data doesn’t by itself make a project spatial data science. A regression on county data that never maps or tests its residuals is ordinary statistics that happens to use places. You also need spatial analysis: a question with spatial aspects, such as the regional ANOVA, the residual map, or a test for spatial autocorrelation.
crumbs: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
20.7 Check your understanding

A list of every county’s median house value, with no summary or map, is: DataInformationKnowledgeWisdom
Which level sits at the top of the DIKW pyramid? 
Running the same code on the same data and getting the same results is called: ReproducibilityReplicabilityVelocitySpatial heterogeneity
The three Vs of big data are volume, velocity, and: VarietyValidityValueVisualization
Which section of a project states the research question? IntroductionBackgroundResultsReferences
A research question should always be phrased as a question. TRUEFALSE
In which section do you discuss what you would do differently next time? Data and methodsResultsConclusionBackground
Any project that uses spatial data is spatial data science. TRUEFALSE
crumbs: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
20.8 Summary

Data are raw values; information is data organized and interpreted. The DIKW pyramid adds knowledge and wisdom on top.
The data science workflow is import, tidy, a loop of transform, visualize, and model, then communicate. Big data is described by volume, velocity, and variety.
Data come from authoritative agencies, web scraping, sensors, and feeds, as files or through APIs, and can be static or dynamic.
Science should be reproducible (same data and methods, same results) and replicable (new data, consistent results). Open science and R Markdown make that easier.
Spatial data are special because of the first law of geography, spatial autocorrelation, and spatial heterogeneity. Map and test residuals, and watch scale, zoning, and projection.
A project has an introduction (the research question), background, data and methods, results, a conclusion, and references.
Spatial data science combines spatial data, maps, and spatial analysis. Spatial data alone aren’t enough.
crumbs: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
20.9 Exercises

Climb the pyramid. Pick a dataset you’ve used this semester. Give one example of it at each level of the DIKW pyramid.
Sharpen a question. Rewrite “Is pollution bad for health?” as a specific, answerable, spatial research question about North Carolina. Name the place, time, units of analysis, and variables.
Find the background. Search Google Scholar for one published study related to your question from Exercise 2. Write two sentences on what it found and how it shapes your own question or methods.
Data and methods. For your question, list each dataset you’d need, who publishes it, whether it’s static or dynamic, and how you’d get it into R.
Peer review. Swap project drafts with a classmate. For each building block in Table 20.3, write one thing that works and one thing to improve. Is their project spatial data science, by the definition in this chapter?

title: 20  Writing a Spatial Data Science Project
text:
20.10 Further reading

R for Data Science (2nd ed.), by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund, free at https://r4ds.hadley.nz. The introduction describes the data science workflow, and the “Quarto” chapters cover writing reproducible reports.
National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2019). Reproducibility and Replicability in Science. National Academies Press. Free at https://doi.org/10.17226/25303. The source of the definitions used in this chapter.
Campbell, H. S., Jr., and James, R. D. (2021). “Place, Space, and Cost of Living in North Carolina: A Research Note.” Southeastern Geographer 61(1): 81–104. The study the example project builds on.




Data, information, knowledge, wisdom: four levels, each built on the one
below, from raw facts to judging what is true and right.
The steps of a data analysis: import, tidy, then a loop of transform,
visualize, and model, and finally communicate.
The ability for anyone to rerun an analysis from its code and data and
get the same result.
When a new study, with new data, answering the same question gets
consistent results.
Doing research so others can check and reuse it: open access papers,
open data, open methods, and open-source software.
The use of data that have a location attached to answer questions about
the world. It combines what we study (the spatial), how we
handle it (data skills), and how we ask and answer questions
(science).
The specific, answerable question a project sets out to answer, usually
with a place and a time.
A language, like R, that runs code one line at a time: an interpreter
reads each line, translates it, and runs it before moving on.
Data too large, fast, or varied for ordinary tools, often described by
three Vs: volume, velocity, and variety.
JavaScript Object Notation: structured text that most web APIs send
back, which R can turn into lists or data frames.
An open, plain-text format for vector features, written in JSON.
Coordinates are longitude first, then latitude, in WGS84.
A plain-text table in which each line is a row and commas separate the
values. Read one into R with read.csv() or
read_csv().
Application Programming Interface: a set of rules for how one program
asks another for data or services, such as your R script asking the
Census Bureau’s server for a table.
Data that are continually updated, so the same request may return
different data later. Static data are a fixed snapshot.
The integrated development environment (IDE) where you write and run R.
R does the computing; RStudio is the workspace around it.
A document format (.Rmd) that mixes formatted text with
chunks of R code. Knitting it runs the code and builds a finished
report.
To build an R Markdown file into a finished document (HTML, PDF, or
Word). Knitting reruns every code chunk from the top in a fresh R
session.
One thing that was measured or recorded, such as a student, a county, or
a flight. In a data frame, each row is an observation.
Waldo Tobler’s statement that “everything is related to everything else,
but near things are more related than distant things.” It is the idea
behind spatial autocorrelation.
The tendency for things that are close together to be more alike than
things that are far apart, such as neighboring counties having similar
incomes.
The assumption, built into most standard statistics, that knowing one
observation tells you nothing about another. Data about places usually
break it, because nearby places tend to be alike.
The idea that relationships between variables change from place to
place. A link that is strong in one city may be weak, or reversed, in
another.
An observation’s actual value minus the value a model predicts for it.
Map them to see where a model fits poorly.
A global measure of spatial autocorrelation, from −1 (dispersed) through
0 (random) to +1 (clustered), with a p-value.
The level of detail at which you study something: addresses,
neighborhoods, counties, or states. A pattern that is clear at one scale
can vanish or reverse at another.
A small area of about 1,200 to 8,000 people (4,000 on average), drawn to
be fairly stable over time. The workhorse unit for neighborhood
analysis.
The way results can change when the same individual data are grouped
into different areas, either larger or smaller ones or the same size
with different boundaries.
A method for flattening the curved graticule onto a flat map. Every
projection distorts shape, area, distance, or direction.
The rules that tie coordinates to places on the Earth, including how the
round Earth is flattened onto a map (the projection). Layers must share
a coordinate system before you can combine them.
In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as
months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic,
such as median income; each Census variable has a code.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
The arrangement of objects in space: clustered, random, or dispersed.
One number that describes many values, such as their mean, median,
maximum, or count. summarize() calculates them.
The outcome a model explains, y. It goes on the left of the
~ in an R formula.
A variable used to explain the dependent variable, x. It goes
on the right of the ~.
A value that is unknown, written NA (“not available”) in R.
Most calculations with NA give NA; test for it
with is.na().
R-squared lowered a little for each independent variable, so adding
useless variables can’t make a model look better. Use it to compare
models.
The weighted average of an observation’s neighbors’ values, calculated
with row-standardized weights. lag.listw() in spdep.
A spatial regression model that allows the errors of neighboring
observations to be correlated.
A statistical model of how one variable (such as home price) changes
with one or more others (such as distance to downtown).
Analysis of variance: a statistical test of whether the averages of
three or more groups differ, such as median age in three regions. It
compares variation between groups with variation within them.
The Census Bureau’s continuous survey of a sample of households every
year. It asks many more questions than the decennial census, but every
value is an estimate with a margin of error.

estimate labeled 2022 describes 2018 to 2022.

Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().

files end in .qmd. This book is written in Quarto.

title: 21  Distance and Neighborhoods
text:
21.1 Distance is a fundamental geographic concept
How far is Chapel Hill from Charlotte? About 179 km in a straight line, but more like 230 km by road, and two and a half hours by car, longer at rush hour. Which answer is right depends on your question.
This chapter has two parts. The first is about distance: what it means, why it matters, and the main ways to measure it. The second uses distance, and shared borders, to decide which features are neighbors, and stores those relationships in a neighborhood weight matrix. That matrix is the input to nearly every spatial statistic in the rest of this book, starting with spatial autocorrelation in Chapter 22.
Distance shapes the relationships and interactions among people, things, and places: where you shop, who you know, which clinic you can reach. Geographers work with two ideas of distance:
The two often work together. Residential segregation is the classic case: two neighborhoods can sit side by side on a map yet be far apart socially.

title: 21  Distance and Neighborhoods
text:
Physical distance is the separation measured across the Earth’s surface, in meters, kilometers, or miles.
Social distance is separation measured by connection, similarity, or interaction: how connected or isolated people and groups are. It shapes social networks, who interacts with whom, and how information or disease moves through a population.



21.1.1 Distance decay
Distance decay is one of the central regularities in geography: interaction between places, actual or potential, decreases as the distance between them increases. Distance has “friction”. Overcoming it costs time, money, or effort, so people choose closer options.

Fewer customers visit a store the farther away they live.
Migration between two cities shrinks as the distance between them grows.
Clinic use drops as travel time rises.

Distance decay is often modeled as an inverse power of distance, such as 1/d or 1/d², or as an exponential function. Keep that idea in mind: we’ll use the same form for continuous neighbor weights later in the chapter.


21.1.2 Why measure distance?
We use distance in three ways:

Explain it: why are some places farther from services than others?
Measure it as an input to other calculations, such as accessibility scores or neighbor weights.
Map it: distance surfaces, service areas, and isochrones, lines of equal travel time, such as the area within a 15-minute drive of a hospital.

In GIS, most work with distance falls into three operations:



Table 21.1: Distance-based operations in GIS.











Operation
What it does
Example
In R




Spatial query
Selects features by distance
All schools within 1 km of a highway
sf::st_is_within_distance()


Buffer
Turns a distance into an area around a feature
A 500 m zone around each transit stop
sf::st_buffer()


Identify neighbors
Finds the features within each feature’s neighborhood
The census tracts that border each tract
spdep::poly2nb()






The question you are asking decides which distance measure fits.

title: 21  Distance and Neighborhoods
text:
21.2 Measuring distance

21.2.1 Euclidean distance
Euclidean distance is straight-line distance, from the Pythagorean theorem. The differences in x and y between two points are the legs of a right triangle, and the distance is the hypotenuse:
\[
d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}
\]
It is a simple calculation that doesn’t need a GIS, but it assumes a flat surface with the same units in x and y. That means projected coordinates. Never use it on latitude and longitude: a degree of longitude is about 111 km at the Equator but shrinks to nothing at the poles (Chapter 12).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Euclidean distance has three limitations:

It assumes a flat Earth. The error grows with distance. Over hundreds of kilometers, use great circle distance.
It assumes flat terrain. It underestimates the real separation in the mountains.
It assumes no barriers. Rivers, fences, buildings, and missing roads all block straight-line travel. A driver can’t cross a lake just because it’s the shortest path.

The next measures each relax one of these assumptions.


21.2.2 Great circle distance
Great circle distance is the shortest distance between two points on a sphere, measured along its surface, like the route a long-haul flight takes. Use it for points stored in longitude and latitude, and always when points are far apart. With longitudes λ and latitudes φ, in radians:
\[
D = R \cdot \arccos\left[\sin\varphi_1 \sin\varphi_2 + \cos\varphi_1 \cos\varphi_2 \cos(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)\right]
\]
where R is the Earth’s radius, about 6,371 km on average. (The haversine formula gives the same answer and is more accurate for very short distances.)

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Chapel Hill to Charlotte is about 179 km, and Chapel Hill to London about 6,252 km. You rarely need to write this yourself: sf::st_distance() computes great circle distances automatically when your data are in longitude and latitude, and Euclidean distances when they are projected.


21.2.3 Manhattan distance
Manhattan distance, or city-block distance, accounts for barriers by restricting travel to routes that run north-south and east-west, as on Manhattan’s grid of streets. Instead of cutting diagonally, it adds the horizontal and vertical differences:
\[
d = |x_2 - x_1| + |y_2 - y_1|
\]

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Manhattan distance is never shorter than the Euclidean distance between the same points. For a purely diagonal trip it is about 1.41 times longer (√2). It works poorly where streets don’t follow a grid.


21.2.4 Network distance and travel time
Network distance restricts travel to the lines, or arcs, of a network, such as streets, rail lines, or rivers. The route is a chain of arcs, and the distance is the sum of their lengths. Real networks add rules: one-way streets, turn restrictions, and speed limits. Esri’s Network Analyst and routing services calculate it, and so do R packages such as sfnetworks and dodgr.
Travel time goes one step further and measures separation in minutes instead of meters, which is closer to how people experience distance. It needs a network with speeds, or a travel-cost surface for off-road travel, and road speeds, turns, and traffic all matter. Calculating it for many origin-destination pairs can take a lot of computing. Most U.S. studies assume everyone travels by car, which overstates access for people who rely on transit or walking; better studies add other modes.


21.2.5 Straight lines or networks?
People usually move along networks, so true separation shouldn’t be measured as a straight line. But Euclidean and network distances are often highly correlated, and where they are, Euclidean distance is a reasonable and much cheaper stand-in. The correlation is weaker in rural areas, near water, and where networks are sparse. Before you choose, compute both for a sample of your data and check how closely they agree.






TipThink about it



You want to measure each North Carolina county’s access to hospitals. Which distance measure would you use for a county in the Triangle? For a county on the Outer Banks, where the nearest hospital may be across a sound? Why?

title: 21  Distance and Neighborhoods
text:
21.3 Neighborhoods and neighbors

21.3.1 Comparing separation between features
There are two basic ways to say how far apart features are, and both become ways to define neighbors:

Absolute distance: the actual distance separating them. Example: everything within 2 km.
Relative distance: separation compared with other features. Examples: the nearest feature, the nearest k features, or features that touch (topology).



21.3.2 Why neighbors matter
The first law of geography says that near things are more related than distant things. Values at nearby locations tend to be similar, and similarity decreases with distance. This dependence is spatial autocorrelation. To measure it, we first have to say which locations are “near”: we need neighbors.
A neighborhood, in spatial analysis, is the zone of influence around a feature: an idea of nearness (things close to one another) or of connectedness (things that affect one another). Neighbors are the features inside a feature’s neighborhood.
Three details matter:

Every observation gets its own set of neighbors.
Neighbors need not be symmetric. With nearest neighbors, A can be B’s neighbor without B being A’s, if B has another feature even closer.
Some observations may have no neighbors at all. An island county, or an isolated point, needs special handling. In spdep, set zero.policy = TRUE.

Nearly every spatial method needs a neighbor definition: global spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I, Geary’s C), local indicators (local Moran’s I, Getis-Ord Gi*), spatial regression (spatial lag and spatial error models), and spatial smoothing and interpolation. In every case, the neighbor definition is a choice you make, and different definitions give different neighbors and different results.


21.3.3 Binary or continuous neighbors
There are two ways to record a neighbor relationship:

Binary (yes or no): a feature either is a neighbor or isn’t, stored as 1 or 0. Binary weights are simpler to interpret and are the default in most software.
Continuous: an amount of “neighborliness”, usually based on distance, so closer features get larger weights. Some neighbors are strong and others weak. Continuous weights are distance decay applied to neighbors.

title: 21  Distance and Neighborhoods
text:
21.4 Three ways to define neighbors



Table 21.2: Three ways to define neighbors.










Approach
Neighbors are
In spdep




Absolute distance
Features within a set distance
dnearneigh()


Relative distance: nearest features
The nearest one, or the nearest k
knearneigh() and knn2nb()


Relative distance: topology
Polygons that share a border
poly2nb(), with queen = TRUE or FALSE







21.4.1 Distance band neighbors
With a distance band, features are neighbors if they fall within a chosen threshold distance. For points, measure between the points. For polygons, measure between their centroids, which can mislead: two large rural counties may share a long border yet have centroids far apart.
The threshold is the key decision:

Too small, and many features have no neighbors.
Too large, and almost everything is a neighbor.
A common start is the smallest distance that gives every feature at least one neighbor, which is the largest of the nearest-neighbor distances.

The top row of Figure 21.1 shows a distance band on 19 points that are dense near the center and sparse at the edges. With d = 8, the central point has four neighbors. The same d gives a point near the edge none. This is the edge effect: features at the boundary of a study area, or in sparse areas, get few or no neighbors, partly because we can’t see past the edge of our data. For these 19 points, every point has at least one neighbor only once d reaches about 20.






Figure 21.1: Distance bands (top) and k nearest neighbors (bottom) for the same 19 points. Each panel shows one focal point (red) and its neighbors (blue). With a distance band of 8, the central point has four neighbors and the edge point has none. With k = 4, both points have four neighbors, but the edge point’s neighborhood stretches much farther.





21.4.2 Inverse distance weights
Distance band neighbors can also be continuous. Each neighbor inside the band gets a weight from an inverse function of distance:
\[
w_{ij} = \frac{1}{d_{ij}^{\,x}}
\]
where wij is the weight from observation i to observation j, dij is the distance between them, and x is the distance-decay parameter: larger values make weights fall off faster. 1 or 2 is common. Features beyond the threshold get a weight of 0.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Inverse distance weights grow very large as distance approaches 0, so check for duplicate or nearly identical points.


21.4.3 k nearest neighbors
The nearest-neighbor approach ignores the actual distance and keeps the k closest features. For polygons, it uses their centroids.

Every feature gets exactly k neighbors, so no one is left out.
It adapts to density. Neighbors are close in dense areas and far apart in sparse ones (bottom row of Figure 21.1).
Relationships are not always symmetric. My nearest neighbor may have someone else even closer. spdep’s make.sym.nb() forces symmetry if a method requires it.

A distance band gives a constant distance and a variable number of neighbors. k nearest neighbors gives a constant number and a variable distance. Choosing k is a trade-off: a small k keeps local detail, while a larger k gives more stable averages but pulls in less related features. Try a few values of k and check whether your conclusions change.


21.4.4 Contiguity: rook and queen
Topology-based neighbors ignore distance altogether and ask whether two polygons touch. Points can’t share a border, so this only works for polygons. (If you need contiguity for points, first build Thiessen or Voronoi polygons around them: each polygon holds the area closer to its point than to any other.) There are two common rules, named after how the chess pieces move (Figure 21.2):

Rook contiguity: polygons must share an edge, a boundary segment of some length. On a grid, each cell has four rook neighbors.
Queen contiguity: a shared edge or a single shared corner is enough. On a grid, each cell has eight queen neighbors.







Figure 21.2: Rook and queen neighbors (N) of cell i on a grid.



Every rook neighbor is also a queen neighbor, so the queen set is always the same size or larger. On irregular real boundaries, such as counties, the two sets are often almost the same (Figure 21.3). The neighbors of the neighbors are called second-order neighbors.






Figure 21.3: Wake County’s contiguity neighbors, from the county boundaries in the sf package’s nc data. Six counties share an edge with Wake. Nash touches it only at a corner, so it is a queen neighbor but not a rook neighbor.



In the nc county boundaries, 14 pairs of counties touch only at a corner, so the queen rule gives 490 neighbor links and the rook rule 462.

title: 21  Distance and Neighborhoods
text:
21.5 The neighborhood weight matrix
However you define neighbors, the result is stored the same way: a neighborhood weight matrix, usually called W. It is a table with n rows and n columns, where n is the number of observations. Entry wij, in row i and column j, describes the relationship between observation i and observation j. The diagonal is 0, because no observation is its own neighbor.
Here are four census tracts in a row, A | B | C | D, so each touches only the tracts beside it. With binary rook contiguity:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Read across a row to find a tract’s neighbors: B’s row has 1s under A and C.

21.5.1 Row standardization
Weights are often row-standardized: each weight is divided by its row’s total, so every row sums to 1. B’s two neighbors then get 0.5 each, and the edge tracts’ single neighbors get 1. In spdep this is style = "W".
Why bother? Multiplying a row-standardized matrix by a variable gives each observation the average of its neighbors’ values. That neighborhood average is called the spatial lag:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
B’s neighbors, A and C, average (10 + 30) ÷ 2 = 20. Moran’s I (Chapter 22) compares each value with exactly this kind of neighborhood average.


21.5.2 Building neighbors and weights in R
In spdep, neighbors are stored as a neighbor list (class nb), a compact version of W that lists only each observation’s neighbors. nb2listw() turns any neighbor list into weights. Assuming library(sf), library(spdep), and an sf polygon layer named tracts in a projected coordinate system:
# Contiguity neighbors (queen is the default)
nb_queen <- poly2nb(tracts, queen = TRUE)
nb_rook  <- poly2nb(tracts, queen = FALSE)

# k nearest neighbors, using tract centroids
coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(tracts))
nb_knn <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 4))

# Distance band: 0 to 5 km (in the CRS's units, meters)
nb_dist <- dnearneigh(coords, d1 = 0, d2 = 5000)

# Row-standardized spatial weights
lw <- nb2listw(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

# Inverse distance weights (x = 1) on the distance band
idw <- lapply(nbdists(nb_dist, coords), function(d) 1 / d)
lw_idw <- nb2listw(nb_dist, glist = idw, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
dnearneigh() measures in the units of your coordinate reference system, so project first. summary(nb_queen) reports how many neighbors each observation has, and warns about any with none.


21.5.3 Weight matrices can encode social distance
Nothing requires the entries of a weight matrix to be geographic. They just record which observations are related and how strongly. They could be commuting flows between counties, airline routes, shared school districts, similarity in income or age structure, or trade and migration ties between countries. Two counties linked by heavy commuting may influence each other more than two counties that merely touch. Any n × n matrix of relationships becomes spatial weights with spdep::mat2listw().

title: 21  Distance and Neighborhoods
text:
21.7 Summary

Physical distance is measured across the Earth’s surface; social distance by connection and similarity. Distance decay says interaction falls as distance grows.
Euclidean distance is the straight line; use it only on projected coordinates. Great circle distance follows the curved Earth and suits longitude and latitude. Manhattan distance follows a street grid. Network distance and travel time follow real routes.
The first law of geography is why neighbors matter: to measure spatial autocorrelation, we must first say who is near whom.
Neighbors can be defined by a distance band (absolute distance), by the k nearest neighbors, or by contiguity: rook (a shared edge) or queen (an edge or a corner). Weights can be binary or continuous, such as inverse distance.
Distance bands give a constant distance and a variable count, and leave edge features short. k nearest neighbors gives a constant count and a variable distance, and can be asymmetric.
Neighbor relationships are stored in a weight matrix, W. Row-standardized weights sum to 1 across each row, so W times a variable gives the spatial lag: each observation’s neighborhood average.
In spdep: poly2nb(), knearneigh() with knn2nb(), and dnearneigh() build neighbors; nb2listw() turns them into weights. Each choice gives a different weight matrix, and can give different results, so justify yours and try more than one.

title: 21  Distance and Neighborhoods
text:
21.8 Exercises

By hand. For the points (2, 3) and (8, 11), calculate the Euclidean and the Manhattan distance, then check both with the functions in this chapter.
Great circles. Find the longitude and latitude of your hometown and calculate its great circle distance from Chapel Hill. Then compare it with the driving distance from an online map. How much longer is the drive, in percent?
Wrong on purpose. Calculate the “Euclidean distance” from Chapel Hill to Charlotte using their longitudes and latitudes as if they were x and y. What units is the answer in, and why is it meaningless?
Your county. Using the sf package’s nc data, build queen and rook neighbors with poly2nb(). How many neighbors does your home county (or Orange County) have under each rule? Which county has the most neighbors?
Three definitions. Project nc with st_transform(32119), find the county centroids, and build neighbors with k = 4 and with a distance band of 50 km. Compare summary() of each. Which counties have no neighbors within 50 km? What is the smallest distance band that gives every county at least one neighbor?
Spatial lag. Make row-standardized queen weights for nc, and calculate the spatial lag of births per square kilometer with lag.listw(). Make a scatterplot of each county’s value against its spatial lag. What does the pattern suggest?
