title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.1 Tobler’s first law
Look at a map of reported Lyme disease cases in the United States and you’ll see cases clustered in the Northeast and the upper Midwest. Look at COVID-19 case rates by ZIP code and you’ll see high-rate ZIP codes next to other high-rate ZIP codes. Our eyes are very good at seeing clusters. They are also very good at seeing clusters that aren’t there.
This chapter is about testing, objectively, whether things on a map are clustered, random, or dispersed. It builds on the neighbors and weight matrices of Chapter 21. We’ll cover spatial pattern, measured with the Average Nearest Neighbor ratio; spatial autocorrelation, measured with Moran’s I; and local hot-spot analysis, with Getis-Ord Gi*.
Waldo Tobler’s first law of geography (1970): “everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.” Values at locations near each other tend to be similar, and the similarity fades with distance. That means phenomena are not distributed randomly across space.
Imagine how the world would look if they were. A map of population density with every county’s value shuffled at random would look like static: no cities, no empty mountains, no suburbs around them. A random elevation map would have no mountain ranges and no river valleys. Real maps almost never look like that. They have structure, and this chapter’s statistics measure it.
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.1.1 Geographic variation
Geographic variation is the change in a phenomenon from place to place. We can list it in a table, but we see it in a map. Three kinds of things vary:

Events, such as disease cases, mapped as points.
Locations, such as hospitals, also points.
Values, such as average income, usually attached to polygons such as counties.



22.1.2 Seeing a pattern is not testing it
Looking at a map is subjective. Two people can look at the same map and disagree about whether it is clustered. And map design changes what we see: the classification breaks and the color ramp (Chapter 10) can make the same data look clustered or not. Spatial statistics give repeatable, testable answers.
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
section: 22.2 Spatial cluster analysis: global and local
text:
22.2 Spatial cluster analysis: global and local
There are two main approaches to finding clusters:

Global methods ask: are the events or values clustered anywhere in the study area? They return one result for the whole dataset, but they don’t tell us where things are happening.
Local methods ask: which areas have clusters of high or low values? They calculate a result for every observation, so the results can be mapped.

A global statistic for income inequality in U.S. counties would look at all 3,000-plus counties at once and return one number. A local statistic would give every county its own value, based on its neighbors, and show where high inequality sits next to high inequality.
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
section: 22.3 Spatial pattern: how objects are arranged
text:
22.3 Spatial pattern: how objects are arranged
A spatial pattern is the arrangement of objects in space. Describing and explaining patterns, how people, objects, and features are distributed across a landscape and why, is one of the central concerns of geography. Based only on where events are, there are three basic patterns (Figure 22.1):

Clustered: events are located near one another.
Random: there is no regular pattern; any location is equally likely.
Ordered or dispersed: events are spread out in a regular, repeating way.


22.3.1 The Average Nearest Neighbor ratio
The Average Nearest Neighbor (ANN) ratio asks: how are my points arranged, compared with a random arrangement?
\[
ANN = \frac{\bar{D}_O}{\bar{D}_E}
\]
\(\bar{D}_O\) is the observed mean distance from each point to its nearest neighbor. \(\bar{D}_E\) is the mean distance you’d expect if the same number of points were placed at random in the same area: \(0.5 / \sqrt{n / A}\), for n points in an area A.

ANN < 1: points are closer together than random: clustered.
ANN > 1: points are more spread out than random: dispersed.
ANN ≈ 1: random.







Figure 22.1: Sixty points in three patterns, with their ANN ratios.




Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Sixty random points give an ANN of 1.10: close to 1, as expected. In the lecture example, a set of crime points in a city gave an ANN of 0.57, well below 1, so the crimes are clustered.


22.3.2 Limits of the ANN ratio

It ignores values. ANN uses only locations. Two datasets with the same point locations but very different attribute values get the same ratio.
It looks at one dataset by itself.
It is global. One ratio for the whole pattern says nothing about where the clusters are.
It depends on the study area. The expected distance depends on A, so a larger boundary makes the same points look more clustered. Always report the study area with an ANN ratio.

To account for values, we need spatial autocorrelation.
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.4 Spatial autocorrelation
The same three patterns apply to attribute values, not just locations. Values can be clustered (similar values next to each other), random, or dispersed (neighbors tend to be different, like a checkerboard). Spatial autocorrelation is the degree of similarity between objects that are located near each other. It describes how values are arranged across a landscape, and it can be measured, for a whole region (a global statistic) or for smaller areas within it (local statistics).
The key distinction:

Spatial pattern cares only about location and arrangement. Use ANN.
Spatial autocorrelation cares about location and values. Use Moran’s I and Getis-Ord Gi.

Notice the “auto”: self. Spatial autocorrelation describes how a single variable relates to itself at nearby locations. Correlation between two different variables, such as income and education, is a different question, answered with regression (Chapter 19).

22.4.1 Which data suit spatial autocorrelation?
It works for areal (polygon), point, or raster data. In each case we measure how the values are arranged. Avoid raw counts, unless the populations generating the counts are the same everywhere: a county with more people will have more cases simply because of its size. Use rates or densities instead, such as cases per 1,000 residents or births per square kilometer.


22.4.2 It depends on who counts as a neighbor
Because spatial autocorrelation is about similarity between things that are near each other, we must define neighbors first: by contiguity (rook or queen), by a distance band, or by the k nearest neighbors (Chapter 21). Queen contiguity is the usual default for polygons such as counties. Different neighbor definitions can give different answers, so report the one you used.
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.5 Moran’s I: a global test
Moran’s I is the most widely used statistic for describing and testing spatial autocorrelation in a region. It is global: it considers the whole study area, and returns a single value, I, that measures the magnitude of spatial autocorrelation, along with a p-value.

22.5.1 How Moran’s I is calculated
\[
I = \frac{N}{W} \cdot \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\]

N is the number of observations.
wij is the spatial weight between i and j: 1 if they are neighbors and 0 if not, in the simplest case.
W is the sum of all the weights.
\(x_i - \bar{x}\) is how far observation i is from the mean.

You won’t compute it by hand, but know what drives it. For every pair of neighbors, multiply how far each is from the mean. If both are above the mean, or both below, the product is positive. If one is above and the other below, it is negative. So when neighbors tend to be alike, the sum is positive and I rises toward 1; when neighbors tend to differ, it is negative and I falls toward −1. The denominator standardizes by the overall variance.


22.5.2 Moran’s I ranges from −1 to 1

−1: perfectly dispersed, like a checkerboard.
0: random.
+1: perfectly clustered.

More precisely, the value expected under complete spatial randomness is −1/(N − 1), which is close to 0 for large datasets. Figure 22.2 shows five arrangements of the same 64 cells, half dark and half light. Only the arrangement changes, and arrangement is all Moran’s I responds to.






Figure 22.2: Moran’s I for five arrangements of the same 64 cells, using rook neighbors.



You can check these values with a few lines of base R. Each cell’s rook neighbors are the cells exactly 1 unit away:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


22.5.3 Is it significant?
How do we know whether an I is bigger than chance? The Monte Carlo (or permutation) test answers it directly: shuffle the values across the locations many times, calculate I each time, and see where the observed I falls among those random results.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The shuffled values give I near 0 (about −0.013, close to −1/63). None comes anywhere near 0.857, so the two-halves pattern is very unlikely to be chance.
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.6 Interpreting Moran’s I
Interpret a Moran’s I result in three steps: its magnitude, its significance, and its importance.

22.6.1 Magnitude: the I value
The closer to 1, the more clustered the values; the closer to −1, the more dispersed. There’s no official scale for describing strength, but this rule of thumb from the GEOG 215 lectures is a useful guide:



Table 22.1: A rule of thumb for describing the strength of Moran’s I.





I value
Interpretation




> 0.5
Highly clustered


0.3 to 0.5
Moderately clustered


0.1 to 0.3
Slightly clustered


0 to 0.1
Barely clustered (≈ random)


0 to −0.1
Barely dispersed (≈ random)


−0.1 to −0.3
Slightly dispersed


−0.3 to −0.5
Moderately dispersed


< −0.5
Highly dispersed








22.6.2 Significance: the p-value
The p-value is the probability of an I this extreme if the values were arranged at random. If p < 0.05, the result is statistically significant. If p > 0.05, the pattern can’t be distinguished from random.


22.6.3 Importance
Beware of a significant but unimportant result. The p-value depends on the number of observations, so:

With many observations, a tiny deviation from random can be significant: I = 0.04, p < 0.001 is significant, but essentially random in practice.
With few observations, a small amount of clustering, say I = 0.11, may not reach significance.

Always report and interpret both I and p (Chapter 18).






TipThink about it



Would you expect Moran’s I for median household income in North Carolina’s census tracts to be positive, near 0, or negative? What about elevation? The number of fast-food restaurants per person? Why?
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.7 Moran’s I in R
In R, the spdep package does the work. Here is Moran’s I for births per square kilometer in North Carolina’s counties from 1974 to 1978, using the sf package’s nc data (Chapter 16) and queen contiguity (Figure 22.3):
library(sf)
library(spdep)

nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf")) |>
  st_transform(32119)
nc$births_per_km2 <- nc$BIR74 / (as.numeric(st_area(nc)) / 1e6)

nb <- poly2nb(nc)                    # queen contiguity neighbors
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")      # row-standardized weights

moran.test(nc$births_per_km2, lw)

set.seed(215)
moran.mc(nc$births_per_km2, lw, nsim = 499)   # Monte Carlo version
    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  nc$births_per_km2
weights: lw
number of simulations + 1: 500

statistic = 0.12675, observed rank = 487, p-value = 0.026
alternative hypothesis: greater






Figure 22.3: Births per square kilometer in North Carolina’s counties, 1974–78.



The two numbers to report are the statistic, I = 0.127, and the p-value, 0.026. By the rule of thumb, 0.127 is slightly clustered, and because p < 0.05 the result is statistically significant. (moran.test(), which uses a formula instead of shuffling, gives the same I and p = 0.015.) Counties with many births per square kilometer tend to be near each other, but the effect is modest.
The lecture used the population of North Carolina’s counties from the ACS and got a very similar result: I = 0.158, p = 0.028, slightly clustered and significant.
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.8 Local hot-spot analysis: Getis-Ord Gi*
A global statistic gives one number for one variable, such as Moran’s I for county population. A local statistic gives a value for each observation: Getis-Ord Gi*, or local Moran’s I, for each county. Because local results are attached to places, we can map them and see where the clusters are.
The Getis-Ord G statistic asks a slightly different question from Moran’s I: are high values near high values, or low values near low values? Like Moran’s I, it has a global and a local version. The local version gives every observation a z-score:

A hot spot is an area of high values surrounded by high values: a large positive z-score.
A cold spot is an area of low values surrounded by low values: a large negative z-score.
Values near 0 are not clustered.

There are two versions. Gi leaves the observation itself out and looks only at its neighbors. Gi* includes the observation along with its neighbors; it is the version most software uses by default. As a rule of thumb, a z-score above 1.96 or below −1.96 is significant at the 0.05 level, and beyond ±2.58 at the 0.01 level.

22.8.1 Local Getis-Ord Gi* in R
The workflow has three steps:

Define neighbors. For counties, queen contiguity; for points, the k nearest neighbors, such as knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 10)).
Convert them to binary weights. For Gi*, include.self() adds each observation to its own neighborhood, and style = "B" makes every neighbor a 1.
Run localG() to get a z-score for every observation, then map it.

nb_self <- include.self(poly2nb(nc))
lw_b <- nb2listw(nb_self, style = "B")

nc$gi <- as.numeric(localG(nc$births_per_km2, lw_b))

nc$gi_class <- cut(nc$gi, c(-Inf, -1.96, 1.96, 2.58, Inf),
                   labels = c("Cold spot (z < -1.96)", "Not significant",
                              "Hot spot (z 1.96 to 2.58)", "Hot spot (z > 2.58)"))

tm_shape(nc) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "gi_class",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                values = c("#2166ac", "grey85", "#f4a582", "#b2182b")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend("Gi* z-score"))






Figure 22.4: Getis-Ord Gi* hot spots of births per square kilometer, 1974–78, with queen contiguity.



Eight counties are significant hot spots (Figure 22.4). The strongest, with z-scores above 2.58, are Gaston (3.9), Lincoln (3.4), and Mecklenburg (3.2): the Charlotte area, where high-density counties are surrounded by other high-density counties. A second group of hot spots is in the Triad: Guilford, Rockingham, and Stokes. No county is a significant cold spot: the lowest z-scores, in the far west and the northeast, reach only about −1.8.
Notice that Wake and Durham, which have high densities themselves, are not hot spots. Their neighbors, such as Johnston, Harnett, Chatham, and Person, had far fewer births per square kilometer in the 1970s, so the neighborhood as a whole isn’t unusual. Gi* finds clusters of high values, not single high values.
The lecture ran the same analysis on county population from the ACS: counties around Charlotte formed the strongest hot spot (z from 3.0 to 4.0), with a second band of positive values across the north-central Piedmont, and low-population cold spots in the northeast and far west.
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.9 Summary: choosing a spatial statistic



Table 22.2: Choosing a spatial statistic.











Method
Uses
Scope
Answers




Average Nearest Neighbor
Locations only
Global
Are points clustered, random, or dispersed?


Moran’s I
Locations and values
Global
Are similar values near each other overall?


Getis-Ord Gi / Gi*
Locations and values
Local
Where are the hot spots and cold spots?






Whichever you use: define your neighbors first, report both the statistic and its p-value, and map local results.

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.10 Check your understanding

A spatial statistic that returns one value for the whole study area is: GlobalLocalDispersedContiguous
An Average Nearest Neighbor ratio of 0.57 means the points are: ClusteredRandomDispersedImpossible to tell
ANN takes the attribute values of the points into account. TRUEFALSE
A perfect checkerboard of two values has a Moran’s I of: -100.51

Why should you usually use rates instead of raw counts for spatial autocorrelation? Places with more people have more cases just because of their sizeCounts can’t be mappedMoran’s I only works on percentagesRates are always normally distributed
A county with a large positive Gi* z-score is a: Hot spotCold spotOutlierRandom value
A Gi* z-score of 2.3 is significant at the 0.05 level. TRUEFALSE
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.11 Summary

The first law of geography means real-world values are rarely random across space. Seeing a pattern on a map is subjective; spatial statistics test it.
Global statistics give one answer for the whole study area; local statistics give one per observation, which you can map.
Spatial pattern uses locations only. The Average Nearest Neighbor ratio compares the observed mean nearest-neighbor distance with the random expectation: below 1 is clustered, above 1 dispersed. It depends on the study area.
Spatial autocorrelation uses locations and values: the similarity of a single variable at nearby locations. Use rates, not counts, and define neighbors first.
Moran’s I is global and runs from −1 (dispersed) through 0 (random) to +1 (clustered). Interpret its magnitude, its p-value, and whether it matters. In R: poly2nb(), nb2listw(), then moran.test() or moran.mc().
Getis-Ord Gi* is local. A large positive z-score is a hot spot, a large negative one a cold spot; |z| > 1.96 is significant at 0.05. In R: include.self(), nb2listw(style = "B"), then localG().
Births per square kilometer in North Carolina’s counties, 1974–78, are slightly clustered (I = 0.127, p = 0.026), with hot spots around Charlotte and in the Triad.
crumbs: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.12 Exercises

ANN by hand. Five points are at (1, 1), (2, 1), (1, 2), (8, 8), and (9, 8), in a 10 × 10 study area. Find each point’s nearest-neighbor distance, the observed mean, the expected mean, and the ANN ratio. Then double the study area to 20 × 20. What happens to the ratio, and why?
Shuffle a map. Shuffle the values of births_per_km2 across North Carolina’s counties with sample(), map the result, and calculate Moran’s I. Compare both with the real map and the real I.
Neighbors matter. Recalculate Moran’s I for births per square kilometer with rook contiguity, with k = 4 nearest neighbors, and with a 50 km distance band (Chapter 21). How much does I change?
Sudden infant deaths. Calculate the rate of sudden infant deaths per 1,000 births, SID74 / BIR74 * 1000, and test it for spatial autocorrelation. Is it more or less clustered than births per square kilometer? Then map its Gi* hot and cold spots.
Residuals. Fit a regression of BIR79 on BIR74 (Chapter 19), and test its residuals with lm.morantest(). Are the residuals spatially autocorrelated? What would you do next?
Local Moran’s I. Run localmoran() on births per square kilometer, and compare which counties stand out with the Gi* map. What does local Moran’s I find that Gi* doesn’t?

title: 22  Spatial Clustering and Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
22.13 Further reading

Spatial Data Science: With Applications in R, by Edzer Pebesma and Roger Bivand (CRC Press, 2023), free at https://r-spatial.org/book/. Chapter 15, “Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation”, covers Moran’s I and local indicators in spdep.
Getis, A., and Ord, J. K. (1992). “The Analysis of Spatial Association by Use of Distance Statistics.” Geographical Analysis 24(3): 189–206. The paper that introduced the G statistics.
Goodchild, M. F. (1986). Spatial Autocorrelation. Concepts and Techniques in Modern Geography (CATMOG) 47. Geo Books. A short, classic introduction, with grid examples like Figure 22.2.
Tobler, W. R. (1970). “A Computer Movie Simulating Urban Growth in the Detroit Region.” Economic Geography 46: 234–240.




Waldo Tobler’s statement that “everything is related to everything else,
but near things are more related than distant things.” It is the idea
behind spatial autocorrelation.
Methods that find groups of similar observations, or groups of places
with similar values that sit close together.
The arrangement of objects in space: clustered, random, or dispersed.
The tendency for things that are close together to be more alike than
things that are far apart, such as neighboring counties having similar
incomes.
The observed mean distance from each point to its nearest neighbor
divided by the mean expected at random. Below 1 is clustered.
A global measure of spatial autocorrelation, from −1 (dispersed) through
0 (random) to +1 (clustered), with a p-value.
A local statistic that gives each observation a z-score: large positive
for hot spots, large negative for cold spots.
A cluster of places with unusually high values, such as a group of
neighborhoods with many burglaries. Finding hotspots is a common goal of
spatial analysis.
An n × n table, W, whose entry
wij records the neighbor relationship
between observations i and j.
The change in a phenomenon from place to place, such as income from
county to county.
A closed shape that represents an area, such as a county, a lake, or a
census tract.
One thing that was measured or recorded, such as a student, a county, or
a flight. In a data frame, each row is an observation.
A statistic that gives one value for a whole study area, such as Moran’s
I. It doesn’t say where clusters are.
A statistic calculated for each observation from its neighbors, such as
Gi*, so its results can be mapped.
In R, a named piece of memory that holds data, such as
months <- 12. In a dataset, a measured characteristic,
such as median income; each Census variable has a code.
Whether two variables move together. It doesn’t say how much one changes
with the other, or which causes which.
A statistical model of how one variable (such as home price) changes
with one or more others (such as distance to downtown).
Spatial data stored as a grid of cells (pixels), each holding a value,
such as a satellite image or an elevation model. In R, the
terra package handles rasters.
Sharing a border. Contiguity neighbors are polygons that touch, by the
rook or queen rule.
A neighbor definition: every feature within a set threshold distance is
a neighbor. dnearneigh() in spdep.
A neighbor definition: each feature’s neighbors are the k
features closest to it. Every feature gets exactly k.
Polygons are neighbors if they share an edge or just a corner. On a
grid, each cell has eight. spdep’s default.
The probability of a result at least as extreme as yours if the null
hypothesis were true. It is not the chance the null hypothesis is true.
The number you divide by to turn a count into a share, usually the total
of the same table, such as total population.
A measure of spread: the standard deviation squared, so its units are
squared too. var() in R.
Points or values placed entirely at random, the baseline that spatial
pattern and autocorrelation statistics compare against.
Polygons are neighbors only if they share an edge. On a grid, each cell
has four.
A test that shuffles values across locations many times and asks how
often the shuffles beat the observed statistic.
The level of detail at which you study something: addresses,
neighborhoods, counties, or states. A pattern that is clear at one scale
can vanish or reverse at another.
By convention, a result with p < 0.05. Significant doesn’t
mean large or important.
The middle value when values are sorted, so half are above and half
below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.
A small area of about 1,200 to 8,000 people (4,000 on average), drawn to
be fairly stable over time. The workhorse unit for neighborhood
analysis.
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
“Simple features”: the R package for spatial vector data. An sf object
is a data frame with a geometry column holding each row’s point, line,
or polygon.
The Census Bureau’s continuous survey of a sample of households every
year. It asks many more questions than the decennial census, but every
value is an estimate with a margin of error.
Moran’s I calculated for each observation, to find clusters and
outliers. localmoran() in spdep.
How many standard deviations a value is from what’s expected. Beyond
±1.96 is significant at the 0.05 level.
An area of low values surrounded by low values: a large negative Gi*
z-score.
Neighbor weights of 1 for a neighbor and 0 for everything else.
The zone of influence around a feature. Features inside it are its
neighbors, defined by a distance, the nearest features, or shared
borders.
An observation’s actual value minus the value a model predicts for it.
Map them to see where a model fits poorly.
The use of data that have a location attached to answer questions about
the world. It combines what we study (the spatial), how we
handle it (data skills), and how we ask and answer questions
(science).

title: Unit 6: Next Steps
text:
Chapter 23: Interactive Map Dashboards
This unit looks beyond the course. It first turns your maps and analysis into interactive dashboards that anyone can explore, then shows where the skills from this book are used, previews the advanced topics that build on them, and maps out the courses, credentials, and careers that come next.
This chapter builds an interactive dashboard of income and poverty by state. It makes interactive maps with leaflet (or tmap in view mode), lays out a map, value box, chart, and table with flexdashboard, links them with crosstalk in a single HTML file, and adds Shiny so the dashboard recalculates when readers make choices. It ends with how to share each kind of dashboard.

title: Unit 6: Next Steps
section: Chapter 24: What’s Next in Spatial Data Science
text:
Chapter 24: What’s Next in Spatial Data Science
This chapter shows spatial data science at work in public health, environmental science, planning, social science, and business. It previews three advanced areas: remote sensing and NDVI, space-time modeling, and GeoAI, including why spatial autocorrelation matters for machine learning. It ends with a path through UNC’s GIS courses, the GIS minor and Geospatial Data Science major, and careers in GIS and spatial data science.



A web page that shows key information on one screen, usually as several
linked, interactive views such as a map, charts, a table, and headline
numbers.
An R package (and JavaScript library) for interactive web maps, built in
layers joined with the pipe.
An R package for making thematic maps quickly, with sensible defaults.
A dashboard panel that shows one headline number, with a caption and an
icon.
An R package that lays out an R Markdown file as a dashboard of columns
or rows of panels, with an optional sidebar.
An R package that links htmlwidgets in one HTML file, so a filter or
selection in one updates the others, with no Shiny.
An R package for web apps that run R code on a server whenever the
reader changes an input.
The use of data that have a location attached to answer questions about
the world. It combines what we study (the spatial), how we
handle it (data skills), and how we ask and answer questions
(science).
Collecting information about Earth without touching it, from sensors on
satellites, aircraft, or drones. It produces most of the world’s raster
data.
Normalized difference vegetation index: (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red). It
ranges from −1 to 1, and dense green vegetation is high.
Artificial intelligence methods, such as deep learning, applied to
spatial data, for example to find buildings in satellite images.
The tendency for things that are close together to be more alike than
things that are far apart, such as neighboring counties having similar
incomes.

title: 23  Interactive Map Dashboards
text:
23.1 What is a dashboard?
All semester you have made maps and analyses and written them up as R Markdown reports. This chapter turns that work into an interactive dashboard: a single web page where a reader can explore a map, a chart, and a table that respond to each other. We build one example dashboard step by step, first from interactive widgets that run in any browser, and then with Shiny. Everything is still an R Markdown file, so it fits the workflow you already know.
A dashboard shows key information on one screen so people can monitor and explore it. It usually has several linked views, such as a map, charts, a table, and a few headline numbers, and it is interactive: readers can zoom, hover, filter, and select. You have certainly used one. During COVID-19, case dashboards from universities and state health departments were checked daily by millions of people, and most were built around a map. Air quality, weather, and traffic dashboards, and city and state open data portals, work the same way. A map is often the anchor, because readers first ask “where?”

title: 23  Interactive Map Dashboards
text:
23.1.1 Reports and dashboards do different jobs



Table 23.1: Reports and dashboards.











R Markdown report
Dashboard




Order
Tells a story in a fixed order
Reader explores in any order


Maps and charts
Static
Interactive and linked


Text
Explains every result
Short labels; the visuals carry the message


Best for
An argument or analysis write-up
Monitoring and exploring data






Your assignments have been reports: you guide the reader through an analysis step by step. A dashboard hands control to the reader. That means less text and more careful design, because the visuals have to explain themselves. A good project often has both: a report that explains the analysis (Chapter 20) and a dashboard that lets people explore the data.


23.1.2 What makes a good dashboard

Answer a few clear questions, and leave out everything else. Write down two or three questions before you start, and cut anything that doesn’t help answer them.
Put the most important view, often the map, largest and first.
Use the map design rules you already know (Chapter 10): sensible classification, a clear legend with units, and a data source.
Link the views, so a filter or selection updates them together.
Design for everyone. Never use color alone to carry meaning; add labels and a table. A table beside the map gives screen reader users and colorblind readers the same information. Check color contrast, and test with a keyboard and on a phone.







TipThink about it



Think of a dashboard you have used: for weather, sports, a class, or public health. What two or three questions does it answer? What would you cut, and what is missing?

title: 23  Interactive Map Dashboards
text:
23.2 The R dashboard toolkit



Table 23.2: Packages for dashboards in R.









Package
What it does




flexdashboard
Lays out an R Markdown file as a dashboard


leaflet
Interactive web maps (tmap makes them too, with tmap_mode("view"))


DT
Searchable, sortable data tables


plotly
Interactive charts


crosstalk
Links widgets, so a filter updates them all


shiny
Runs R code in response to what the reader does






leaflet, DT, and plotly are all htmlwidgets: R functions that produce JavaScript, which runs in the browser with no R needed.

23.2.1 Two kinds of interactivity
The most important design decision is which of two kinds of dashboard to build:



Table 23.3: Static and Shiny dashboards.











htmlwidgets + crosstalk
Shiny




How it works
Knit once to a single HTML file; interactivity runs in the browser
R runs on a server while people use it


What readers can do
Show and hide the data that was knitted in
Trigger any R code: recalculate statistics, rebuild maps, query APIs


Sharing
No R needed; share it like any file
Needs a server






A static dashboard can be emailed, uploaded to Canvas, or hosted on GitHub Pages, and it works with no R installed. But it can only show and hide the data that was baked in when you knitted it. Shiny can do anything R can do in response to a click, like recalculating a weighted average or refitting a model, but it needs a running R process. Start static, and move to Shiny only when you need it.


23.2.2 Our example: income and poverty by state
Figure 23.1 shows where we are headed. A sidebar holds filters. The large map shows median income by state. On the right are a value box, a scatter plot of poverty rate against median income, and a table.






Figure 23.1: The finished static dashboard. The map’s gray background is only because the basemap tiles didn’t load when this screenshot was taken; on your computer you will see a light basemap.



The data are us_states and us_states_df from the spData package, the same data you joined in Chapter 15, so everything loads with library() and nothing needs downloading. Preparing the data looks just like the joins chapter:
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(spData)

states <- us_states |>
  left_join(us_states_df, by = c("NAME" = "state")) |>
  mutate(
    REGION = fct_recode(REGION, Northeast = "Norteast"),  # fix a typo in spData
    poverty_rate_15 = poverty_level_15 / total_pop_15 * 100
  ) |>
  st_transform(4326)  # leaflet expects WGS84 longitude and latitude
Three details. spData spells the Northeast region “Norteast”, so fct_recode() from forcats fixes the label. poverty_level_15 is a count of people, so dividing by population gives a rate. And leaflet works in longitude and latitude on WGS84, EPSG:4326 (Chapter 12), so we transform the data. Doing the data preparation once, at the top of the file, keeps the rest of the dashboard simple.

title: 23  Interactive Map Dashboards
text:
23.3 Interactive maps with leaflet
The map is the heart of the dashboard.

23.3.1 Your first leaflet map
library(leaflet)

leaflet(states) |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) |>
  addPolygons(color = "white", weight = 1,
              fillColor = "steelblue", fillOpacity = 0.6)
A leaflet map is built in layers, like tmap and ggplot2, but the layers are joined with the pipe instead of +. leaflet() creates an empty map from the data. addProviderTiles() adds basemap tiles; CartoDB Positron is a light gray basemap that works well under choropleth colors. addPolygons() draws the states. Run this in RStudio and the map appears in the Viewer pane, where you can already zoom and pan.


23.3.2 Coloring a choropleth
Unlike tmap, leaflet doesn’t classify data for you. First you build a palette function: a function that takes data values and returns colors.
pal <- colorBin("Blues", domain = states$median_income_15, bins = 5)

leaflet(states) |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) |>
  addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(median_income_15),
              fillOpacity = 0.8, color = "white", weight = 1) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~median_income_15,
            title = "Median income ($)")
colorBin() takes a ColorBrewer scheme, here Blues, and the range of the data, and returns a function that turns values into colors. The tilde in ~pal(median_income_15) tells leaflet to look up the column in the data. Use the same palette in addLegend() so the legend matches the map. The other palette functions are colorNumeric() for a continuous ramp, colorQuantile() for quantile classes, and colorFactor() for categories.


23.3.3 Labels, popups, and highlighting
Interactivity is what makes a web map worth the effort:
addPolygons(
  fillColor = ~pal(median_income_15), fillOpacity = 0.8,
  color = "white", weight = 1,
  label = ~NAME,                                     # shows on hover
  popup = ~paste0("<b>", NAME, "</b><br>Poverty rate: ",
                  round(poverty_rate_15, 1), "%"),   # shows on click
  highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
    weight = 3, color = "#13294B", bringToFront = TRUE)
)
A label appears when the reader hovers over a state, and a popup when they click. Popups accept simple HTML, so the state name can be bold, with a line break after it. highlightOptions() outlines the state under the mouse, so readers know exactly which polygon they are on. Labels also help accessibility, because readers don’t have to match a color to the legend.


23.3.4 A shortcut: tmap in view mode
If you prefer tmap, you don’t have to learn leaflet first. Chapter 10 showed that tmap_mode("view") turns tmap code into an interactive map, and that map is a leaflet map:
library(tmap)
tmap_mode("view")   # interactive; tmap_mode("plot") for static

tm_shape(states) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "median_income_15",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks",
                                    values = "brewer.blues"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Median income ($)"),
    id = "NAME",
    popup.vars = c("median_income_15", "poverty_rate_15"))
id sets the hover label, and popup.vars chooses the variables shown on click. tmap is quicker to write and classifies the data for you. leaflet gives you more control and works with crosstalk, which we use below. Both work in a dashboard.

title: 23  Interactive Map Dashboards
text:
23.4 Laying out a flexdashboard

23.4.1 A flexdashboard is an R Markdown file
A flexdashboard is an R Markdown file with a different output format in its YAML header. You knit it the same way you knit your assignments.
---
title: "US States: Income and Poverty, 2015"
output:
  flexdashboard::flex_dashboard:
    orientation: columns
    vertical_layout: fill
---
orientation: columns lays out the page as side-by-side columns; rows is the other option. vertical_layout: fill stretches the panels to fill the browser window; scroll lets the page scroll instead. In RStudio, File > New File > R Markdown > From Template > Flex Dashboard starts one for you.


23.4.2 Columns, panels, and a sidebar
The layout comes from Markdown headings:
Inputs {.sidebar}
--------------------------------------------

Column {data-width=600}
--------------------------------------------
### Median income by state, 2015

Column {data-width=400}
--------------------------------------------
### States {data-height=120}
### Poverty rate vs. median income
### Data table

A heading underlined with dashes starts a column.
A ### heading starts a panel inside that column, and its text becomes the panel’s title. Under each panel heading goes one R chunk that draws the map, chart, or table (left out above).
The attributes in curly braces set relative widths and heights. 600 and 400 mean the map column gets 60% of the space after the sidebar.
The special {.sidebar} column holds inputs and filters on the left.

Figure 23.2 shows how those headings become the page. Sketching the layout on paper before you code is a good habit.






Figure 23.2: How the headings above lay out the dashboard: a sidebar, a wide map column, and a narrower column that stacks a value box, a scatter plot, and a data table.





23.4.3 Value boxes, tables, and charts
Each of the other panels gets one of these:
# Headline number
valueBox(nrow(states), caption = "States in the map", icon = "fa-map")

# Searchable, sortable table
datatable(state_table, rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 5))

# Interactive scatter plot
plot_ly(state_table, x = ~median_income_15, y = ~poverty_rate_15,
        text = ~NAME, type = "scatter", mode = "markers")
A value box shows a single headline number with an icon from Font Awesome. datatable() from DT makes a table readers can search and sort, and plot_ly() makes a scatter plot with hover labels. The table and chart use state_table, a copy of the data without geometry, made with st_drop_geometry() and select(). Tables and charts don’t need polygons, and dropping the geometry keeps the file small.


23.4.4 Linking views with crosstalk
crosstalk makes the views talk to each other:
library(crosstalk)

# Same key and group = linked widgets
shared_table <- SharedData$new(state_table, key = ~NAME, group = "states")

# Filters go in the sidebar
filter_checkbox("region", "Census region", shared_table, ~REGION)
filter_slider("income", "Median income ($)", shared_table, ~median_income_15)
Wrap a data frame in SharedData$new(), with a key that identifies each row, here the state name, and a group name. Pass shared_table instead of state_table to datatable() and plot_ly(), and every widget built from a SharedData object in the same group is linked: filtering one filters the others, and selecting points in the scatter plot highlights the same states in the table. filter_checkbox() and filter_slider() make filter controls that work without Shiny; they go in the sidebar.


23.4.5 crosstalk and leaflet: points, not polygons
Here is a limitation you will run into: leaflet links only point layers, markers and circles, with crosstalk. A crosstalk filter won’t hide polygons, so a region filter can’t hide states on a choropleth.
A simple workaround is one point per state. Draw the choropleth normally as context, then add the points as a shared layer on top:
state_points <- states |>
  st_transform(5070) |>        # find points in a projected CRS...
  st_point_on_surface() |>
  st_transform(4326) |>        # ...then go back to longitude and latitude
  select(NAME, REGION, median_income_15, poverty_rate_15)

shared_points <- SharedData$new(state_points, key = ~NAME, group = "states")

# in the map chunk, after addPolygons():
addCircleMarkers(data = shared_points, radius = 5, label = ~NAME)
st_point_on_surface() is better than st_centroid() here, because its point always falls inside the polygon. Run it on projected data, such as EPSG:5070, and transform the points back to 4326 afterward.
Figure 23.3 shows the result. The reader has checked only the South: the points on the map, the scatter plot, and the table all show only the 17 southern states. The choropleth colors and the value box didn’t change, because value boxes are fixed when you knit. That is the static dashboard’s limit. Even so, this single HTML file is already a useful, shareable product.






Figure 23.3: The static dashboard filtered to the South. The red points, scatter plot, and table show 17 states; the choropleth and value box are unchanged.









TipThink about it



In Figure 23.3, a reader filtered to the South but the value box still says 49. Is that misleading? How could you change the dashboard’s labels so a reader isn’t confused, without switching to Shiny?

title: 23  Interactive Map Dashboards
text:
23.5 Adding Shiny

23.5.1 When do you need Shiny?
Use Shiny when a reader’s choice should trigger new R calculations, not just hide data:

Filter the polygons themselves on the map.
Update headline numbers, such as an average for the selected states.
Let readers choose which variable to map.
Rerun a model or query an API with the reader’s choices.

In a flexdashboard, add one line, runtime: shiny, to the YAML header. Then you need three pieces: inputs that collect the reader’s choices, reactive expressions that recompute data, and render functions that redraw the outputs.


23.5.2 Inputs in the sidebar
variables <- c("Median income, 2015 ($)" = "median_income_15",
               "Poverty rate, 2015 (%)"  = "poverty_rate_15",
               "Population, 2015"        = "total_pop_15")

selectInput("variable", "Map variable", choices = variables)

checkboxGroupInput("region", "Census region",
                   choices  = levels(states$REGION),
                   selected = levels(states$REGION))
selectInput() makes a drop-down menu. The named vector shows readers friendly labels while giving your code the column names. checkboxGroupInput() makes the region checkboxes, all checked to start. Every input has an ID, its first argument, and anywhere else in the dashboard input$variable or input$region holds the reader’s current choice.


23.5.3 Reactive data and render functions
selected_states <- reactive({
  req(input$region)
  states |> filter(REGION %in% input$region)
})

renderLeaflet({
  df  <- selected_states()
  val <- df[[input$variable]]
  pal <- colorBin("Blues", domain = val, bins = 5)
  leaflet(df) |> addPolygons(fillColor = pal(val))
})
A reactive expression is code that reruns automatically when the inputs it uses change. selected_states filters the data to the checked regions, and req() stops it from running if no region is checked. You call it like a function: selected_states().
Render functions, such as renderLeaflet(), renderValueBox(), and renderDT(), draw outputs. Because this renderLeaflet() uses both selected_states() and input$variable, Shiny redraws the map whenever either changes. You don’t write any code to watch the inputs; Shiny tracks the dependencies for you. That is the core idea of reactive programming. (The full app, at the end of the chapter, also adds basemap tiles, labels, and a legend.)
Figure 23.4 shows the Shiny version. The reader chose poverty rate and unchecked the Northeast and West. Now the polygons themselves are filtered, the color classes are recalculated for just these states, and the value boxes show 29 states and a population-weighted poverty rate of 15.6% for them.






Figure 23.4: The Shiny dashboard mapping poverty rate for the Midwest and South. The polygons, the value boxes, and the table all recalculate.

title: 23  Interactive Map Dashboards
text:
23.6 Sharing your dashboard



Table 23.4: How to share each kind of dashboard.









Static (crosstalk)
Shiny




Knit to one self-contained HTML file
Needs R running on a server


Email it or upload it to Canvas
shinyapps.io or Posit Connect Cloud (free tiers)


Host it free on GitHub Pages or RPubs
Or a campus or company Shiny server


Open it in any browser
Run it locally with RStudio’s Run Document button







23.6.1 Common pitfalls and fixes

The map is blank or in the wrong place: transform to EPSG:4326 first.
The file is huge or slow: simplify the polygons and drop columns you don’t need. Use st_simplify() on projected data, or rmapshaper::ms_simplify().
The legend and map disagree: use the same palette function for both.
Missing values: set na.color in the palette, and say what gray means.
A filter doesn’t hide polygons: crosstalk only filters leaflet points.
The design isn’t accessible: add labels and a table; never rely on color alone.



23.6.2 Looking ahead: Quarto dashboards
Quarto, the successor to R Markdown (and what built this book), has its own dashboard format: format: dashboard in the YAML header. The ideas are the same: rows, columns, cards instead of panels, value boxes, and a sidebar. It works with R and Python, and with leaflet, DT, plotly, and Shiny, so everything in this chapter carries over.

title: 23  Interactive Map Dashboards
23  Interactive Map Dashboards
text:
23.8 Summary

A dashboard puts a map, charts, a table, and key numbers on one interactive screen, with linked views. A report tells a story in order; a dashboard lets the reader explore.
leaflet builds the map, in layers joined with the pipe: basemap tiles, polygons colored with a palette function, a legend, labels on hover and popups on click. tmap_mode("view") makes the same kind of map.
flexdashboard lays out an R Markdown file as a dashboard: a sidebar, columns, and panels, with value boxes, DT tables, and plotly charts.
crosstalk links htmlwidgets in a single HTML file that anyone can open, using SharedData with a key and a group. It filters only leaflet points, not polygons.
Shiny (runtime: shiny) reruns R code when readers make choices, with inputs, reactive expressions, and render functions, but it needs a server.
Start simple and static; add Shiny only when you need it.

title: 23  Interactive Map Dashboards
text:
23.9 Exercises

Questions first. Before building anything, write the two or three questions a dashboard about North Carolina’s counties should answer. Which views would answer each one?
Map a change. Start from states-dashboard.Rmd. Add a column for the change in median income from 2010 to 2015, and map it instead of 2015 income. Which palette function fits a variable that can be negative?
Another headline. Add a second value box that shows the highest-income state.
Another filter. Add a filter_select() to the static dashboard, or a new Shiny input to the Shiny version.
tmap instead. Replace the leaflet map with tmap_mode("view") and the tmap code from Section 23.3. What did you gain, and what did you lose?
Usability test. Knit your dashboard and give it to a classmate with your questions from Exercise 1. Can they answer them without asking you anything?

text:

A web page that shows key information on one screen, usually as several
linked, interactive views such as a map, charts, a table, and headline
numbers.
An R package (and JavaScript library) for interactive web maps, built in
layers joined with the pipe.
In leaflet, a function, made by colorBin(),
colorNumeric(), colorQuantile(), or
colorFactor(), that turns data values into colors. Use the
same one for the map and its legend.

map.

interactive map.

or rows of panels, with an optional sidebar.

holds one map, chart, table, or value box.

icon.

selection in one updates the others, with no Shiny.
A closed shape that represents an area, such as a county, a lake, or a
census tract.

reader changes an input.
A control, such as a drop-down menu or checkboxes, that collects a
reader’s choice. Its value is read as input$id.
Shiny code, made with reactive(), that reruns automatically
when the inputs it uses change. Call it like a function.

renderDT(), that draws an output and redraws it when the
inputs or reactives it uses change.
A document format (.Rmd) that mixes formatted text with
chunks of R code. Knitting it runs the code and builds a finished
report.
The integrated development environment (IDE) where you write and run R.
R does the computing; RStudio is the workspace around it.
A bundle of code, written by other users, that adds new functions to R.
Install it once with install.packages(), then load it in
each session with library().
Maps, charts, and tables that respond to each other, so filtering or

R functions, such as those in leaflet, DT, and plotly, that produce

To build an R Markdown file into a finished document (HTML, PDF, or

below. Unlike counts, medians can’t be added across areas.

left_join().

title: 24  What’s Next in Spatial Data Science
text:
24.1 Spatial data science in action
This chapter looks forward instead of teaching a new method. You can now do a full spatial data science workflow in R:
That is the core workflow of spatial data science. This chapter shows where it is used, previews three advanced topics that build on it, and maps out what to take next at UNC and where spatial skills can take you. As you read, notice which application excites you most. That is a good clue to which course to take next.
Almost any question that involves “where” is a spatial question:
The methods are shared; the questions change by discipline. For each application below, notice which methods from this book show up: joins, distance, neighbors, autocorrelation, regression, or mapping.
crumbs: 24  What's Next in Spatial Data Science

title: 24  What’s Next in Spatial Data Science
text:
Where are disease cases clustering?
Which neighborhoods are farthest from a clinic or grocery store?
How fast is forest being cleared, and where?
Who lives in the flood zone?
Where should a new store, bus route, or fire station go?



24.1.1 Public health: where disease happens
Spatial epidemiology studies how health outcomes vary across places. Its classic origin story is John Snow’s map of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak in London, which tied deaths to a single water pump.
Today we don’t just look at the map; we test whether a cluster is bigger than chance would produce. Local Moran’s I and hot spot statistics such as Getis-Ord Gi* (Chapter 22) find unusual clusters of cases, and scan statistics, in software such as SaTScan, search through both space and time for outbreaks. During COVID-19, case maps and dashboards were updated daily, and wastewater testing added a new signal for tracking infection by sewershed. A sewershed is just another polygon you can join data to.


24.1.2 Public health: access to care
Access to care depends on distance, travel time, and who can make the trip. Chapter 21 compared straight-line, network, and travel-time distance, and health access is where that choice matters most: a clinic 10 miles away is not the same for someone with a car and someone who relies on a bus. Analysts draw drive-time and transit-time areas around hospitals, pharmacies, and clinics, and track how rural hospital and maternity unit closures lengthen trips for patients.
Accessibility models weigh supply against demand. The two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) method is a common example: it combines how many providers there are, how many people need them, and how long it takes to get there.


24.1.3 Public health: environmental exposure and justice
Where people live shapes what they breathe, drink, and are exposed to. Researchers link air pollution monitors and satellite estimates to asthma rates, and measure distance to highways, factories, and hazardous waste sites. Environmental justice asks who bears that burden.
A well-known North Carolina example comes from UNC epidemiologists, including the late Steve Wing, who showed that industrial hog operations in eastern North Carolina were concentrated near Black, Latino, and low-income communities. The methods are ones you know: spatial joins, buffers, census data, and regression, controlling for spatial autocorrelation. Maps can reveal inequities, and spatial data science has real policy consequences.


24.1.4 Environmental science: watching the planet change
Satellites give a consistent, repeated view of the whole Earth. Hansen and colleagues (2013) used Landsat imagery to map forest loss worldwide at 30-meter resolution, and Global Forest Watch now serves that kind of data to the public. Satellite data also show land cover change, such as farms turning into suburbs or wetlands into development, and urban heat islands: paved, treeless neighborhoods that run hotter, which is a health issue too.
Ecologists use species distribution models, which are essentially regression with spatial predictors, to predict where plants and animals can live, and GPS collars and tags to record how animals move through landscapes.


24.1.5 Environmental science: hazards and resilience
GIS is central to preparing for and responding to disasters: flood maps, evacuation routes, and shelter locations before a storm, and rapid damage mapping from aerial and satellite imagery after it. North Carolina has plenty of examples:

Hurricane Helene’s 2024 flooding in western North Carolina, when imagery and GIS were used to map flooding, landslides, and damaged roads.
Sea-level rise and shoreline change along the Outer Banks.
Statewide lidar elevation data, collected for floodplain mapping.

The key question, who is exposed, is an overlay of hazard zones with census data: exactly the kind of spatial join you did in Chapter 15.


24.1.6 Cities, transportation, and planning
Urban and regional planners use GIS every day, for zoning, land use, and housing affordability. Transportation questions are almost always network questions. Who lives within a 10-minute walk of a bus stop? Where are the bike and pedestrian crash hot spots?
Choosing where to put new schools, parks, or fire stations is a classic GIS problem. Location–allocation models take demand locations and candidate sites and choose the sites that minimize travel or serve the most people. Network distance, from Chapter 21, is the core tool.


24.1.7 Social science, history, and politics

History. The Mapping Inequality project digitized the 1930s Home Owners’ Loan Corporation “redlining” maps, including several North Carolina cities such as Durham. Researchers join those historic polygons to today’s data on health, heat, and wealth.
Politics. Redistricting and gerrymandering are spatial problems by definition, and North Carolina has been at the center of many redistricting court cases. Compactness measures and simulated district maps test whether a plan is fair.
Archaeology. Lidar sees through forest canopy to reveal buried sites.
Sociology and economics. Segregation, mobility, and neighborhood effects are studied with neighbor-based measures like the weight matrices from Chapter 21.



24.1.8 Business, agriculture, and humanitarian work

Business. Site selection, delivery routing, market areas, and real estate, often called location intelligence.
Agriculture. Precision farming with GPS-guided equipment, drones, and crop imagery puts water and fertilizer only where they are needed.
Humanitarian mapping. Volunteers trace roads and buildings in OpenStreetMap, and responders use those maps after earthquakes, floods, and conflicts. Anyone can contribute, including you, this week.
Insurance and finance. Insurers price risk from floods, wildfire, and climate change with hazard models.







TipThink about it



Pick the application in this section that interests you most. Which chapters of this book would you need for a first project on it? What data would you need, and who publishes them?

title: 24  What’s Next in Spatial Data Science
section: 24.2 Remote sensing: seeing Earth from above
text:
24.2 Remote sensing: seeing Earth from above
The next three sections preview advanced areas: remote sensing, space-time modeling, and GeoAI. Each is a full course or career on its own, so the goal is vocabulary and a sense of what is possible, not mastery.
Remote sensing is collecting information about Earth without touching it, and it produces most of the raster data in the world (Chapter 11). Sensors come in two kinds:

Passive sensors record reflected sunlight or the heat a surface gives off, like a camera or a multispectral scanner.
Active sensors send their own signal and measure what comes back. Radar can see through clouds and at night, and lidar measures distance with laser pulses to build 3D models of terrain and trees.


24.2.1 Four kinds of resolution
Every sensor is described by four kinds of resolution:

Spatial resolution: the size of a pixel on the ground.
Spectral resolution: the number and width of wavelength bands it records.
Temporal resolution: how often it revisits the same place.
Radiometric resolution: how finely it records brightness.

Each sensor trades these off. A satellite with tiny pixels usually covers a smaller area or revisits less often. Choosing data means choosing the resolution that fits your question, just as Chapter 21 chose the distance measure that fits the question.



Table 24.1: Remote sensing data you will meet most often. Pixel sizes are approximate.











Sensor
Type
Pixel size
Good for




Landsat (since 1972)
Passive
30 m
Decades of change


Sentinel-2
Passive
10–60 m
Crops, forests, cities


MODIS
Passive
250 m–1 km
Daily fires and snow


Sentinel-1, NISAR
Active radar
About 5–20 m
Floods, ground motion


Lidar
Active laser
Under 1 m
Elevation, tree height


Drones
Mostly passive
Centimeters
Small study sites






Landsat is the longest continuous record of Earth’s surface, which makes it ideal for change over decades. Sentinel-2, from the European Space Agency, has finer pixels and frequent revisits. MODIS is coarse but images the whole planet about every day. Radar, from Sentinel-1 and the NASA–ISRO NISAR mission launched in 2025, works through clouds, so it maps floods during storms. Most of these data are free from NASA, the USGS, and the European Space Agency, a big change from twenty years ago.


24.2.2 From pixels to information
Different surfaces reflect different wavelengths of light, so each has a spectral signature. Healthy plants absorb red light, because chlorophyll uses it, and reflect near-infrared (NIR) light strongly. The normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) turns that contrast into one number for each pixel:
\[
\text{NDVI} = \frac{\text{NIR} - \text{Red}}{\text{NIR} + \text{Red}}
\]
NDVI ranges from −1 to 1, and dense green vegetation is high (Figure 24.1).






Figure 24.1: Typical shares of red and near-infrared light reflected by four surfaces, and the NDVI each gives. Values are illustrative.



Two more steps turn imagery into maps:

Classification assigns each pixel a land cover class, such as forest, water, or developed land, increasingly with machine learning.
Change detection compares images of the same place from different dates.

In R, the terra and stars packages handle rasters. NDVI is two lines of raster algebra in terra. Google Earth Engine, taught in GEOG 567, runs the same analyses in the cloud on petabytes of imagery, without downloading anything.

title: 24  What’s Next in Spatial Data Science
text:
24.3 Space-time modeling
Almost every dataset in this book was a snapshot: one ACS period, or one year. But real processes change over both space and time:

Disease spreading from county to county.
Air pollution changing by the hour and by neighborhood.
Cities growing over decades.

Tobler’s first law extends to time: nearby moments are related, just as nearby places are. A useful mental model is the space-time cube: a map for every time step, stacked on top of each other, with x, y, and time as its three axes.
Some space-time methods to explore:

Emerging hot spot analysis runs a hot spot statistic, like Gi* from Chapter 22, for every time step and classifies each location’s trend: new, intensifying, persistent, or diminishing. The sfdep package has a function for it.
Space-time scan statistics detect disease outbreaks early, and are widely used in disease surveillance.
Spatiotemporal kriging predicts values at places and times with no measurements, for example air pollution exposure.
Movement and trajectory analysis works with GPS tracks of people, vehicles, and animals.

In R, look at the sfdep, stars, sftime, and gstat packages. At UNC, ENEC 468, Temporal GIS and Space/Time Geostatistics for the Environment and Public Health, focuses on these methods.

title: 24  What’s Next in Spatial Data Science
text:
24.4 GeoAI
GeoAI is artificial intelligence applied to spatial data, and it is one of the fastest-growing parts of the field.

Deep learning reads imagery at massive scale. Models trained to recognize objects in images have extracted building footprints for whole countries (Microsoft released its global footprints as open data), and map roads, rooftop solar panels, crops, and flood extent. Work that once took armies of people digitizing by hand is now automatic.
Machine learning predicts. Random forests and gradient boosting, with spatial predictors, estimate air quality, poverty, or crop yield in places with no measurements.


24.4.1 Foundation models and AI assistants
Geospatial foundation models are large models pretrained on huge image archives, which can then be adapted to many tasks. In 2023 NASA and IBM released Prithvi, an open model trained on Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery, which can be fine-tuned to map floods, burn scars, or crop types with little labeled data. Segmentation models can outline buildings or fields with minimal training.
Large language models can help write R code, explain error messages, and geocode place names in text. They are most useful to people who know enough to check the answer, such as noticing that a model used the wrong coordinate system. The course AI policy asks you to use them that way.


24.4.2 Spatial thinking keeps AI honest
This is where this book pays off directly. Most machine learning assumes observations are independent, and spatial data are not: you measured that with Moran’s I in Chapter 22.

Random train–test splits mislead. If you split spatial data at random, near-duplicate neighbors end up in both the training set and the test set. Accuracy looks great, and then the model fails in new places.
Spatial cross-validation holds out whole regions instead, so the test really is a new place. The R packages spatialsample and blockCV do this.
Training data can be biased toward wealthy or well-mapped places, so models do worst where better data are most needed.
Location data raise privacy concerns. A few GPS points can be enough to identify a person.

Understanding spatial data is what separates someone who can run an AI model from someone who can trust its results.






TipThink about it



A model predicts poverty from satellite images of North Carolina’s census tracts. It is trained on a random 80% of tracts and scores 95% accuracy on the other 20%. Why might it do much worse in South Carolina? How would you test it more honestly?




24.4.3 Scaling up: cloud, big data, and open science
Datasets are growing faster than laptops. Planet-wide imagery and billions of GPS points don’t fit on one computer, so analysis is moving to the cloud, where the data sit next to the computing:

Cloud platforms: Google Earth Engine, Microsoft Planetary Computer, and AWS open data.
Spatial databases: PostGIS adds spatial queries, such as spatial joins, to SQL.
Cloud-ready formats: Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF and GeoParquet let you read only the piece of a file you need.

Reproducibility (Chapter 20) matters more as projects grow. The habits you built with R Markdown scale up to Quarto (which built this book), Git, and GitHub, with shared code and data. GEOG 586 Scaling Up Geospatial Analysis and GEOG 592 GIS Programming go deeper.

section: 24.6 Careers in GIS and spatial data science
text:
24.6 Careers in GIS and spatial data science
Whether or not you major in geography, spatial skills make you more employable in many fields. Job titles vary a lot, so search broadly:

GIS analyst or technician: builds, maintains, and analyzes spatial data. The most common entry point.
Geospatial data scientist: statistics, machine learning, and code at scale.
Remote sensing analyst: turns imagery into maps and measurements.
Cartographer or geovisualization designer: maps, dashboards, and web maps.
Geospatial developer: web mapping apps, spatial databases, and APIs.
Domain roles that use GIS: planner, spatial epidemiologist, environmental consultant, emergency manager.

Many of you will end up in the last group, using GIS as a core skill in another field. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects much faster than average growth for data scientists, and spatial skills set you apart within that field.

24.6.1 Where geospatial professionals work

State and local government: nearly every North Carolina city and county has GIS staff, as do NCDOT and the NC Center for Geographic Information and Analysis, which runs NC OneMap.
Federal agencies: USGS, NOAA, NASA, the Census Bureau, CDC, and EPA, which has a large campus in Research Triangle Park.
Research and nonprofits: universities, RTI International, and conservation groups.
Private sector: engineering and environmental consulting, utilities, real estate, tech, and insurance.
Software and data companies: Esri and other mapping, imagery, and analytics firms.

Look at job boards for these employers to see which skills they ask for.


24.6.2 Skills employers look for



Table 24.3: Skills that geospatial job postings ask for.









Technical skills
Professional skills

Clear maps and visual communication


ArcGIS Pro and QGIS
Writing for non-technical audiences


SQL and PostGIS
Asking good spatial questions

Working on teams and managing projects


Git and reproducible workflows







You already have R, spatial statistics, and reproducible reports from this book. Adding ArcGIS Pro or QGIS, through GEOG 370 or 491, makes a strong combination. Don’t underestimate the second column: employers consistently say they need people who can explain results clearly, make a good map, and think carefully about ethics.


24.6.3 Start building your portfolio now
You don’t need to wait until graduation. Two or three polished projects matter more than a list of courses.

Put your best maps and R projects on GitHub or a personal website. Your final project, cleaned up with a clear write-up and map, is a strong first piece.
Contribute to OpenStreetMap or a humanitarian mapping task.
Look for internships with city, county, and state GIS offices, state agencies, and research centers.
Join a professional community, such as the NC GIS Conference, URISA, or the American Association of Geographers. Most have student rates.
Later in your career, consider the GISP certification from the GIS Certification Institute and Esri’s technical certifications.
Keep learning: free online books, such as Geocomputation with R, pick up right where this book ends.

title: 24  What’s Next in Spatial Data Science
text:
24.7 Summary

Spatial data science answers “where” questions in nearly every field: spatial epidemiology, accessibility to care, environmental justice, environmental change and hazards, planning, history, politics, business, and humanitarian mapping. The methods are the ones in this book.
Remote sensing collects information about Earth from a distance, with passive or active sensors, each with a spatial, spectral, temporal, and radiometric resolution. NDVI uses the contrast between red and near-infrared light to measure vegetation; classification and change detection turn imagery into maps.
Space-time modeling extends Tobler’s first law to time. The space-time cube, emerging hot spot analysis, and spatiotemporal kriging are starting points.
GeoAI reads imagery and makes predictions at massive scale, and foundation models adapt to new tasks with little labeled data. Because of spatial autocorrelation, honest testing needs spatial cross-validation.
At UNC, take GEOG 370 next, then electives or GEOG 515, and consider the GIS minor or the Geospatial Data Science B.S.
Spatial skills are in demand in government, research, and the private sector. Start a portfolio now.

24.8 Exercises

Spot the methods. Choose one application from Section 24.1. List every method from this book it uses, with the chapter where you learned it.
Compute NDVI. A pixel reflects 0.08 of red light and 0.40 of near-infrared light. Compute its NDVI by hand, then in R. Is it more likely forest, bare soil, or water? Why?
Pick a sensor. For each question, choose a sensor from Table 24.1 and justify it with one kind of resolution: (a) How much did Wake County’s developed land grow from 1990 to 2025? (b) Which roads flooded during last night’s storm? (c) How tall are the trees in Duke Forest?
Space-time question. Write a research question about North Carolina that needs a space-time method. What would one time slice of your space-time cube be?
Plan your path. Using Figure 24.2 and Table 24.2, write a four-semester plan of GIS courses that fits your interests, and check each course’s prerequisites in the UNC catalog.
Portfolio piece. Choose your best map or analysis from this semester. Write a one-paragraph description of it for a non-technical reader, as you would on a personal website.

the world. It combines what we study (the spatial), how we

(science).

data.

ranges from −1 to 1, and dense green vegetation is high.

but near things are more related than distant things.” It is the idea
behind spatial autocorrelation.
The tendency for things that are close together to be more alike than

to explain or predict anything with it.

compares variation between groups with variation within them.
